docs.title: Commissioning
docs.text:
Commissioning is the systematic process of verifying that a building's systems have been installed and perform according to the owner's requirements and the design intent. Testing begins during construction and continues after the systems are complete. A commissioning agent, who may be independent of the contractor, reviews the design, observes installation, and then directs functional tests, in which each system is operated through its modes to show that it responds correctly. The building systems introduced in Chapter 1 depend on each other, and commissioning is the point at which that interdependence is tested.

Worked example: testing at Riverbend. The commissioning agent tests the heating system by lowering the thermostat setpoint and confirming that the rooftop unit starts, the dampers open, and the temperature responds. For the electrical system, the agent interrupts the normal power to confirm that emergency lights switch on and the exit signs remain lit. A common finding is a control sequence that was programmed incorrectly, for example lighting that remains on in an empty classroom. The test produces a list of deficiencies that the contractor must correct before the owner accepts the system.

docs.title: Occupancy and Closeout
docs.text:
Occupancy and closeout is the final phase, in which the building is handed to the owner and the project is administratively completed. The sequence has several steps. When the work is sufficiently complete for the owner to use, the architect certifies substantial completion, and the team prepares a punch list, a list of minor items still to be finished or corrected. The building official conducts final inspections, and if the building complies with the code, issues a certificate of occupancy, which is the legal permission to use the building.

The contractor also delivers the records the owner needs to operate the building: operation and maintenance manuals, warranties, equipment training, and record drawings that show the building as actually built, including changes made along the way. Warranties commonly cover at least one year for the contractor's work. When the punch list is complete and the records have been delivered, the owner makes final payment and releases the retainage. The completed building then enters its long service life, the subject of the final chapter of this book.

You Know the Whole Journey

You can now name the phases of a project from programming through closeout, tell design-bid-build from design-build and construction manager at risk, and trace an RFI, a submittal, and a change order through the team. That is the map of how every building gets made, and the rest of the book fills in the science behind each stage.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Design is iterative and convergent: each phase repeats the define, generate, evaluate, and select cycle at a finer level of detail, and each decision constrains the next.
  • A project moves through programming, schematic design, design development, construction documents, bidding and procurement, construction, commissioning, and occupancy and closeout, with owner approval at each gate.
  • Changes are cheapest in the early phases, when they are lines on paper, and cost the most after the work has been built.
  • The architect leads design and observes construction. The general contractor holds the contract to build and controls means and methods. Subcontractors perform specialty work under the general contractor.
  • Delivery methods differ in whom the owner contracts with, when the builder joins, and how the price is set: design-bid-build, design-build, construction manager at risk, and integrated project delivery.
  • Submittals, requests for information, and change orders are the written channels that carry information and changes during construction. Work should not begin on a change until it is authorized in writing.
  • The critical path is the longest chain of dependent activities, and any delay on it delays the project. Activities off the path have float until a delay uses it up.
  • Commissioning tests that the systems work as intended, and closeout transfers the building, its records, and its warranties to the owner.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: The Design and Construction Process
docs.text: Test your understanding of the concepts in this chapter with these review questions, one for each of the 24 concepts covered.

docs.title: 1. Why is the design process described as both iterative and convergent?
docs.text:
1. The team repeats the same drawings until the owner approves, and each decision adds new alternatives
  2. The team repeats a define, generate, evaluate, and select cycle at finer detail, and each decision removes options
  3. The team designs each system once in sequence, and every system converges on the same material
  4. The team revises drawings only after construction starts, and each revision lowers the cost of the finished work
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. No one can pick the best answer on the first pass, so the team cycles through define, generate, evaluate, and select at progressively finer levels, from site placement down to a single breaker. It is convergent because each choice, such as a wood-framed roof, narrows the options for ceilings, ducts, and lighting. Repetition alone would not make it convergent.

Concept Tested: Design Process

See: The Design Process

docs.title: 2. Which three flows must the contractor manage simultaneously during the construction process?
docs.text:
1. Materials, labor, and information
  2. Drawings, permits, and inspections
  3. Design, bidding, and payment
  4. Owners, architects, and engineers
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The construction process turns documents into a building, and the contractor must coordinate materials (ordered and delivered on time), labor (the right trades in the right order), and information (current drawings and answers). Drawings, permits, inspections, bidding, and payment all matter, but they are not the three flows, and owners and designers are participants, not flows.

Concept Tested: Construction Process

See: The Construction Process

docs.title: 3. What do project phases accomplish for the owner and the team?
docs.text:
1. Each phase is completed by a different contractor who is chosen through competitive bidding for that phase
  2. Each phase allows earlier decisions to be reversed at no cost to the owner
  3. Each phase produces defined deliverables and ends with an owner approval, called a phase gate
  4. Each phase combines design and construction so that work overlaps without approvals
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The standard phases answer different questions, produce defined deliverables, and end with an owner approval before the next phase begins, which protects everyone from building on unconfirmed decisions. Phases are not tied to separate contractors, and reversing early decisions gets more expensive as the project proceeds, so approvals matter most before physical work begins.

Concept Tested: Project Phases

See: Project Phases

docs.title: 4. A program lists 4,200 ft² of net area and the owner expects a building efficiency of 0.70. What gross area should the team plan for?
docs.text:
1. 2,940 ft²
  2. 4,200 ft²
  3. 5,460 ft²
  4. 6,000 ft²
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Gross area equals net area divided by efficiency: 4,200 / 0.70 = 6,000 ft². Multiplying (2,940) inverts the relationship, using the net area alone (4,200) forgets that corridors, walls, and shafts are not part of any room, and simply adding 30 percent (5,460) is not the same as dividing by the efficiency ratio.

Concept Tested: Programming

See: Programming

docs.title: 5. What does the architect explore during schematic design?
docs.text:
1. The final dimensions, product models, and installation details for every system
  2. The competitive prices that contractors offer for the work described in the finished drawings and specifications
  3. The written approval that allows the owner to occupy the finished building
  4. The overall form of the building: site placement, shape, height, and room arrangement
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Schematic design compares a few genuinely different options for where the building sits, its shape and height, and how rooms are arranged. Deliverables are a site plan, preliminary floor plans, rough elevations, and a preliminary estimate. Fixing dimensions and products belongs to later phases, pricing belongs to bidding, and occupancy approval belongs to closeout.

Concept Tested: Schematic Design

See: Schematic Design

docs.title: 6. Why is the end of design development sometimes called a design freeze?
docs.text:
1. After owner approval, the building official stops reviewing any change to the design for the building permit
  2. After owner approval, changes become costly because the next phase turns each decision into detailed drawings
  3. After owner approval, the contractor takes over responsibility for all design decisions
  4. After owner approval, the design team may no longer coordinate with other disciplines
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Design development settles how the building will be built: systems are chosen and sized, materials selected, and dimensions fixed. Because construction documents will build on every decision, later changes ripple across many sheets and cost much more. The term describes cost and effort, not a legal ban on review, a transfer of design responsibility, or an end to coordination.

Concept Tested: Design Development

See: Design Development

docs.title: 7. Why does the team run a coordination review before releasing the construction documents?
docs.text:
1. Bidders are barred from asking questions after the documents have been released
  2. The building official requires an overlay of drawings before issuing any permit
  3. Conflicts between disciplines are cheaper to fix on paper than to discover on site
  4. Specifications can be replaced by drawings once all sheets have been compared
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Gaps and conflicts do not disappear; they turn up during construction as questions, delays, or change orders. In the duct and beam example, a clash cost a revised sheet on paper but would have stopped the framers on site. The review is a professional practice, not a permit rule, and specifications remain part of the project manual.

Concept Tested: Construction Documents

See: Construction Documents

docs.title: 8. Which term describes products such as switchgear, elevators, or custom windows that take months to manufacture and can control the schedule?
docs.text:
1. Long-lead items
  2. Alternates
  3. Addenda
  4. Punch-list items
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Procurement includes ordering long-lead items early so their delivery does not delay construction. Alternates are priced options the owner may add or subtract from the base bid, addenda are written changes to the documents during bidding, and punch-list items are minor corrections at closeout. Only long-lead items are defined by their long manufacturing time.

Concept Tested: Bidding and Procurement

See: Bidding and Procurement

docs.title: 9. A contract is for $2,000,000 with 10 percent retainage. The architect certifies that 25 percent of the work is complete, and $300,000 has been paid previously. What is the payment due this month?
docs.text:
1. $450,000
  2. $150,000
  3. $200,000
  4. $50,000
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Earned to date is 0.25 × $2,000,000 = $500,000. Retainage is 10 percent of that, or $50,000, so payment due is $500,000 − $50,000 − $300,000 = $150,000. The value of $450,000 forgets to subtract earlier payments, $200,000 forgets retainage, and $50,000 is only the retainage itself.

Concept Tested: Construction Administration

See: Construction Administration

docs.title: 10. In design-bid-build, when does the builder join the project?
docs.text:
1. At the start of design, as an adviser to the architect
  2. During schematic design, under a single contract with the architect
  3. At the start, as a signer of a multi-party agreement
  4. After the design is complete and the documents have been bid
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Design-bid-build is strictly sequential: the architect completes the design, the finished documents are bid, and the contract goes to the low bidder. The owner holds separate contracts with the architect and contractor. Joining at the start as an adviser describes construction manager at risk, and the multi-party agreement describes integrated project delivery.

Concept Tested: Design-Bid-Build

See: Design-Bid-Build

docs.title: 11. What is the purpose of commissioning?
docs.text:
1. To certify that the contractor's pay application is accurate before the monthly payment is released
  2. To compare the bids received and award the contract to the lowest responsible bidder
  3. To verify that installed systems perform to the owner's requirements and the design intent
  4. To record the building as actually built, including changes made during construction
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Commissioning uses functional tests, in which each system is operated through its modes, to show that heating, emergency lighting, and controls work as intended. Certifying payment is a construction administration task, awarding a contract is part of bidding, and recording as-built conditions is the job of record drawings at closeout.

Concept Tested: Commissioning

See: Commissioning

docs.title: 12. Which statement best describes the role of the architect?
docs.text:
1. A licensed design professional who leads the design team and is primarily responsible for the design
  2. A contractor who manages the site, schedules the trades, and decides means and methods
  3. A building official who reviews drawings and inspects the finished work for compliance with the adopted code
  4. A specialty firm hired by the general contractor to perform part of the physical work
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Licensing exists because design errors endanger the public, so a state board verifies the architect's education, experience, and examination record. The architect coordinates the engineers' work and usually holds the design contract with the owner. Managing the site belongs to the general contractor, code review to the building official, and trade work to subcontractors.

Concept Tested: Architect

See: The Architect

docs.title: 13. Which document gives legal permission to use a building after the building official's final inspections?
docs.text:
1. A certificate of substantial completion
  2. A punch list
  3. A certificate of occupancy
  4. A set of record drawings
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The building official issues the certificate of occupancy if the building complies with the code. Substantial completion is certified by the architect when the owner can use the work, the punch list is a list of minor items still to be corrected, and record drawings show the building as actually built. None of those three grants legal permission to occupy.

Concept Tested: Occupancy and Closeout

See: Occupancy and Closeout

docs.title: 14. Why does the architect observe the construction work but not supervise it?
docs.text:
1. The general contractor controls means and methods and answers for all of the work, including others' work
  2. The architect lacks a license that permits regular observation visits to the site during construction work
  3. The owner holds the contract for means and methods and delegates them to subcontractors
  4. The building official supervises construction, so the architect's visits are only advisory
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The documents describe the finished result, not the process of reaching it. The general contractor holds the prime contract and decides how the work is carried out and in what order, plus schedule and site safety. The architect's periodic visits protect the owner by checking consistency with the design, not by directing the work.

Concept Tested: General Contractor

See: The General Contractor

docs.title: 15. Why can design-build shorten the schedule compared with design-bid-build?
docs.text:
1. The owner skips the design phase and instead uses documents from a similar project built elsewhere
  2. The contractor submits a sealed bid, so the bidding period is eliminated from the project schedule entirely
  3. The architect works for the owner independently, so approvals happen in a single step
  4. One entity holds the contract for design and construction, so early work like foundations can start during design
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Under design-build the owner signs a single contract with one entity responsible for both design and construction, so phases overlap. The trade-offs are less independent oversight of the design and a price set earlier, when less is known. Design is still performed, bids are not the mechanism, and the architect is part of the design-build team, not an independent party.

Concept Tested: Design-Build

See: Design-Build

docs.title: 16. What does the construction manager at risk agree to deliver?
docs.text:
1. The project for the lowest bid submitted by any qualified general contractor
  2. The project for a guaranteed maximum price, bearing the risk of overruns above it
  3. The design and the construction under a single multi-party agreement with shared rewards
  4. The construction administration services that the architect would normally perform
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. In CMAR the owner hires a construction manager during design as an adviser, and the same firm then agrees to build for a guaranteed maximum price. The owner keeps separate contracts with the architect and the construction manager. Selection is based on qualifications and fee, not lowest price alone, and the shared-reward multi-party agreement describes integrated project delivery.

Concept Tested: Construction Manager at Risk

See: Construction Manager at Risk

docs.title: 17. Why does a Minnesota contractor try to finish the foundation and dry-in before hard winter?
docs.text:
1. Interior work can proceed in heated, protected space without the cost of cold-weather measures
  2. Building codes prohibit pouring foundations or framing walls at any time between December and March
  3. Subcontractors are unavailable in winter, so only exterior work can be scheduled
  4. Dried-in buildings no longer need inspections before interior finishes are applied
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Sequencing orders activities for physical reasons, to protect completed work, and to allow inspections. In Minnesota, the calendar adds a constraint: a project not dried in before freezing weather faces temporary heat, cold-weather concrete practices, and delays. Winter work is not prohibited by code, trades remain available, and inspections still occur.

Concept Tested: Construction Sequencing

See: Construction Sequencing

docs.title: 18. Why should a project team identify a single person with authority to speak for the owner at the outset?
docs.text:
1. Only one person may sign the contract documents under public procurement laws
  2. The building official will communicate only with a single representative
  3. Slow or reversed owner decisions are a common source of delay and expense
  4. The architect cannot hold a design contract with more than one person
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The owner commissions and pays for the project and approves each phase gate. When several people give conflicting answers or reverse decisions, the team loses time and money. Public procurement laws, official communication channels, and architect contracts do not require a single representative, though identifying one is a practical safeguard.

Concept Tested: Project Owner

See: The Project Owner

docs.title: 19. Why do payments and questions from a subcontractor flow through the general contractor?
docs.text:
1. The subcontractor is not licensed to communicate with the architect or engineers
  2. The subcontractor is paid by the building official after each inspection
  3. The subcontractor works only on public projects, where direct contact is prohibited
  4. The subcontractor has a contract with the general contractor and none with the owner
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A subcontractor is a specialty firm hired by the general contractor for a portion of the work, so its contractual relationship runs up to the GC, who remains responsible for the entire chain, including any sub-tier firms. Questions and payments therefore follow that contract path. The reasons given in the other statements are not part of how projects are organized.

Concept Tested: Subcontractor

See: The Subcontractor

docs.title: 20. Which feature of integrated project delivery makes it extend construction manager at risk?
docs.text:
1. The builder adds cost advice during design but still holds a separate contract directly with the owner
  2. Designers and builders sign one multi-party agreement and share risk and reward instead of separate contracts
  3. The owner awards a single lump sum to the lowest bidder after the design is complete and permitted
  4. The contractor guarantees a maximum price and absorbs any overrun by itself
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. IPD brings the owner, architect, contractor, and key subcontractors under one agreement with shared incentives, so decisions move earlier, when change is cheapest. CMAR brings the builder into design but keeps separate contracts and puts the overrun risk on the construction manager. Lowest-bid lump sums describe design-bid-build, and bearing overruns alone describes the GMP in CMAR.

Concept Tested: Integrated Project Delivery

See: Integrated Project Delivery

docs.title: 21. An electrical subcontractor wants to order a main switchboard. What should happen before the switchboard is ordered?
docs.text:
1. The subcontractor orders the switchboard and sends the invoice to the architect for approval
  2. The subcontractor prepares a submittal, the general contractor checks it, and the engineer reviews it
  3. The subcontractor sends a request for information asking the owner to approve the manufacturer's switchboard
  4. The subcontractor asks the building official to approve the switchboard before purchase
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Submittals such as product data and dimensions let the design team confirm that the product meets the specification before it is ordered. The sub prepares it, the GC checks it, and the engineer returns it with a status such as approved or revise and resubmit. An RFI asks a question, not for product approval, and the building official reviews code compliance, not product selection.

Concept Tested: Submittals

See: Submittals

docs.title: 22. Why do requests for information protect both the contractor and the design team?
docs.text:
1. They automatically change the contract price when the design team replies
  2. They allow the contractor to start extra work without waiting for a signed change order from the owner
  3. They create a written record of the question, the date, and the answer for any later dispute
  4. They transfer responsibility for the question to the building official
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. An RFI is a written question that clarifies unclear, incomplete, or conflicting documents, and the written answer may become a change to the documents. Because the exchange is on file, both sides can show what was intended. An RFI does not by itself adjust price or authorize extra work; that requires a change order or written directive.

Concept Tested: Requests for Information

See: Requests for Information

docs.title: 23. A superintendent is told verbally at the site to add a small extra wall, and the schedule is tight. What is the best course of action?
docs.text:
1. Wait for a signed change order or written directive stating price and time
  2. Begin the work and settle the price after the extra wall is built
  3. Build the wall and submit it as a punch-list item at closeout
  4. Ask the building official to approve the extra wall as a field change before any work starts
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A change order is a written modification of scope, price, or time signed by the owner, architect, and contractor. Starting extra work on a verbal go-ahead leaves price unagreed, so a dispute can leave the contractor unpaid. Punch-list items are minor corrections to contract work, and the building official reviews code compliance, not contract changes.

Concept Tested: Change Orders

See: Change Orders

docs.title: 24. Activity A takes 3 days. Activities B (4 days) and C (6 days) both follow A. Activity D takes 2 days and follows both B and C. How many days is the shortest possible project duration?
docs.text:
1. 9 days
  2. 13 days
  3. 15 days
  4. 11 days
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The critical path is the longest chain of dependent activities. A-B-D totals 9 days and A-C-D totals 11 days, so the critical path is A-C-D and the project takes 11 days, with B holding 2 days of float. Choosing 9 follows the shorter chain, 13 adds A, B, and C, and 15 adds every duration as though no activities could overlap.

Concept Tested: Critical Path

See: The Critical Path

docs.title: References: The Design and Construction Process
docs.text:
1. Design-bid-build - Wikipedia - Describes the traditional delivery method in which the owner contracts separately with a designer and a contractor, then bids the work. It covers sequence, advantages, and drawbacks, matching this chapter's central delivery method.

  2. Integrated project delivery - Wikipedia - Explains the collaborative delivery approach in which owner, designer, and builder share risk and reward under a multi-party agreement. It clarifies how IPD differs from design-bid-build and design-build in contracts and early collaboration.

  3. Critical path method - Wikipedia - Explains the scheduling algorithm that finds the longest chain of dependent activities, which sets the minimum project duration. It includes forward and backward pass examples that support this chapter's treatment of critical path and sequencing.

  4. The Architect's Handbook of Professional Practice (15th Edition) - American Institute of Architects - Wiley - The AIA's handbook is credited with codifying the standard phases of schematic design, design development, construction documents, bidding, and administration. It explains each phase's deliverables and the architect's role during construction.

  5. Construction Project Management: A Practical Guide to Field Construction Management (6th Edition) - S. Keoki Sears, Glenn A. Sears, Richard H. Clough, Jerald L. Rounds, and Robert O. Segner - Wiley - Most praised for its field-level clarity, it works through critical path scheduling networks, submittals, requests for information, and change orders with practical examples that mirror the paperwork students will meet on real jobs.

  6. Project Delivery Systems: CM at Risk, Design-Build, Design-Bid-Build - Construction Industry Institute - Research report RR133-11 comparing how each delivery system defines roles, responsibilities, and activity sequence. It gives the evidence base for this chapter's delivery methods and is paired with a selection workbook.

  7. An Owner's Guide to Project Delivery Methods - Construction Management Association of America - A plain-language PDF guide written for owners comparing design-bid-build, construction manager at risk, and design-build. It clarifies contract relationships and risk, helping students see the owner's decision-making role.

  8. Minnesota Statutes 16C.32: Design-Build Contracts - Office of the Revisor of Statutes, State of Minnesota - The state law defining design-build and its qualification-based and price-based selection processes. It shows how delivery methods are regulated in Minnesota public work, which makes the chapter's terms legally concrete.

  9. A Guide to Building Commissioning - Pacific Northwest National Laboratory - A U.S. Department of Energy guide explaining how commissioning verifies that building systems perform to the owner's requirements. It describes activities in each project phase, linking directly to this chapter's commissioning and closeout concepts.

  10. Construction Manager / General Contractor - Minnesota Department of Transportation - Explains how MnDOT uses a construction manager who advises during design and then builds the project. It is a Minnesota example of the construction manager at risk model discussed in this chapter.

docs.title: Forces, Heat, and the Physics of Buildings
Forces, Heat, and the Physics of Buildings
Summary
docs.text: The forces, stress, strain, heat transfer, and thermal resistance principles that explain how buildings carry loads and resist heat flow. It has no prerequisites within the book and starts the learning progression. After completing this chapter, students will be able to define, explain, and apply the 16 concepts listed below.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 16 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Forces 473 Heat 326 Heat Transfer 282 Equilibrium 153 Stress 121 Conduction 62 Thermal Resistance 56 R-Value 32 Radiation 20 Strain 10 Thermal Bridging 5 Convection 4 U-Value 4 Daylight 4 Thermal Mass 3 Sound Transmission 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter assumes only the prerequisites listed in the course description.

Two Kinds of Physics, One Building

Every roof that stays up and every winter morning that stays warm comes down to two pieces of physics: forces that balance, and heat that flows slowly. Once you can run the numbers on both, you can look at a wall or a beam and say whether it will do its job. Let's build it right!

Chapter 1 described what a building is and the four jobs it performs: it supports, separates, serves, and protects. Those jobs sound like architecture, but each one is governed by ordinary physics. A building supports because forces are balanced, so that every pound of load finds a path to the ground. A building separates because the enclosure slows the flow of heat from a warm interior to a cold exterior. This chapter builds the working vocabulary for both ideas.

The chapter has two halves. The first half covers forces, equilibrium, stress, and strain, which explain how structures carry load. The second half covers heat, the three ways heat travels, and the measures of how well a wall resists it, and then closes with two other forms of energy that every designer must manage: light and sound. To keep the numbers concrete, we occasionally return to the invented Riverbend Youth Center from Chapter 2: a one-story Minneapolis building with a 40 ft multipurpose room spanned by glued-laminated wood beams. All Riverbend loads and dimensions here are illustrative.

docs.title: Forces
docs.text:
A force is a push or a pull that can change an object's motion or change its shape. A force has two properties that matter: a magnitude, which says how strong it is, and a direction, which says which way it acts. A quantity with both properties is called a vector, and it is drawn as an arrow whose length represents the magnitude and whose orientation shows the direction. Two people pushing a stalled truck in the same direction add their efforts. Two people pushing in opposite directions cancel each other, and the sum of the arrows tells you the result.

In US customary units, force is measured in pounds-force (lbf, usually written lb), and a kip is 1,000 lbf. In the International System of Units (SI), force is measured in newtons (N), where 1 lbf is about 4.45 N. The most important force in building design is weight, the force of gravity acting on a mass. Near the Earth's surface, a mass of 1 lb weighs 1 lbf, which is why designers can speak of "pounds" without separating mass from force. Builders also rarely deal with a single force at a point. They deal with force spread over an area, called a load, and measure it in pounds per square foot (psf). Chapter 6 classifies loads in detail, but the four sources you will meet first are gravity (the weight of the structure and its contents), snow, wind, and the pressure of soil against buried walls.

A single inclined force can be replaced by two components, one horizontal and one vertical, that together have the same effect. Using the angle \( \theta \) measured from the horizontal, the components are:

\[ F_x = F \cos\theta \qquad F_y = F \sin\theta \]

The horizontal component \( F_x \) tries to slide the connection sideways, and the vertical component \( F_y \) tries to lift or press it. Splitting forces this way lets us check each direction separately, which is the foundation of every structural calculation in later chapters.

Worked example: forces on the Riverbend roof. The roof over the multipurpose room covers 2,400 ft². Suppose the roof assembly weighs 30 psf (its dead load) and the design snow load is 40 psf (a live load; both values are illustrative). The total vertical force is \( (30 + 40) \times 2{,}400 = 168{,}000 \) lb, or 168 kips, which is about the weight of 40 midsize cars sitting on the roof. Now consider a diagonal steel brace in the wall that carries 5,000 lb at an angle of 45 degrees from the horizontal. Its horizontal component is \( 5{,}000 \cos 45^\circ = 3{,}536 \) lb, and its vertical component is \( 5{,}000 \sin 45^\circ = 3{,}536 \) lb. At 45 degrees, the brace splits its force equally between sliding and lifting.

The table below collects the units we have just defined, so you can return to it when a later chapter mixes systems.

Quantity US customary unit SI unit Conversion Force pound-force (lb), kip newton (N), kilonewton (kN) 1 lb is about 4.45 N Distributed load pounds per square foot (psf) pascals (Pa) 1 psf is about 47.9 Pa Line load pounds per linear foot (plf) newtons per meter (N/m) 1 plf is about 14.6 N/m

Before you open the simulation below, note that the arrow's angle is measured from the horizontal and that the components always sum back to the original arrow.

docs.title: Equilibrium
docs.text:
A body is in equilibrium when all of the forces and turning effects acting on it balance, so that it does not accelerate. Buildings are designed to remain in static equilibrium, meaning they stay at rest. The wording matters: equilibrium does not mean that nothing pushes on the building. It means that for every push there is an equal and opposite resistance somewhere else, and the building stays put. This is Newton's third law at work. A beam pressing down on a wall is pushed up by the wall with exactly the same force.

The Ground Pushes Back

Notice that a standing building is not a thing at rest but a stalemate of forces. Every load pushing down is met by a support pushing up, all the way to the soil, and the building fails the moment any link in that chain can no longer push back.

Three conditions guarantee equilibrium in a plane. The sum of the horizontal forces must be zero, the sum of the vertical forces must be zero, and the sum of the moments must be zero. A moment is the turning effect of a force about a point. It equals the force times the perpendicular distance from the point to the line along which the force acts, and it is measured in foot-pounds (ft-lb). A door handle placed far from the hinges lets a gentle push produce a large moment, which is why the handle is not placed next to the hinge. In symbols, the three conditions are:

\[ \sum F_x = 0 \qquad \sum F_y = 0 \qquad \sum M = 0 \]

The forces that a support supplies to keep a structure in equilibrium are called reactions. Because each equation can be solved for one unknown, a beam resting on two supports with two unknown reactions can be solved completely using only these three conditions.

Moments Take Practice

Moments are where many students first stumble in statics, and that is normal. You already know how to balance a seesaw, so try the example below as a seesaw problem and pick the pivot point yourself.

Worked example: reactions on a Riverbend beam. A 40 ft glued-laminated beam spans the multipurpose room, resting on a support at each end, labeled A (left) and B (right). A mechanical unit hung from the beam applies a downward point load of 6,000 lb located 10 ft from A. We want the reactions \( R_A \) and \( R_B \). Choose A as the pivot point, so that \( R_A \) has no moment about it. The unit's moment is \( 6{,}000 \times 10 = 60{,}000 \) ft-lb in one direction, and \( R_B \) must balance it at a distance of 40 ft:

\[ R_B \times 40 = 6{,}000 \times 10 \quad\Rightarrow\quad R_B = 1{,}500 \text{ lb} \]

The vertical forces must also sum to zero, so \( R_A + R_B = 6{,}000 \) and \( R_A = 4{,}500 \) lb. As a check, take moments about B instead: \( R_A \times 40 = 6{,}000 \times 30 = 180{,}000 \), which again gives 4,500 lb. The support nearer the load carries more of it, in proportion to how close the load sits. If the beam instead carried an evenly spread line load of 800 plf (illustrative) over its whole length, the total would be \( 800 \times 40 = 32{,}000 \) lb, and by symmetry each support would receive 16,000 lb. Those reactions then become loads on the walls, footings, and soil beneath, which is the load path described in Chapter 6.

docs.title: Stress
docs.text:
Stress is the internal force per unit area that a material carries in response to the loads applied to it. It is calculated by dividing the force by the area over which it acts:

\[ \sigma = \frac{F}{A} \]

where \( \sigma \) (the Greek letter sigma) is stress, \( F \) is the force, and \( A \) is the cross-sectional area. Stress has units of pounds per square inch (psi) or pounds per square foot (psf) in US practice, and pascals (Pa) in SI, where 1 psi is about 6,895 Pa. The reason to divide by area is that materials do not fail because of the total force. They fail when the stress at some location reaches the limit that the material can sustain. A 1,000 lb pull is trivial for a thick steel bar and fatal for a thin thread.

Stress, Not Force, Breaks Things

Think of a person standing on a snowfield: in boots they sink, and on wide snowshoes they float, though the weight is identical. The load stays the same, but the area changes, and that changes the stress.

The direction of the force relative to the area gives stress its type. Tensile stress pulls the material apart, compressive stress squeezes it together, and shear stress slides one part of the material past the adjacent part. A real member often experiences a mix, as when a beam bends and the top squeezes while the bottom stretches. Chapter 5 examines how much of each type different materials can tolerate.

Type Action Everyday example Building example Tension Pulls apart Stretching a rope Steel hanger rod holding a ceiling Compression Squeezes together Standing on a block Concrete column, wall stud Shear Slides layers past each other Cutting paper with scissors A bolt joining two timbers

Worked example: a steel rod and a footing. First consider a 3/4 in diameter steel rod that hangs a load of 8,000 lb. Its cross-sectional area is \( A = \pi r^2 = \pi (0.375)^2 = 0.442 \text{ in}^2 \), so the tensile stress is \( \sigma = 8{,}000 / 0.442 = 18{,}100 \) psi. Common structural steel begins to deform permanently at about 36,000 psi, so this rod works at roughly half of that limit. The ratio of the limit to the working stress, about 2.0, is a factor of safety, a margin that designers include because loads and material properties are never known exactly.

Now consider a wood post, 3.5 in by 3.5 in, that carries 6,000 lb. Its area is 12.25 in², so the compressive stress is \( 6{,}000 / 12.25 = 490 \) psi. The post sits on a square concrete footing 2 ft by 2 ft, an area of 4 ft², so the load pressing on the soil is \( 6{,}000 / 4 = 1{,}500 \) psf, which is only 10.4 psi. The footing exists to spread the same force over a bigger area so that the weak soil beneath is stressed no more than it can bear. Allowable soil pressures commonly fall in the range of about 1,500 to 3,000 psf for competent soils, and Chapter 9 explains how they are determined.

docs.title: Strain
docs.text:
Strain is the measure of how much a material deforms under stress, expressed as the change in length divided by the original length:

\[ \varepsilon = \frac{\Delta L}{L} \]

where \( \varepsilon \) (epsilon) is strain, \( \Delta L \) is the change in length, and \( L \) is the original length. Strain is dimensionless because the two lengths cancel, so a strain of 0.001 means that the material stretched by one thousandth of its length, whatever units were used. Engineers also report strain in microstrain, where 1,000 microstrain equals 0.001.

Stress and strain are cause and effect. Applying a stress produces a strain. Over the working range of most structural materials, the two are proportional, a relationship called elastic behavior: when the load is removed, the material returns to its original length. If the stress exceeds the material's elastic limit, part of the strain remains after the load is removed, which is plastic deformation. A bent steel bar that does not spring back has been strained plastically.

Worked example: stretching the steel rod. Suppose the 3/4 in rod from the Stress section is 10 ft (120 in) long, and a measurement under its 8,000 lb load shows that it has stretched by 0.075 in. The strain is \( \varepsilon = 0.075 / 120 = 0.000625 \), or 625 microstrain. We can now divide the stress by the strain: \( 18{,}100 / 0.000625 \approx 29{,}000{,}000 \) psi. This ratio, which describes how stiff the material is, comes out near 29 million psi for steel regardless of the rod's size, and Chapter 5 gives it the name modulus of elasticity. Strain is small, but it matters. It governs how much a floor deflects under a crowd and how much a long wall expands on a hot day, and a floor that is strong enough but too bouncy still fails the occupants.

docs.title: Heat
docs.text:
Heat is the energy that transfers between objects because of a difference in temperature. It is not the same as temperature, which measures the average motion of the molecules in a material. A bathtub of lukewarm water contains much more heat than a spark from a sparkler, although the spark is far hotter. The distinction explains why a large mass at a modest temperature can warm a room while a tiny hot object cannot.

Heat is measured in the British thermal unit (BTU) in US practice, which is the heat needed to raise one pound of water by 1 degree Fahrenheit. In SI, the unit is the joule (J). The rate at which heat flows is measured in BTU per hour (BTU/h) or in watts (W). Heating and cooling equipment is rated in these rate units, and a "ton" of cooling is 12,000 BTU/h. The table below relates the units that appear most often.

Unit Quantity measured Equivalent BTU Energy (heat) 1 BTU is about 1,055 J kilowatt-hour (kWh) Energy (electricity, heat) 1 kWh is 3,412 BTU BTU/h Rate of heat flow 3.412 BTU/h is 1 W ton of cooling Rate of heat flow 12,000 BTU/h

When heat changes a material's temperature without changing its phase, it is called sensible heat, and the amount is found from the mass, the temperature change, and a property called specific heat (\( c \)), which is the heat needed to raise one pound of a material by 1°F:

\[ Q = m \, c \, \Delta T \]

Water has a specific heat of 1.0 BTU/lb·°F, and air has about 0.24. When heat changes a material's phase, such as turning water to vapor, it is called latent heat. Evaporating a pound of water absorbs roughly 1,000 BTU without changing its temperature, and condensing it releases that heat again. Chapter 4 uses this idea to explain why condensation matters.

Worked example: warming a classroom's air. One Riverbend classroom has 600 ft² of floor and a 9 ft ceiling, so its volume is 5,400 ft³. Air weighs about 0.075 lb/ft³, so the room holds \( 5{,}400 \times 0.075 = 405 \) lb of air. Raising it from 50°F to 70°F takes \( Q = 405 \times 0.24 \times 20 = 1{,}944 \) BTU, which is only 0.57 kWh. That is surprisingly little, because air holds very little heat. Per cubic foot, water holds about 3,500 times more heat than air (62.4 lb/ft³ at 1.0 versus 0.075 lb/ft³ at 0.24). The real work of a heating system is therefore not warming the air once, but replacing the heat that keeps escaping through the enclosure, which is the subject of the next section.

docs.title: Heat Transfer
docs.text:
Heat transfer is the movement of heat from a region of higher temperature to a region of lower temperature. It always goes in that direction, from hot to cold, until the two reach the same temperature. In a heated Minnesota building in January, the interior is the hot region and the outdoors is the cold one, so the heat flows outward through the walls, roof, windows, and floor. A building does not let in cold. It loses heat, and the colder it is outside, the faster the heat leaves.

Cold Is Not a Thing That Comes In

Think of heat as water running downhill, with temperature as the height of the hill. A draft on a winter day is not cold flowing in. It is warm air leaving, and replacement air arriving that your furnace must now heat.

Heat moves by three mechanisms, each treated in its own section below. Conduction is transfer through direct contact between molecules in a solid, such as heat moving along a metal spoon. Convection is transfer by the motion of a fluid, such as warm air rising from a radiator. Radiation is transfer by electromagnetic waves, such as the warmth from the sun or a campfire, which needs no material at all. In a real wall, all three mechanisms act in sequence, as the table below shows for a wall on a winter night.

Location along the heat path Dominant mechanism Warm room air to the inside wall surface Convection, with some radiation Through the solid wall layers Conduction Through an air gap or a cavity Convection and radiation Outside wall surface to cold air and sky Convection and radiation

The rate of heat flow depends on the temperature difference \( \Delta T \) driving it, so the same wall loses heat faster on a colder day. This proportionality is one of the most useful ideas in building science, because it lets you scale from one condition to another without redoing the calculation.

Worked example: a design day and a fall day. Suppose the room is kept at 70°F. On a Minneapolis design day with an outdoor temperature of about −10°F (an illustrative value), \( \Delta T = 70 - (-10) = 80 \)°F. On a mild fall day at 50°F outside, \( \Delta T = 20 \)°F. The ratio is \( 80/20 = 4 \), so the same wall loses four times as much heat per hour on the design day as on the fall day. A heating system sized for the design day therefore runs at a quarter of that load on a fall day, which is why heating equipment spends most of the year at partial output.

docs.title: Conduction
docs.text:
Conduction is the transfer of heat through a material by the collisions of neighboring molecules, without any bulk motion of the material. A fast-vibrating, hot molecule bumps its slower neighbors and passes along some of its energy, and the energy migrates step by step to the cold side. Conduction is the main mechanism in solid building materials such as wood, concrete, steel, and insulation.

How easily a material conducts heat is measured by its thermal conductivity, denoted \( k \). A high \( k \) means the material passes heat readily, and a low \( k \) means it resists. In US practice, \( k \) is given in BTU·in/(h·ft²·°F), which is the heat per hour that passes through a 1 in thick, 1 ft² slab for each degree of temperature difference across it. For steady conditions, the heat flow rate through a flat layer follows from Fourier's law:

\[ \dot{Q} = \frac{k \, A \, \Delta T}{L} \]

where \( \dot{Q} \) is the heat flow rate in BTU/h, \( A \) is the area in ft², \( \Delta T \) is the temperature difference across the layer in °F, and \( L \) is the thickness in inches. Heat flow rises with conductivity, area, and temperature difference, and falls with thickness. The approximate conductivities in the table are typical, and actual products vary.

Material Approximate \( k \) (BTU·in/h·ft²·°F) Comment Still air 0.17 Excellent insulator if it cannot circulate Polyisocyanurate foam board 0.17 Rigid foam insulation Fiberglass batt 0.27 Traps still air among fibers Softwood lumber 0.8 A moderate insulator Gypsum board 1.1 Interior wall finish Normal-weight concrete 10 Conducts heat readily Structural steel 310 Conducts heat extremely well

Insulation works because it holds air still in thousands of tiny pockets, so the heat has to conduct through a material that is mostly air and only a little solid.

Worked example: stud versus insulation. Take a 3.5 in thick layer, 1 ft² in area, and a 70°F temperature difference across it. Through a softwood stud, \( \dot{Q} = 0.8 \times 1 \times 70 / 3.5 = 16 \) BTU/h. Through a fiberglass batt of the same size, \( \dot{Q} = 0.27 \times 1 \times 70 / 3.5 = 5.4 \) BTU/h. The wood passes about three times as much heat as the insulation. For the same thickness, an 8 in concrete layer would pass \( 10 \times 70 / 8 = 87.5 \) BTU/h, more than 16 times the batt. A steel stud conducts so well that it can carry roughly 1,000 times the heat of insulation at an equal thickness, a fact that returns when we discuss thermal bridging.

docs.title: Convection
docs.text:
Convection is the transfer of heat by the movement of a fluid, either a liquid or a gas, that carries thermal energy from one place to another. A moving fluid brings fresh warm or cold material against a surface, so the exchange is faster than conduction alone. There are two kinds. In natural convection, differences in temperature make the fluid's density differ, and the lighter warm fluid rises while the heavier cool fluid sinks. In forced convection, a fan, a pump, or the wind drives the motion.

At the surface of a wall, a thin layer of nearly still air clings to the material, and heat must cross it. This layer is called a surface film or air film, and its effect can be described by a film coefficient \( h \) in BTU/(h·ft²·°F), so the heat exchanged with the air is:

\[ \dot{Q} = h \, A \, \Delta T \]

A standard value for the inside surface of a vertical wall in still indoor air is about \( h = 1.47 \). The outside surface of a wall in a 15 mph winter wind has a much larger coefficient, about \( h = 5.9 \), because the wind sweeps away the still layer.

Worked example: wind on the outside film. Consider 100 ft² of wall surface with a 10°F temperature difference between the air and the surface. On the inside, in still air, \( \dot{Q} = 1.47 \times 100 \times 10 = 1{,}470 \) BTU/h. On the outside in a 15 mph wind, \( \dot{Q} = 5.9 \times 100 \times 10 = 5{,}900 \) BTU/h, which is about four times larger. This is why a windy day feels colder than a calm one at the same air temperature, and why the outside surface of a wall in the wind sits very close to the outdoor air temperature. The same physics creates the air movement inside buildings that Chapter 4 calls the stack effect.

docs.title: Radiation
docs.text:
Radiation is the transfer of energy by electromagnetic waves, which travel through empty space and need no material to carry them. Every object above absolute zero emits thermal radiation, and the amount rises steeply with its absolute temperature, in proportion to the fourth power. Surfaces also absorb the radiation that arrives. A property called emissivity, from 0 to 1, describes how well a surface emits and absorbs radiation. Most building materials, such as paint, wood, and glass, have emissivities near 0.9. Polished metal foil is as low as 0.05, so it emits very little and reflects most of the radiation that arrives.

Radiation is the reason you feel cold standing next to a large window on a winter day even when the thermostat reads 70°F. Your skin radiates heat toward every colder surface it can "see." Windows also admit solar radiation, which is the sun's energy, and this heats the room's interior surfaces. In Minnesota, that is welcome in winter and a burden in summer.

Worked example: the cold window. Treat your skin as a surface at 91°F with an emissivity of 0.95, facing a surface of the same emissivity. Using the Stefan-Boltzmann law with absolute temperatures, the net radiant exchange is about 23 BTU/h for each ft² of skin when the other surface is a 68°F interior wall. It is about 48 BTU/h per ft² when the other surface is a 40°F window pane, which is roughly double. The air in the room is the same temperature in both cases. The loss of radiant heat to the cold glass is what you perceive as a chill. This is an approximation that assumes the skin sees only that one surface. A window with a low-emissivity coating, covered in Chapter 12, reduces the radiant loss, and a pane that stays warmer on the inside surface makes the room feel more comfortable at a lower thermostat setting.

docs.title: Thermal Resistance
docs.text:
Thermal resistance is a measure of how strongly a material or assembly opposes the flow of heat. Rearranging Fourier's law shows that the resistance of a flat layer is its thickness divided by its conductivity, and that the heat flow follows from the temperature difference and the resistance:

\[ R = \frac{L}{k} \qquad \dot{Q} = \frac{A \, \Delta T}{R} \]

Where electrical resistance is measured in ohms, \( R \) in this chapter is expressed per unit area, in the units h·ft²·°F/BTU. A thick layer or a low-conductivity material has high resistance, and heat flows slowly through it. Electrical designers will recognize this structure because it is Ohm's law in a thermal costume. Chapter 15 introduces the electrical version, and the analogy is useful in both directions.

Thermal quantity Electrical analogue Temperature difference \( \Delta T \) Voltage \( V \) Heat flow \( \dot{Q} \) Current \( I \) Thermal resistance \( R \) Resistance \( R \) Layers in series Resistors in series (resistances add)

The analogy gives a rule that is easy to remember: when heat must pass through several layers one after another, their resistances add. The total resistance is the sum of each layer's \( R \), and the temperature difference splits across the layers in proportion to their resistances. A layer with high resistance takes the largest share of the temperature drop.

Worked example: following the temperature through a wall. Consider a 2×4 wood-framed wall at a cavity location (between studs), with the layers listed in the table, and take the inside air as 70°F and the outside as −10°F, a difference of 80°F. The layers include the inside and outside air films from the Convection section, whose resistances are the reciprocals of their coefficients (1/1.47 = 0.68 and 1/5.9 = 0.17). The total is 15.4 h·ft²·°F/BTU, so the heat flow per ft² is \( 80 / 15.4 = 5.2 \) BTU/h. The temperature drop across each layer is this flow times the layer's resistance.

Layer R Drop across layer (°F) Temperature at the cold side of the layer (°F) Inside air film 0.68 3.5 66.5 1/2 in gypsum board 0.45 2.3 64.1 3.5 in fiberglass batt 13.0 67.5 −3.4 7/16 in sheathing 0.5 2.6 −6.0 Vinyl siding 0.6 3.1 −9.1 Outside air film 0.17 0.9 −10.0 Total 15.4 80.0

Nearly all of the 80°F drop, 67.5°F, happens across the insulation. The inner face of the sheathing, which is the cold side of the insulation, sits at about −3°F, far below freezing, and the inside face of the gypsum board stays at about 66°F. A cold layer inside a wall is exactly where moisture problems start, which is a central theme of Chapter 4.

docs.title: R-Value
docs.text:
The R-value is the thermal resistance of a material or assembly, expressed in the units h·ft²·°F/BTU, and it is the number printed on insulation packages and listed in energy codes. A higher R-value means better resistance to heat flow. Manufacturers and codes usually quote the R-value of a product per inch of thickness or for a specific thickness, and the R-value of a layer is the per-inch value times the thickness. SI practice uses RSI, in m²·K/W, where an R-value of 1 equals an RSI of about 0.176.

The R-values below are approximate and vary by product and temperature, but they are close enough to estimate with.

Material Approximate R per inch Softwood lumber 1.25 Fiberglass or mineral-wool batt 3.7 Dense-pack cellulose 3.7 Extruded polystyrene (XPS) board 5.0 Polyisocyanurate board 6.0 Normal-weight concrete 0.1

Minnesota lies in climate zones 6 (the southern and central parts of the state, including Minneapolis) and 7 (the north) of the model energy codes, which are the cold and very cold zones. The Minnesota Energy Code therefore requires higher R-values for roofs, walls, and floors than milder states do. Chapter 11 covers the specific insulation strategies, and Chapter 19 covers the code requirements.

Worked example: reaching R-30 in a roof. Suppose the design team wants a roof insulation layer of R-30 (an illustrative target) at Riverbend. The thickness needed equals the target R divided by the R per inch. Using polyisocyanurate board at R-6 per inch, \( 30 / 6 = 5 \) in. Using fiberglass at R-3.7 per inch, \( 30 / 3.7 = 8.1 \) in. Using XPS at R-5 per inch, \( 30 / 5 = 6 \) in. The foam board reaches the target in a thinner layer, which matters when the roof is shallow, but it usually costs more per R. The designer therefore compares thickness, cost, and fire behavior together, a theme of Chapter 5's discussion of material selection.

Adding R-value brings diminishing returns, because heat loss depends on the reciprocal of the total. Suppose we add a 1 in layer of XPS (R-5) outside the cavity wall, which has a total R of 15.4. The total becomes 20.4, and the U-value falls from 0.0649 to 0.0490, a 24 percent cut in heat loss. A second inch brings the total to 25.4 and the U-value to 0.0394, which is only a further 20 percent cut from the 0.0490 value. Each added inch of insulation saves less than the one before it, so designers look for the thickness at which the extra cost no longer repays itself in saved energy.

Two cautions apply to every R-value you read. First, a labeled R-value describes the insulation alone, not the wall that contains it. Second, the number can fall if insulation is compressed, wet, or installed with gaps, because it depends on trapped still air. Both matter more than most beginners expect.

docs.title: U-Value
docs.text:
The U-value, also called the U-factor, is the rate at which heat flows through an assembly per square foot per degree of temperature difference, and it equals the reciprocal of the assembly's total R-value:

\[ U = \frac{1}{R_{\text{total}}} \qquad \dot{Q} = U \, A \, \Delta T \]

Its units are BTU/(h·ft²·°F). A low U-value means low heat loss, and it is the number that energy codes commonly use for windows and for whole assemblies. The total R-value includes every layer plus the air films. Because the total form multiplies by area and temperature difference, the U-value gives the whole heat loss in a single step.

Worked example: a wall and a window. The cavity wall from the previous section has a total \( R = 15.4 \), so \( U = 1/15.4 = 0.065 \). A window with an illustrative U-value of 0.30 has a total resistance of only \( 1/0.30 = 3.3 \). On the 80°F design day, 1,000 ft² of this wall loses \( 0.065 \times 1{,}000 \times 80 = 5{,}200 \) BTU/h. Only 100 ft² of the window loses \( 0.30 \times 100 \times 80 = 2{,}400 \) BTU/h. Per square foot, the window loses \( 0.30/0.065 \approx 4.6 \) times as much heat as the wall, and a tenth of the area produces nearly half as much loss. That is why window area is one of the biggest decisions in cold-climate design.

Beau's Tip: R Adds in Layers, U Adds in Areas

Add R-values when heat passes through layers one after another, and add U-times-area when heat flows through different parts of a wall side by side. When you need to combine the two situations, convert to R for the layers, then to U for the areas.

docs.title: Thermal Bridging
docs.text:
Thermal bridging is the flow of heat around or through insulation by way of a higher-conductivity material that spans from the warm side to the cold side. Examples include wood or steel studs that interrupt insulation, concrete slab edges that pass through the wall, steel beams that penetrate the enclosure, and window frames. Heat chooses the easiest path, and in a wall the studs are an easier path than the insulation between them.

In a conventional 2×4 wall, studs and plates make up roughly 25 percent of the wall's area (a common estimate that includes headers and corners). We can calculate the wall's overall performance with the parallel path method: calculate \( U \) separately for the cavity and for the stud path, then average the two by their areas. The two paths sit side by side, so we average U-values, not R-values.

Worked example: the R-13 batt in a wall that is not R-13. The cavity path, which adds the R-13 batt to the gypsum, sheathing, siding, and air films, has a total R of 15.4, as in the previous sections. That total is higher than the batt's label only because the other layers add resistance; the framing is what pulls the whole wall back down. In the stud path, the 3.5 in of wood replaces the batt, giving a layer R of \( 3.5/0.8 = 4.4 \) and a total R of 6.8. The two U-values are \( 1/15.4 = 0.0649 \) and \( 1/6.8 = 0.1476 \). With 75 percent of the area as cavity and 25 percent as stud:

\[ U_{\text{avg}} = 0.75 \times 0.0649 + 0.25 \times 0.1476 = 0.0856 \]

The effective total resistance is \( 1/0.0856 = 11.7 \), about 24 percent lower than the 15.4 that a quick calculation suggests. The 1,000 ft² wall from the previous section then loses \( 0.0856 \times 1{,}000 \times 80 = 6{,}850 \) BTU/h, which is 1,650 BTU/h more than the 5,200 BTU/h predicted for the cavity alone. The remedy, covered in Chapter 11, is to add a continuous layer of insulation outside the framing, so that no stud touches both sides without interruption.

Watch Out: The Label Is Not the Wall

A common trap is to read "R-13" on a batt and assume the wall is R-13. Studs, headers, and gaps bypass the batt, so the whole wall performs lower. Calculate the effective R of the full assembly, or ask for it, before you compare options.

The next simulation lets you build the wall layer by layer, so you can see the framing penalty directly.
