docs.title: Movement Joints
docs.text: Concrete and masonry change size with temperature and moisture, and if the change is prevented they crack. Designers therefore build planned joints into slabs and walls, so that the movement and the cracking happen where they are intended. The two kinds of joint do different jobs, and the table compares them after the definitions.

docs.title: Control Joints
docs.text: A control joint is a deliberately weakened line in a concrete slab or masonry wall that is meant to crack, so that shrinkage cracking occurs in a straight, controlled location. Concrete shrinks as it dries, and a restrained slab would otherwise crack at random. In a slab, a control joint is made by sawing a groove, usually to one-quarter of the slab depth, within hours of finishing. A common spacing rule is 2 to 3 times the slab thickness in inches, expressed in feet, so a 5 in. slab has joints every 10 to 15 ft. In concrete masonry walls, vertical control joints are placed at intervals, commonly on the order of 25 ft or less, and at openings and changes in height, with the joint filled with sealant.

docs.title: Expansion Joints
docs.text:
An expansion joint is a full-depth gap, filled with a compressible material, that lets two parts of a structure expand and contract independently without pushing against each other. Expansion joints (also called isolation joints in slabs) separate a slab from columns and walls, so that they can move independently, and they divide long runs of brick veneer. Clay brick expands slowly over its life as it absorbs moisture, while concrete products shrink, so a common rule is that clay expands and concrete shrinks.

Worked example: movement over a Minnesota year. Concrete expands about \( 5.5 \times 10^{-6} \) per °F. Assume a temperature range of 115 °F between a cold winter morning and a hot summer afternoon, an illustrative figure. A 100 ft run (1,200 in.) of concrete changes in length by

\[ 1{,}200\ \text{in.} \times 5.5 \times 10^{-6} \times 115 = 0.76\ \text{in.} \]

This is the change if the concrete is free to move. A clay brick wall of the same length, with an expansion coefficient of about \( 3.6 \times 10^{-6} \) per °F, would change by about 0.5 in. These movements explain why long runs are broken by joints. The table compares the two types.

Joint Purpose Typical locations Depth and filler Control Direct shrinkage cracking to a line Slabs, concrete and CMU walls Partial depth, sealant Expansion Allow growth and separate elements Slab edges, brick veneer, building seams Full depth, compressible filler and sealant

You Can Read a Pour and a Wall

You can now explain how cement, water, and aggregates become concrete, balance a mix by absolute volume, spot a water-cement ratio gone wrong, size rebar for a beam, schedule a pour, and tell brick, block, mortar, and grout apart. That is the vocabulary the foundation chapters build on next.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Concrete is cement, water, and aggregates that harden by hydration, a chemical reaction that needs moisture. It is strong in compression (typically 3,000 to 5,000 psi), weak in tension (about 10 percent as strong), and in Minnesota it must be air-entrained to survive freezing.
  • Cement is the binder and aggregates make up 60 to 75 percent of the volume. The maximum aggregate size is limited by the narrowest form dimension, the rebar spacing, and the slab depth.
  • The water-cement ratio is the most influential property of a mix: lower ratios mean stronger, denser, more durable concrete, and adding water at the chute raises the ratio and weakens the concrete.
  • Mix design balances strength, workability, durability, and cost, and the absolute volume method requires the solid volumes of the ingredients to add up to 27 ft³ per cubic yard.
  • Rebar carries tension and concrete carries compression, and the two work together because of bond, similar thermal expansion, and the protective alkaline environment of concrete. Prestressing keeps concrete in compression before the loads arrive.
  • Cast-in-place concrete moves through forms, reinforcement, placement, consolidation, finishing, and curing. Formwork must resist the fluid pressure of fresh concrete, and curing keeps water in the concrete so that it reaches its design strength.
  • Precast concrete is made in a plant and erected by crane, and slabs on grade combine a compacted base, a vapor retarder, and insulation in cold climates.
  • Masonry builds walls from brick, concrete block, or stone bound by mortar, with grout and steel in reinforced masonry to resist tension and sideways forces.
  • Control joints direct shrinkage cracks to chosen lines, and expansion joints let parts move freely. Clay expands, and concrete shrinks.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Concrete and Masonry
docs.text: Test your understanding of the concepts in this chapter with these review questions, one for each of the 23 concepts covered.

docs.title: 1. Why can concrete harden under water, and why does concrete that dries out too early stop gaining strength?
docs.text:
1. It hardens by evaporation of the mixing water, so a wet environment only slows the process down
  2. It hardens by cooling of the cement paste, so added water speeds up the change of state
  3. It hardens by hydration, a chemical reaction that needs moisture, so drying out stops the reaction
  4. It hardens by compaction of the aggregates, so moisture only affects the surface finish of the slab
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Hydration is the combination of cement with water to form interlocking crystals that bind the mixture. It releases heat and continues for weeks, as long as moisture and moderate temperatures are available. Hydration is not drying, so water is an ingredient and not a solvent that must leave. Concrete that dries too early stops gaining strength, which is why the goal after the pour is keeping the water in.

Concept Tested: Concrete

See: Concrete

docs.title: 2. What is the role of cement in concrete?
docs.text:
1. It is the granular material that makes up most of the volume and limits shrinkage of the paste
  2. It is the binder that reacts with water to form a paste that glues the aggregates together
  3. It is the steel that carries the tension the concrete cannot carry on its own in a beam
  4. It is the chemical added in small doses to change the workability or the set time of a mix
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Portland cement is made by heating limestone and clay in a kiln and grinding the clinker with a little gypsum. It reacts with water in hydration, so cement is the glue and not the product. A sidewalk is concrete, never cement. The granular material is aggregate, the tension carrier is rebar, and the small-dose chemicals are admixtures.

Concept Tested: Cement

See: Cement

docs.title: 3. A #4 reinforcing bar has a cross-sectional area of 0.20 in² and a yield strength of 60 ksi. About how much tension can it carry at yield?
docs.text:
1. 0.33 kips
  2. 120 kips
  3. 60 kips
  4. 12 kips
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Force equals area times stress: 0.20 in² × 60 ksi = 12 kips. The value 0.33 kips divides the stress by the area, 120 kips overstates by a factor of ten, and 60 kips simply repeats the yield strength. Rebar provides in a thin bar the tension capacity that concrete, at about 10 percent of its compressive strength, cannot provide at all.

Concept Tested: Reinforcing Steel

See: Reinforcing Steel

docs.title: 4. In masonry vocabulary, what is a wythe?
docs.text:
1. A vertical layer of masonry one unit thick
  2. A horizontal layer of units laid in a wall
  3. The pattern in which vertical joints are staggered
  4. The thin facing of brick attached to a structural backup
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A course is a horizontal layer of units, a wythe is a vertical layer one unit thick, and the bond is the pattern in which vertical joints are staggered from course to course, commonly running bond. A thin facing attached to a structural backup is a veneer. Masonry is strong in compression and weak in tension, like concrete.

Concept Tested: Masonry

See: Masonry

docs.title: 5. A wall form has a narrowest dimension of 8 in., rebar with a 3 in. clear spacing, and an adjoining slab 6 in. deep. Using the one-fifth, three-quarters, and one-third rules, what maximum aggregate size controls?
docs.text:
1. 2.0 in., from one-third of the 6 in. slab depth
  2. 2.25 in., from three-quarters of the clear bar spacing
  3. 3.0 in., from the clear spacing between the bars
  4. 1.6 in., from one-fifth of the narrowest form dimension
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The limits are 8/5 = 1.6 in. for the form, 0.75 × 3 = 2.25 in. for the bars, and 6/3 = 2.0 in. for the slab. The smallest result controls, because a larger stone would jam and leave voids. Aggregates make up 60 to 75 percent of concrete's volume and should be hard, clean, and well graded.

Concept Tested: Aggregates

See: Aggregates

docs.title: 6. A concrete mix contains 600 lb of cement and 270 lb of water per cubic yard. What is its water-cement ratio?
docs.text:
1. 0.45
  2. 2.22
  3. 0.25
  4. 0.55
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The water-cement ratio is the mass of water divided by the mass of cement: 270 / 600 = 0.45. The value 2.22 inverts the ratio, and 0.25 is only about what hydration itself needs by mass. A lower ratio produces stronger, denser, less permeable concrete, and exposed Minnesota concrete commonly needs 0.45 or lower, so adding water at the chute can push it out of specification.

Concept Tested: Water-Cement Ratio

See: Water-Cement Ratio

docs.title: 7. In the absolute volume method of mix design, why does the aggregate volume equal whatever remains after the other ingredients are accounted for?
docs.text:
1. The aggregate must always make up exactly 60 percent of the mix by mass
  2. The masses of all ingredients must add up to 27 lb per cubic foot of concrete
  3. The solid volumes of all ingredients must add up to exactly 27 ft³, one cubic yard
  4. The cement and water must fill all of the space that the air does not occupy
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Absolute volume is bookkeeping: each ingredient's volume is its mass divided by its specific gravity times 62.4 lb/ft³, and the totals must equal 27 ft³. In the example, cement, water, and air take 8.56 ft³, so the aggregate fills 18.44 ft³. Aggregates usually occupy 60 to 75 percent of the volume, and the mix's mass totals thousands of pounds, not 27.

Concept Tested: Concrete Mix Design

See: Concrete Mix Design

docs.title: 8. Why do form designers either space ties closer together or use stronger ties near the bottom of a tall wall pour?
docs.text:
1. Concrete hardens first at the bottom, so the ties must resist its early shrinkage
  2. Fresh concrete acts like a heavy liquid, so pressure on the form increases with depth
  3. The top of the pour carries the weight of the crew, so the bottom must be braced
  4. Vibration is applied only at the base, so the pressure there is higher than anywhere else
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Fresh concrete behaves like a fluid, so the pressure at the base of an 8 ft pour is at most about 150 × 8 = 1,200 psf, falling to zero at the top. A tie one foot above the base on a 2 ft grid could see about 4,200 lb. A form designed for less than full fluid pressure can burst. Slower pours and cooler concrete reduce the actual pressure.

Concept Tested: Formwork

See: Formwork

docs.title: 9. Which three reasons explain why steel and concrete work well together in reinforced concrete?
docs.text:
1. Deformed bars bond to the concrete, both expand by nearly the same amount, and concrete's alkalinity protects steel from rust
  2. Steel is lighter than concrete, both have the same tensile strength, and concrete's porosity absorbs the steel's heat
  3. Steel stiffens the aggregates, both shrink at the same rate, and concrete's acidity cleans the steel surface of rust
  4. Steel is cheaper than concrete, both resist compression equally, and concrete's moisture hydrates the steel bars
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Ribs on deformed bars create a strong bond, steel and concrete expand about 6 millionths per °F so they do not pull apart with the seasons, and concrete forms a protective film on steel as long as it stays sound. Concrete is weak in tension, steel is strong in tension, and the partnership assigns compression to concrete and tension to steel.

Concept Tested: Reinforced Concrete

See: Reinforced Concrete

docs.title: 10. Why should concrete be placed close to its final position instead of being dropped from a great height or pushed far?
docs.text:
1. Dropping it speeds hydration, so the concrete sets before it can be consolidated
  2. Dropping or pushing it can segregate the mix, so the stone separates from the paste
  3. Pushing it allows air bubbles to escape, so the concrete loses its freeze-thaw resistance
  4. Dropping it adds water to the mix, so the water-cement ratio rises
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Placement delivers fresh concrete to the forms, spreads it, consolidates it, and finishes it. Segregation weakens the mix. Concrete is also normally discharged within about 90 minutes of mixing because hydration has begun. Consolidation with an internal vibrator releases trapped air, and under-vibration leaves honeycombing while over-vibration causes segregation.

Concept Tested: Concrete Placement

See: Concrete Placement

docs.title: 11. What is the main advantage of cast-in-place concrete compared with assembled precast pieces?
docs.text:
1. The concrete is cured in a factory, so its quality does not depend on site weather or labor
  2. The forms are not required, so the pour can proceed immediately after the excavation is complete
  3. The reinforcement is eliminated, because the concrete cures in its final position in the building
  4. The pieces form a single monolithic structure that can carry moment connections and unusual shapes
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Cast-in-place concrete is placed and cured in its final location in forms built on site, which makes it monolithic. Its disadvantages are dependence on weather, site labor, and time, since each pour must cure before it is loaded. Factory curing describes precast, and forms and reinforcement are always needed for cast-in-place work.

Concept Tested: Cast-in-Place Concrete

See: Cast-in-Place Concrete

docs.title: 12. From the top down, what is the order of layers in a typical slab on grade in a cold climate?
docs.text:
1. Concrete slab, rigid insulation, compacted subgrade, vapor retarder, compacted granular base
  2. Vapor retarder, concrete slab, compacted granular base, rigid insulation, compacted subgrade
  3. Concrete slab, vapor retarder, rigid insulation where needed, granular base, compacted subgrade
  4. Compacted subgrade, compacted granular base, concrete slab, rigid insulation, vapor retarder
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A slab on grade rests directly on soil. The vapor retarder sits beneath the slab to block ground moisture, rigid insulation keeps the ground from drawing heat away, and the compacted granular base rests on the compacted subgrade prepared during site work. A suspended slab, by contrast, spans between beams or walls as a structural member and needs reinforcement.

Concept Tested: Concrete Slabs

See: Concrete Slabs

docs.title: 13. Why is mortar deliberately made a little weaker and more flexible than the masonry units?
docs.text:
1. Weaker mortar bonds better to the units, so it prevents any cracking from forming in the wall
  2. Any cracking then occurs in the joint, which can be repaired by repointing, not by replacing units
  3. Weaker mortar hydrates faster, so the wall can be loaded sooner after construction is complete
  4. Flexible mortar absorbs all of the wall's compressive load, so the units themselves can be thinner
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Mortar bonds the units and seals the joints, and standard types M, S, N, and O range from 2,500 psi down to 350 psi minimum. Type N is common above grade, and Type S is used where higher bond or lateral strength is needed. A softer joint localizes cracks where they can be tooled and repointed. Mortar does not carry all the load, and weakness is a design choice, not a way to prevent cracking.

Concept Tested: Mortar

See: Mortar

docs.title: 14. A modular brick face needs about 6.75 bricks per square foot of wall. About how many bricks are needed for a 100 ft² wall, before any allowance for breakage?
docs.text:
1. 675 bricks
  2. 15 bricks
  3. 1,440 bricks
  4. 6,750 bricks
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Multiply the bricks per square foot by the wall area: 100 × 6.75 = 675. The value 15 divides the area by 6.75, 1,440 treats the wall as 144 ft², and 6,750 is a decimal-place error. A typical estimate then adds an allowance such as 5 percent for breakage. Minnesota brick exposed to the weather should be Grade SW, severe weathering.

Concept Tested: Brick

See: Brick

docs.title: 15. Which description of a standard concrete masonry unit is correct?
docs.text:
1. Nominally 4 in. by 2⅔ in. by 8 in., with an actual size ⅜ in. more in each direction, solid sides, and no cores
  2. Nominally 8 in. by 8 in. by 16 in., with an actual size ⅜ in. more in each direction and no hollow cores
  3. Nominally 8 by 8 by 16 in., with an actual size ⅜ in. less in each direction and hollow cores that can be grouted
  4. Nominally 12 in. by 12 in. by 24 in., with an actual size equal to the nominal size and a solid face
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. CMUs are hollow or solid units of molded concrete. The actual size is ⅜ in. smaller than nominal in each direction so that the unit plus its mortar joint fits the module. The cores reduce weight and can be filled with grout and rebar, and the thick sides are called face shells. The 4 × 2⅔ × 8 module describes brick with its joint.

Concept Tested: Concrete Masonry Units

See: Concrete Masonry Units

docs.title: 16. Why is grout made much more fluid than ordinary concrete, with a slump of 8 to 11 in.?
docs.text:
1. It must evaporate quickly from the cores so that the units can be loaded on the same day
  2. It must stay on the surface of the wall to seal the mortar joints against wind-driven rain
  3. It must replace the mortar, so it fills each joint without any other bonding agent being used
  4. It must flow into narrow block cores and around bars to bond the steel and add strength
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Grout is a concrete-like mixture of cement, fine aggregate or pea gravel, and water poured into the cores of concrete blocks or between wythes. It is consolidated by vibrator or puddling and placed in lifts of limited height so the pressure does not blow out the block face shells. Mortar bonds units and seals joints, while grout bonds steel and strengthens cells.

Concept Tested: Grout

See: Grout

docs.title: 17. A slab is finished on a hot, dry, windy afternoon, and fine cracks appear within hours. What practice would best prevent this problem?
docs.text:
1. Let the surface dry quickly so that the excess water leaves the slab before hydration begins
  2. Add water to the surface as it stiffens so the finish stays workable for the finishing crew
  3. Wait for the 28-day cylinder results to come back before beginning any curing of the slab
  4. Keep the surface moist from the start with curing compound, wet burlap, or plastic sheeting
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Hot, dry, or windy conditions pull water from the surface faster than it rises from within, causing plastic shrinkage cracks. Curing keeps freshly placed concrete moist and in a suitable temperature range so hydration continues and the concrete reaches its design strength. Moist curing is commonly required for at least seven days, and adding surface water or waiting for tests does not protect the slab.

Concept Tested: Curing

See: Curing

docs.title: 18. A contractor wants to core-drill an unmarked post-tensioned slab without locating the tendons first. Why is this dangerous?
docs.text:
1. The tendons carry no load, so drilling through them only damages the slab's insulation layer
  2. The tendons hold great stored energy, so cutting one can cause a violent release and weaken the slab
  3. The tendons are made of brittle cast iron, so drilling shatters the concrete around them
  4. The tendons are filled with grout under pressure, so drilling releases wet concrete into the room below
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. In post-tensioning, high-strength strands run through ducts and are stretched with jacks after the concrete hardens, which keeps the concrete in compression before loads arrive. That stored energy is why an unmarked post-tensioned slab must never be cut or drilled until tendons are located. Prestressing allows longer spans and thinner slabs, as in parking structures and office floors.

Concept Tested: Prestressed Concrete

See: Prestressed Concrete

docs.title: 19. What are the main advantages and limits of precast concrete?
docs.text:
1. Pieces are cast in their final positions on site, but weather and labor affect quality and schedule
  2. Pieces are always unreinforced, but they are cheaper than any cast-in-place alternative at any size
  3. Factory conditions give precise forms and consistent quality, but size limits and critical connections apply
  4. Pieces are poured on the building's own slab, but they cannot be lifted by a crane or tilted up
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Precast concrete is cast in a plant and lifted into place, so it has precise forms and controlled curing regardless of weather, and many pieces are also prestressed. Hollow-core planks, double-tee beams, wall panels, beams, and columns are common. Connections between pieces, made by welded plates, bolts, or grouted joints, are critical details. Casting on the building's slab describes tilt-up construction.

Concept Tested: Precast Concrete

See: Precast Concrete

docs.title: 20. Why is reinforced masonry the standard way to build a masonry shear wall?
docs.text:
1. Unreinforced masonry is brittle and weak against sideways forces, and grouted bars let the wall resist tension and shear
  2. Unreinforced masonry is too heavy for lateral loads, and grouted bars reduce the wall's weight enough to resist them
  3. Unreinforced masonry cannot resist compression, and grouted bars carry the vertical load of the floors above
  4. Unreinforced masonry is not fire resistant, and grouted bars supply the fire-resistance rating of the wall
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Reinforced masonry places steel bars or wires in grout-filled cells or joints. Vertical bars go at corners, openings, and regular spacing; bond beams tie courses together; and joint reinforcement controls cracking. Masonry is strong in compression but weak in tension, so steel is needed where wind or seismic forces are significant. Masonry is already heavy and fire resistant.

Concept Tested: Reinforced Masonry

See: Reinforced Masonry

docs.title: 21. How is stone masonry used in modern buildings?
docs.text:
1. Mainly as thick walls that carry load by their weight alone, as in historic buildings and old mills
  2. Mainly as rough rubble placed in the forms to replace the aggregates in a concrete mix
  3. Mainly as a thin veneer anchored to a backup wall, with anchorage designed for the stone's weight
  4. Mainly as lightweight panels that weigh less than 50 pcf and are glued to the wall surface
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Historic buildings used very thick stone walls carrying load by weight, but modern buildings use stone mostly as veneer. Stone weighs roughly 150 to 170 pcf, so anchorage must be designed for that weight, and the stone must be chosen for its resistance to freezing when wet. Common building stones include granite, limestone, and sandstone, and Minnesota has quarried limestone and granite for generations.

Concept Tested: Stone Masonry

See: Stone Masonry

docs.title: 22. Using the rule of 2 to 3 times the slab thickness in inches, expressed in feet, what spacing of control joints is appropriate for a 6 in. slab?
docs.text:
1. 6 to 9 ft
  2. 24 to 36 ft
  3. 2 to 3 ft
  4. 12 to 18 ft
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The rule multiplies the thickness in inches by 2 to 3 and reads the answer in feet: 6 × 2 = 12 ft and 6 × 3 = 18 ft. A control joint is a deliberately weakened line, sawn to about one-quarter of the slab depth within hours of finishing, that directs shrinkage cracking to a straight, controlled line. A restrained slab would otherwise crack at random.

Concept Tested: Control Joints

See: Control Joints

docs.title: 23. What does the rule "clay expands and concrete shrinks" imply for joints in a brick veneer over a concrete block backup?
docs.text:
1. Brick veneer needs control joints directing its shrinkage cracks, while concrete block needs full-depth expansion joints
  2. Brick veneer needs full-depth expansion joints, while concrete block needs control joints directing shrinkage cracks
  3. Neither material needs joints, because both change size by the same amount with temperature and moisture
  4. Both materials need only expansion joints, because both of them shrink as they dry and then stay stable
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Clay brick expands slowly over its life as it absorbs moisture, while concrete products shrink as they dry. An expansion joint is a full-depth gap with compressible filler that lets two parts move independently, and it divides long runs of brick veneer. A control joint is a partial-depth weakened line that directs shrinkage cracks, which suits concrete and block.

Concept Tested: Expansion Joints

See: Expansion Joints

docs.title: References: Concrete and Masonry
docs.text:
1. Concrete - Wikipedia - Thorough article on cement, aggregates, the water-cement ratio, mix design, placement, and curing. Its sections on hydration and strength development tie together most of this chapter's materials concepts.

  2. Reinforced concrete - Wikipedia - Explains why steel bars are added to concrete, which is strong in compression but weak in tension. Covers rebar, prestressing, and corrosion, with diagrams of reinforced beams and slabs.

  3. Masonry - Wikipedia - Overview of brick, stone, and concrete masonry units, mortar, and construction methods. Its coverage of bonds, load-bearing walls, and reinforced masonry gives students a broad vocabulary for the masonry half of the chapter.

  4. Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures (16th Edition) - Steven H. Kosmatka and Michelle L. Wilson - Portland Cement Association - The standard industry reference, most praised for clarity. Its charts relating water-cement ratio to strength and durability, and its curing guidance, make mix design concepts concrete for students.

  5. Why Buildings Stand Up: The Strength of Architecture - Mario Salvadori - W. W. Norton - Salvadori explains masonry arches, vaults, and reinforced concrete beams in non-mathematical language, showing how compression-only materials carry load and why steel reinforcement is needed where tension develops.

  6. Concrete Technology and Applications of Cement - Portland Cement Association - Describes ready mixed, precast, prestressed, and tilt-up concrete, along with concrete masonry units and insulating concrete forms. Helpful for comparing cast-in-place, precast, and prestressed systems.

  7. Mechanics and Design of Concrete Structures - MIT OpenCourseWare - Free undergraduate course by Prof. Oral Buyukozturk with lecture notes and problem sets on concrete behavior, reinforced members, and slab design. Offers a rigorous extension of this chapter's reinforced concrete topics.

  8. Rebar Properties - Concrete Reinforcing Steel Institute - Explains why steel suits concrete: a uniform modulus, ductility, matching thermal expansion, and fire resilience, with yield strengths and ASTM specifications. Directly supports the reinforcing steel concept.

  9. Masonry Movement Joints - Masonry Advisory Council - Distinguishes expansion joints in brick from control joints in concrete masonry and works a spacing example. Matches the chapter's point that clay expands while concrete shrinks.

  10. Accommodating Expansion of Brickwork (Technical Note 18A) - Brick Industry Association - Industry technical note on designing expansion joints to prevent cracking in brick walls. Offers placement guidance and details useful for the expansion joints and brick concepts.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: How site analysis, excavation, soil properties, groundwater, and frost conditions shape what can be built on a site. It builds on the prerequisite concepts from Chapters 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. After completing this chapter, students will be able to define, explain, and apply the 11 concepts listed below.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 11 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Site Analysis 47 Soil Types 32 Soil Bearing Capacity 21 Site Preparation 13 Excavation 8 Groundwater 5 Grading 4 Frost Depth 3 Site Drainage 3 Soil Testing 1 Frost Heave 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
  • Chapter 2: The Design and Construction Process
  • Chapter 3: Forces, Heat, and the Physics of Buildings
  • Chapter 4: Moisture, Air Movement, and Thermal Comfort
  • Chapter 5: Properties of Building Materials

Every Building Starts With the Ground

Before a single wall goes up, the ground has already made some of your biggest decisions for you. Learn to read a site and its soil, and you will know what a building can safely stand on, what it will cost to get there, and what surprises to expect in a Minnesota spring. Let's build it right!

Every load that Chapter 6 will trace through a structure ends in the same place: the soil beneath the building. A beam, a column, and a footing can each be perfectly designed, and the building will still fail if the ground cannot carry what it is given. This chapter therefore starts before construction does. We examine how the project team studies a site, how soil is classified and tested, how groundwater and frost change soil behavior, and how the site is cleared, excavated, shaped, and drained so that a foundation can be built on it.

To keep the numbers concrete, we return to the Riverbend Youth Center from Chapter 2, the one-story, 9,000 ft² community building in Minneapolis. For this chapter we imagine it on a 300 ft by 200 ft lot. The lot size, soil values, and quantities are illustrative, chosen to make the arithmetic clear and not to represent a real site.

docs.title: Site Analysis
docs.text:
Site analysis is the systematic collection and evaluation of information about a parcel of land, its surroundings, and the rules that govern it, so that the design team can decide where and how to build. It begins during programming and schematic design, which Chapter 2 described, because the findings shape the building rather than merely adjust it. A site that slopes steeply, floods in spring, or sits above soft peat will change the foundation, the budget, and sometimes the decision to buy the land at all.

The team gathers information in several categories. Each category answers a different question, and each can add cost or restrict the design.

  • Legal and regulatory. Property boundaries, zoning, setbacks (the minimum distances a building must keep from the property lines), and easements (rights of others to cross or use part of the land, such as a utility line).
  • Topography. The shape of the ground, shown on a survey by contour lines that connect points of equal elevation. Tightly spaced contours mean a steep slope.
  • Soils and groundwater. What the ground is made of, how strong it is, and where water stands in it. The rest of this chapter explores these.
  • Climate. Sun path, prevailing wind, snow load and drifting, and the depth to which the ground freezes.
  • Utilities and access. Where water, sewer, electric, gas, and communication lines are located, and how people and delivery trucks reach the site.
  • Environmental constraints. Wetlands, floodplains, mature trees, and past uses of the land that may have left contamination.

The electrical designer, introduced in Chapter 1, uses the same analysis. The location of the utility's transformer and the route of the service line from the street affect the length of the electrical service and its cost.

Worked example: the buildable area at Riverbend. The imagined lot is 300 ft by 200 ft, which is 60,000 ft² or about 1.38 acres. Suppose the zoning requires setbacks of 25 ft at the front, 10 ft on each side, and 20 ft at the rear. The buildable envelope is the part of the lot where the building may sit. Its width is \( 300 - 10 - 10 = 280 \) ft, and its depth is \( 200 - 25 - 20 = 155 \) ft, so its area is \( 280 \times 155 = 43{,}400 \) ft². The 9,000 ft² building occupies about 21 percent of that envelope and 15 percent of the lot. The remaining area must still hold parking, a stormwater basin, and the entry court from the schematic design. A sewer easement along the rear 10 ft, a mapped wetland, or a 15 percent slope would each shrink the usable area further, which is why the team prepares this map before deciding on a floor plan.

The diagram below lets you turn each category of site information on and off as a layer, so you can see how the constraints stack up on one parcel.

docs.title: Soil Types
docs.text:
Soil is the loose mixture of mineral particles, organic matter, water, and air that lies above solid rock. For a builder, soil is a construction material that arrives already in place and whose properties cannot be specified, only discovered. Engineers sort soils by the size of their particles, because particle size largely controls how a soil drains, how much load it carries, and how it behaves when wet or frozen.

The common soil types, from coarsest to finest, are gravel, sand, silt, and clay. Gravel and sand are coarse-grained, or granular, soils whose particles are visible to the eye. Gravel particles are larger than about 4.75 mm, which is the opening of a No. 4 sieve, and sand particles range from that size down to 0.075 mm. Silt and clay together are called fines, particles smaller than 0.075 mm that pass the No. 200 sieve, and they are fine-grained soils. Clay particles, smaller than about 0.002 mm, are flat and carry an electric charge, so they hold water tightly and can be sticky and plastic. A fifth category, organic soil and peat, consists of partly decayed plant material. It is compressible and weak, and is almost always removed from beneath a foundation.

Two terms help describe behavior. A soil's permeability is how easily water flows through it, which is high for gravel and very low for clay. A soil's plasticity is its ability to be molded without crumbling when moist. The laboratory measures plasticity with the Atterberg limits, the moisture contents at which a soil changes from liquid to plastic to solid. With these terms defined, the table below summarizes how the types compare for building.

Soil type Particle size Drainage Relative strength Frost susceptibility Typical concern Gravel Larger than 4.75 mm Excellent High Low Few; excellent bearing and drainage Sand 0.075 to 4.75 mm Good Moderate to high Low Loose sand can settle Silt 0.002 to 0.075 mm Poor Low to moderate Very high Frost heave, strength lost when saturated Clay Smaller than 0.002 mm Very poor Moderate when dry, low when wet Moderate to high Slow settlement over years Organic and peat Plant fibers Variable Very low Variable Large settlement; must be removed

The engineering profession uses the Unified Soil Classification System (USCS) to give each soil a two-letter symbol, such as GW for well-graded gravel, SM for silty sand, and CL for low-plasticity clay. The first letter names the dominant type (G, S, M for silt, C for clay, O for organic), and the second describes grading or plasticity. The classification procedure follows a short decision path based on a sieve analysis, a laboratory test in which a dry sample is shaken through a stack of sieves of decreasing opening size and the weight retained on each is recorded.

Worked example: classifying a Riverbend soil. A sample taken from a boring at 4 ft depth has the following results (illustrative): 8 percent gravel, 62 percent sand, and 30 percent fines. First, the portion retained on the No. 200 sieve is \( 8 + 62 = 70 \) percent, which is more than half, so the soil is coarse-grained. Second, sand makes up \( 62 / 70 \approx 89 \) percent of that coarse fraction, more than half, so the soil is a sand and not a gravel. Third, the fines exceed 12 percent, so the symbol depends on the fines' plasticity. The laboratory reports that they have low plasticity, which makes them silty, and the symbol is SM, silty sand. A silty sand drains moderately, carries load well when dry, and is somewhat frost-susceptible because of its fines. That last property matters in Minneapolis, as the frost sections below explain.

Much of Minnesota's ground consists of glacial till (a mixture of clay, silt, sand, and gravel deposited by ice sheets) and layers of lake clay, with peat in low, wet areas. Local conditions change within a few city blocks, which is the reason no one should assume the soil from a neighboring site.

docs.title: Diagram: USCS Soil Classifier
docs.text:
Run USCS Soil Classifier Fullscreen

USCS Soil Classifier

Type: microsim sim-id: uscs-soil-classifier Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Learning objective: Students will apply (Bloom Level 3, Apply) the simplified USCS decision path to a sieve analysis to classify a soil as a gravel, sand, silt, or clay, and will predict (Bloom Level 2, Understand) its drainage, strength, and frost behavior.

Visual: On the left, a column of three stacked sieves (No. 4, No. 200, and a pan) with a stacked bar showing the percentage of the sample retained in each. On the right, a flowchart of the decision path (more than 50 percent retained on No. 200? more than half of coarse fraction sand or gravel? more than 12 percent fines? plasticity low or high?) with the current path highlighted. At the bottom, a result card shows the symbol, a name, and icons for drainage, strength, and frost susceptibility. The canvas is responsive, 460 px tall, and redraws on window resize.

Controls: Three sliders for percent gravel, sand, and fines that always sum to 100 (adjusting one rescales the others). A dropdown for "plasticity of the fines" with options low and high. A "Load Riverbend boring B-2" button sets 8, 62, and 30 percent with low plasticity. A "Random sample" button generates a new soil.

Interactions: Hovering over a sieve shows its opening size and the particle size category it separates. Clicking any decision box opens a one-sentence explanation of why that test is applied. The result card updates immediately when any control changes.

Default state: Riverbend boring B-2 loaded, result SM (silty sand).

Implementation: p5.js with built-in sliders, select, and buttons, a rule-based classifier, and a responsive canvas.

The Soil Is a Structural Member

Think of the soil as the last member in the load path, the one that no one sized, ordered, or inspected before it arrived. Everything in this chapter is the work of finding out what that member can actually carry.

docs.title: Soil Testing
docs.text:
Soil testing is the combination of field exploration and laboratory analysis that tells the design team what the soil is and how it will behave. A geotechnical engineer, a civil engineer who specializes in soil and rock behavior, directs the work. A drilling crew advances soil borings, small-diameter holes that bring up samples at regular depth intervals, and records the depth at which water appears. Many borings include the standard penetration test, in which a weighted hammer drives a sampler into the soil and the number of blows needed to advance it one foot, called the N-value, indicates how dense or stiff the soil is.

Samples go to a laboratory for grain size, Atterberg limits, moisture content, and, if fill will be placed, a Proctor test that finds the moisture content at which the soil compacts best. The engineer then writes a geotechnical report with the soil profile, recommended allowable bearing capacity, frost and groundwater observations, and requirements for fill and compaction. The cost of borings is a small fraction of the project budget, and it buys protection from the largest unknowns in the foundation design.

Beau's Tip: Hire the Borings Early

Ask the owner to order the geotechnical investigation during schematic design, not after the foundation is drawn. A report that arrives with the building already laid out can force a redesign, while one that arrives first can guide where the building goes.

docs.title: Soil Bearing Capacity
docs.text:
Soil bearing capacity is the pressure that a soil can support from a foundation without failing in shear or settling excessively. The pressure is the load divided by the area it acts on, in pounds per square foot (psf). Engineers work with two values. The ultimate bearing capacity is the pressure at which the soil would fail, and the allowable bearing capacity is that value divided by a factor of safety, commonly about 3, so that the building stays well below failure. A second limit also applies: even soil that will not fail may compress under load, and if one part of a building settles more than another, walls and floors crack. This uneven movement is called differential settlement.

Soil is much weaker than the concrete and steel placed on it, so the footing must spread the load over a larger area. The required footing area follows directly from the definition of pressure:

\[ A_{\text{required}} = \frac{P}{q_{\text{allow}}} \]

where \( P \) is the column load in pounds or kips (1 kip equals 1,000 lb) and \( q_{\text{allow}} \) is the allowable bearing capacity in psf. Prescriptive code tables list conservative presumptive values, commonly on the order of 1,500 psf for clays and silts, 2,000 psf for sands, and 3,000 psf for gravels, but the geotechnical report governs when one exists.

Worked example: sizing a footing for three soils. Suppose a column supporting one of the glulam beams over the Riverbend multipurpose room carries 40 kips (an illustrative load). Chapter 10 treats footing design in detail; here we ask only how much area the soil demands. In clay at 1,500 psf the area is \( 40{,}000 / 1{,}500 = 26.7 \) ft², a square about 5.2 ft on a side, which we round up to 5 ft 3 in. In sand at 2,000 psf the area is 20 ft², about 4.5 ft square. In gravel at 3,000 psf the area is 13.3 ft², about 3.7 ft square, rounded to 3 ft 9 in. Weaker soil requires nearly twice the footing area, and weaker soil also costs more to excavate and fill with concrete. This estimate ignores the weight of the footing itself, which a real design adds.

Watch Out: Fill and Frozen Ground Are Not Bearing Soil

Never found a footing on topsoil, loose fill, or frozen ground, because each will compress or thaw and let the footing settle. Remove the topsoil, replace any loose or organic layer with compacted engineered fill, and keep winter pours on thawed, protected subgrade.

docs.title: Groundwater
docs.text:
Groundwater is water that fills the spaces between soil particles below a certain depth. The top of this saturated zone is the water table. Above it, soil may still be damp because fine soils pull water upward by capillary action, the same force that draws water up a paper towel. In Minnesota the water table rises with spring snowmelt and rain and falls in late summer, so its depth depends on the date. Occasionally a layer of clay holds a pocket of water above the main table, called perched water.

Groundwater matters to builders in three ways. Saturated soil usually has less strength than the same soil when dry. Water below a floor pushes upward with hydrostatic pressure, which increases with depth below the water table, and the pressure acts on basement floors and walls. Finally, an excavation that reaches the water table fills with water, and the contractor must pump it out, a practice called dewatering, to work in the dry.

Worked example: uplift under a basement slab. Water weighs about 62.4 lb/ft³, so the pressure at a depth \( d \) below the water table is \( 62.4 \times d \) psf. Suppose a below-grade slab (illustrative) sits 6 ft below the water table, giving a pressure of \( 62.4 \times 6 = 374 \) psf pushing up on the underside. A 6 in concrete slab weighs about \( 0.5 \times 150 = 75 \) psf, so the net uplift is about 299 psf. That is roughly 4 times the slab's weight, enough to crack and lift the slab. Designers respond by keeping floors above the water table, adding drainage that lowers the water level, or designing the slab as a thick, anchored structure.

Watch Out: The Boring Reflects That Day's Water

A boring drilled in a dry August can record a water table several feet lower than the spring high. Ask the geotechnical engineer to report the expected seasonal high water level, and design below-grade space for that level, not the day of the borings.

docs.title: Frost Depth
docs.text: Frost depth is the depth to which the ground freezes in winter. It depends on the climate: air temperatures, how long the cold lasts, snow cover, and the soil's water content. Frost depth is an input to the building code, which sets a minimum depth for the bottom of exterior footings so that they sit below frozen soil. In the Twin Cities area this depth is commonly 42 inches, and it is greater farther north, but the local building official and the Minnesota State Building Code establish the value for a given project. Frost depth is not the same as the frost line seen on a single cold morning, because it records the deepest freezing expected in a severe winter. Chapter 10 applies frost depth to footing design, and Chapter 11 introduces frost-protected foundations, which use insulation to reduce the needed depth.

docs.title: Frost Heave
docs.text: Frost heave is the upward movement of the ground, and of anything resting on it, when soil freezes. Many people attribute it to water expanding about 9 percent when it turns to ice, but that expansion alone would produce only modest movement. The larger cause is the growth of ice lenses, layers of nearly pure ice that form as freezing soil draws more water upward from below by capillary action, thickening the lens until it lifts the soil above. Heave requires three conditions together: frost-susceptible soil, a supply of water, and freezing temperatures. Silt is the worst offender, because it is fine enough to pull water up strongly and permeable enough to let it move. Removing any one of the three stops heave, which is the basis of the cures: place footings below frost depth, replace silty soil with clean gravel, or drain the water away.

docs.title: Site Preparation
docs.text:
Site preparation is the set of activities that make a site ready for foundation construction. It begins as soon as the contract is signed and the permits are in hand. Preparation is as much about protecting the surroundings as it is about changing the land, because disturbing soil produces mud, runoff, and sediment that can leave the site.

The main tasks, in a typical order, are as follows.

  1. Locate utilities. In Minnesota, contractors must call 811 (Gopher State One Call) before digging so that buried gas, electric, and communication lines are marked.
  2. Survey and stake. Surveyors mark building corners and elevations, which give the crew a reference for every later measurement.
  3. Install erosion and sediment controls. Silt fences, inlet protection on storm drains, and a stabilized rock construction entrance keep sediment from leaving the site.
  4. Protect what stays. Fencing around trees and areas to be preserved prevents damage to roots.
  5. Clear, grub, and strip. Clearing removes trees and brush, grubbing removes stumps and roots, and stripping removes the topsoil layer, which is stockpiled for later landscaping because it is rich in organic matter that is unsuitable for supporting a building.
  6. Establish access and temporary facilities. Construction roads, a staging area, and temporary power and water.

Large projects need more than good practice. In Minnesota, a project that disturbs about one acre or more typically needs a construction stormwater permit with a written pollution-prevention plan. The imagined Riverbend lot is 1.38 acres, and if the work disturbs even 1.1 acres, the permit would apply.

Worked example: sequencing Riverbend. The superintendent plans the first three weeks. The utility locate request goes in first because markings take several working days. While waiting, the survey crew stakes the building and installs the silt fence along the downhill property line. On the day after the locates arrive, the excavator strips 6 in of topsoil from the building pad and stockpiles it at the back of the lot, away from the stormwater basin. Stripping first would have exposed bare soil with no sediment control in place, which is the most common mistake in sequencing, and it would invite a stop-work order after the first rain.

Beau's Tip: Controls Before Cuts

Use a simple rule on every site: install the silt fence and rock entrance before the first scoop of dirt is moved. The inspector will check for them first.

docs.title: Excavation
docs.text:
Excavation is the removal of soil or rock to create space for foundations, utilities, and basements, and to bring the ground to the planned elevations. Excavation is described in terms of cut, the soil removed, and of the bank volume, the volume of soil as it lies undisturbed. Once dug, soil is loosened and occupies more space. The ratio of that increase is the swell factor, which is commonly 10 to 40 percent depending on the soil. When the soil is later placed and compacted as fill, it shrinks again, so quantities should be tracked in bank, loose, and compacted volumes and never mixed.

Excavation is also the most dangerous part of site work, because trench walls can collapse without warning. The federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) generally requires a protective system for trenches 5 ft or deeper unless the walls are in stable rock. The protective system may be sloping the walls back, shoring them with braces, or using a trench box, and a competent person must inspect the excavation daily. For sloping, OSHA classifies soil as Type A, B, or C, which is a separate system from the USCS and describes stability only. The maximum allowable slope, written as horizontal to vertical, is commonly 3/4:1 for Type A, 1:1 for Type B, and 1.5:1 for Type C. The table below restates these limits and what they mean for a 5 ft deep cut.

OSHA soil type Typical soil Maximum slope (horizontal:vertical) Sideways run for a 5 ft cut Type A Firm, cohesive clay 3/4:1 3.75 ft Type B Silt, angular gravel, some stiff till 1:1 5 ft Type C Sand, loose or wet soil 1.5:1 7.5 ft

Worked example: hauling the Riverbend pad cut. Suppose the building pad plus 3 ft of working space on each side measures \( 126 \times 81 = 10{,}206 \) ft² and the cut averages 1.5 ft deep. The bank volume is \( 10{,}206 \times 1.5 = 15{,}309 \) ft³, which is \( 15{,}309 / 27 = 567 \) yd³. With a swell factor of 25 percent (illustrative), the loose volume is \( 567 \times 1.25 \approx 709 \) yd³. A tandem dump truck hauling 12 yd³ per trip needs \( 709 / 12 \approx 59.1 \), so 60 loads. If the cut were instead 6 ft deep in Type B soil, the trench would need either walls sloped at 1:1, which adds 6 ft of width on each side, or a trench box.

docs.title: Grading
docs.text:
Grading is the shaping of the ground surface to the elevations and slopes shown on the plans. Where the existing ground is higher than the design elevation, the crew cuts, and where it is lower, the crew fills. A good grading plan balances cut and fill so that little soil must be hauled onto or off the site, since hauling is expensive. Fill that supports a building is placed in thin layers, commonly about 8 in loose, and each layer is compacted before the next is added, so that the fill carries load without settling later. Compaction is commonly specified as a percentage, such as 95 percent, of the maximum density found in the Proctor test.

Grading serves two other purposes. It directs surface water away from the building, and it creates accessible paths. Building codes commonly require the ground to fall at least 6 in within the first 10 ft away from the foundation, a 5 percent slope. Accessibility standards generally treat a walking surface steeper than 1:20, which is 5 percent, as a ramp with additional requirements. Slopes are written as a percent, a ratio, or a drop over a distance, and the table below converts among them for the values that matter most on a building site.

Slope Percent Where it appears 1:48 about 2.1 Commonly the maximum cross slope of an accessible walk 6 in in 10 ft 5 Minimum fall away from the foundation; also 1:20, the limit before a walk becomes a ramp 1:12 about 8.3 Commonly the steepest slope allowed for an accessible ramp 1:1 100 A 45 degree slope, such as a Type B excavation wall

Worked example: checking the Riverbend entry. The finished floor of the entry is set at elevation 100.00 ft, and the parking lot edge, 60 ft away, is at 98.00 ft. The drop of 2.00 ft over 60 ft is \( 2/60 = 0.033 \), or 3.3 percent. That is gentler than 5 percent, so the walk stays a regular route and not a ramp. The ground within 10 ft of the building must fall at least 6 in, so at 10 ft away it must be no higher than 99.50 ft, which is a 5 percent slope. Both conditions can be satisfied with one gently sloped walk and a slightly steeper lawn beside it.

docs.title: Site Drainage
docs.text:
Site drainage is the system of surfaces, channels, and pipes that collects stormwater and groundwater and carries it away from buildings and paved areas. Surface drainage relies on the grading described above, plus swales (shallow, vegetated channels), catch basins (inlets that collect water from pavement), and storm sewers that carry it to a discharge point. Subsurface drainage uses perforated pipe in gravel, commonly called a French drain, to intercept groundwater. In cold climates, the water must also not pool where it will freeze on walkways. Minnesota municipalities and watershed districts commonly require projects to hold back stormwater in a basin and release it slowly, so that downstream flooding does not increase. Chapter 10 returns to drainage at the foundation itself, where it keeps water away from basement walls and floors.

You Can Read the Ground

You can now analyze a site's constraints, classify a soil from a sieve analysis, size a footing from the soil's bearing capacity, and explain how groundwater and frost can lift or crack a structure. You also know how a site is prepared, excavated, graded, and drained before the first footing is poured. That is the knowledge a foundation depends on.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Site analysis gathers legal, topographic, soil, climate, utility, and environmental information early, because it can reduce the buildable area and drive cost.
  • Soils are classified by particle size into gravel, sand, silt, clay, and organic soil. The USCS assigns symbols such as SM from a sieve analysis and plasticity.
  • Soil testing by borings and laboratory work, directed by a geotechnical engineer, replaces assumptions about the ground with data.
  • Required footing area equals load divided by allowable bearing capacity, so weaker soil demands a larger footing.
  • Groundwater lowers soil strength, creates hydrostatic uplift of about 62.4 psf per foot of depth below the water table, and must be designed for at its seasonal high.
  • Frost depth sets how deep footings must go. Frost heave needs frost-susceptible soil, water, and freezing temperatures together, and removing any one stops it.
  • Site preparation puts erosion controls in place before stripping, and excavation volumes must be tracked as bank, loose, and compacted quantities.
  • Grading balances cut and fill and slopes the ground away from the building, and site drainage carries stormwater and groundwater away safely.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Site Work, Soils, and Groundwater
docs.text: Test your understanding of the concepts in this chapter with these review questions, one for each of the 11 concepts covered.

docs.title: 1. A lot is 200 ft wide and 150 ft deep. Zoning requires setbacks of 10 ft on each side, 25 ft at the front, and 15 ft at the rear. What is the area of the buildable envelope?
docs.text:
1. 30,000 ft²
  2. 19,800 ft²
  3. 27,000 ft²
  4. 22,500 ft²
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The envelope's width is 200 − 10 − 10 = 180 ft, and its depth is 150 − 25 − 15 = 110 ft, so the area is 180 × 110 = 19,800 ft². The lot area (30,000) ignores all setbacks, 27,000 ignores the front and rear setbacks, and 22,500 ignores the rear setback. Easements, wetlands, or steep slopes would shrink the usable area further.

Concept Tested: Site Analysis

See: Site Analysis

docs.title: 2. A sieve analysis finds 5 percent gravel, 25 percent sand, and 70 percent fines of low plasticity. Which classification and behavior fit best?
docs.text:
1. A coarse-grained silty sand with good drainage, high strength, and low frost susceptibility
  2. A well-graded gravel with excellent bearing capacity and excellent drainage
  3. A fine-grained, silt-like soil with poor drainage and very high frost susceptibility
  4. An organic soil that is very strong when saturated and easy to compact in lifts
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Fines are particles smaller than 0.075 mm that pass the No. 200 sieve. When more than half of a sample passes it, the soil is fine-grained. With low-plasticity fines, the soil behaves like a silt: poor drainage, low to moderate strength, strength lost when saturated, and very high frost susceptibility. The coarse-grained options contradict the 70 percent fines, and organic soil is weak and compressible.

Concept Tested: Soil Types

See: Soil Types

docs.title: 3. A column carries 60 kips and the soil's allowable bearing capacity is 2,000 psf. What footing area is required?
docs.text:
1. 30 ft²
  2. 3 ft²
  3. 60 ft²
  4. 120 ft²
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Required area equals load divided by allowable bearing capacity: 60,000 lb / 2,000 psf = 30 ft², about 5.5 ft square. The value 3 ft² comes from using kips against psf with the wrong decimal, and 60 and 120 ft² use capacities of 1,000 and 500 psf. Weaker soil demands a larger footing, and a real design also adds the footing's own weight.

Concept Tested: Soil Bearing Capacity

See: Soil Bearing Capacity

docs.title: 4. A crew strips topsoil from the whole building pad before installing any silt fence. What problem does this sequence invite?
docs.text:
1. Compaction of the topsoil by the equipment, which makes the stockpile unusable for later landscaping
  2. Loss of the utility markings, which are removed along with the topsoil layer during stripping
  3. Settlement of the future footings, which would rest on the thin layer of topsoil left behind
  4. Bare soil with no sediment control, which can wash off the site in the first rain and draw a stop-work order
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Preparation is as much about protecting the surroundings as changing the land. The recommended order is to locate utilities, survey, install erosion and sediment controls, protect what stays, then clear, grub, and strip. Stripping first exposes bare soil with nothing to stop runoff, which is the most common sequencing mistake. Topsoil is stripped because it is unsuitable for supporting a building.

Concept Tested: Site Preparation

See: Site Preparation

docs.title: 5. An excavation removes 300 yd³ of soil measured in place (bank volume). With a swell factor of 25 percent, what loose volume must the trucks haul?
docs.text:
1. 240 yd³
  2. 325 yd³
  3. 375 yd³
  4. 300 yd³
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Once dug, soil is loosened and occupies more space. The loose volume is the bank volume times (1 + swell factor): 300 × 1.25 = 375 yd³. Dividing by 1.25 gives 240 yd³, adding 25 yd³ gives 325, and 300 ignores swell entirely. Quantities should be tracked separately as bank, loose, and compacted volumes, because compacted fill shrinks again.

Concept Tested: Excavation

See: Excavation

docs.title: 6. Why should below-grade space be designed for the seasonal high water level and not the water level observed on the day of the borings?
docs.text:
1. The water table rises with spring snowmelt and rain, and a dry-season boring can read too low
  2. The water table stays constant all year, so any boring date gives a reliable value for design
  3. Groundwater only exerts pressure in spring, so the other seasons are not important for design
  4. Saturated soil is stronger than dry soil, so the high level is the safest assumption for bearing
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Groundwater fills the spaces between soil particles below the water table, and hydrostatic pressure increases by about 62.4 psf per foot of depth. A slab 6 ft below the water table sees about 374 psf of uplift, which can crack and lift it. Saturated soil is usually weaker, not stronger, and the water table varies with season.

Concept Tested: Groundwater

See: Groundwater

docs.title: 7. An entry sits at elevation 100.00 ft and the parking lot edge, 50 ft away, is at 98.50 ft. What is the walk's slope, and how does it compare with the 5 percent threshold between a walk and a ramp?
docs.text:
1. 3 percent, which is below 5 percent, so it must be treated as a ramp
  2. 3 percent, which is below 5 percent, so it remains a regular walking route
  3. 33 percent, which is above 5 percent, so it must be treated as a ramp
  4. 0.03 percent, which is below 5 percent, so it needs no slope at all
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The drop is 1.5 ft over 50 ft, or 0.03, which is 3 percent. Accessibility standards generally treat a walking surface steeper than 1:20 (5 percent) as a ramp with additional requirements, so this walk is a regular route. The value 33 percent inverts the ratio. Codes also commonly require ground to fall at least 6 in within the first 10 ft away from the foundation.

Concept Tested: Grading

See: Grading

docs.title: 8. What is the practical purpose of the code's frost depth requirement for exterior footings?
docs.text:
1. It places the bottom of footings at the depth where the water table is found in spring
  2. It places the bottom of footings at the depth where the soil changes from silt to granular
  3. It places the bottom of footings above frozen soil so they can be inspected in winter
  4. It places the bottom of footings below the depth to which ground freezes in a severe winter
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Frost depth is the depth to which the ground freezes, and the code sets a minimum depth for the bottoms of footings so they sit below frozen soil. In the Twin Cities area it is commonly 42 inches and greater farther north, but the local building official establishes the project value. It records the deepest freezing expected in a severe winter, not the frost line seen on a single cold morning.

Concept Tested: Frost Depth

See: Frost Depth

docs.title: 9. What does a French drain do?
docs.text:
1. It uses perforated pipe in gravel to intercept groundwater
  2. It uses a shallow vegetated channel to carry surface water away from pavement
  3. It uses an inlet in the pavement to collect surface runoff
  4. It uses a basin to hold stormwater and release it slowly
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Subsurface drainage uses perforated pipe in gravel to intercept groundwater. Surface drainage uses grading, swales (shallow vegetated channels), catch basins (pavement inlets), and storm sewers. Municipalities and watershed districts commonly require basins that hold back stormwater and release it slowly so downstream flooding does not increase.

Concept Tested: Site Drainage

See: Site Drainage

docs.title: 10. Why does the geotechnical investigation order borings early, during schematic design, rather than after the foundation is drawn?
docs.text:
1. Borings are cheaper in schematic design because the soil is easier to sample before drawings begin
  2. The code requires foundation plans to be drawn before the soil's allowable bearing capacity is known
  3. The standard penetration test cannot be performed once the building footprint is staked
  4. A report that arrives first can guide where the building goes, while a late report can force a redesign
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Soil testing combines field exploration and laboratory analysis, directed by a geotechnical engineer, and replaces assumptions with data on grain size, Atterberg limits, moisture, and compaction. The report recommends allowable bearing capacity and records frost and groundwater observations. Borings are a small fraction of the project budget and protect against the largest foundation unknowns.

Concept Tested: Soil Testing

See: Soil Testing

docs.title: 11. A slab edge rises each winter over wet silt. Which measure removes one of the three conditions needed for frost heave?
docs.text:
1. Add a second layer of concrete to increase the slab's weight
  2. Replace the silt beneath the slab edge with clean gravel
  3. Seal the slab surface so snow cannot melt onto it
  4. Increase the slab thickness so the freezing front cannot reach it
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Frost heave requires frost-susceptible soil, a supply of water, and freezing temperatures together. The main cause is the growth of ice lenses as freezing soil draws water upward by capillary action. Silt is the worst offender. Removing any one condition stops heave, so options include footings below frost depth, replacing silty soil with clean gravel, or draining the water away.

Concept Tested: Frost Heave

See: Frost Heave

docs.title: References: Site Work, Soils, and Groundwater
docs.text:
1. Bearing capacity - Wikipedia - Defines ultimate and allowable bearing capacity and shows how soil strength, footing size, and groundwater affect foundation design. Directly supports the soil bearing capacity concept and the failure modes it illustrates.

  2. Frost heaving - Wikipedia - Explains how ice lenses grow in frost-susceptible soil, lifting pavements and foundations. Describes the conditions needed (freezing temperatures, fine soil, water supply), which explains why frost depth matters in Minnesota.

  3. Soil classification - Wikipedia - Introduces the Unified Soil Classification System and other schemes sorting gravel, sand, silt, and clay. Gives students the vocabulary for soil types and soil testing results.

  4. Soil Mechanics in Engineering Practice (3rd Edition) - Karl Terzaghi, Ralph B. Peck, and Gholamreza Mesri - Wiley - Terzaghi's effective stress principle and bearing capacity analysis, with Peck's practical, experience-based commentary, explain how groundwater changes soil strength. Foundational for the chapter's soil and groundwater concepts.

  5. An Introduction to Geotechnical Engineering (2nd Edition) - Robert D. Holtz, William D. Kovacs, and Thomas C. Sheahan - Pearson - Most praised for clarity, it builds soil classification, permeability, and bearing concepts with many worked examples and diagrams. Useful for students meeting soil testing for the first time.

  6. Web Soil Survey - USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service - Free tool that maps soil units for most U.S. counties and generates reports on suitability, drainage, and properties. Students can define a site and perform a real site analysis.

  7. Minnesota Rule 1303.1600: Footing Depth for Frost Protection - Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes - The state code text setting minimum footing depths by frost zone and exceptions for slab-on-grade on suitable soils. Primary source for Minnesota frost depth requirements.

  8. Revised Builder's Guide to Frost Protected Shallow Foundations - Building America Solution Center - HUD, PATH, and NAHB guide showing how perimeter insulation lets footings sit 12 to 16 inches deep in cold climates. Demonstrates a practical response to frost heave.

  9. Aquifers and Groundwater - U.S. Geological Survey - Explains the zone of saturation, the water table, porosity, and permeability, with diagrams of aquifers and wells. Builds the physical understanding behind groundwater and site drainage concepts.

  10. Groundwater and Aquifers in Minnesota - University of Minnesota Extension - Describes glacial sand and gravel, sedimentary, and crystalline aquifers across Minnesota, plus unconfined versus confined conditions. Localizes groundwater concepts for regional site analysis.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The shallow and deep foundations, foundation walls, slabs, and retaining walls that transfer building loads to the soil. It builds on the prerequisite concepts from Chapters 6, 8, 9. After completing this chapter, students will be able to define, explain, and apply the 15 concepts listed below.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 15 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Foundation Systems 19 Shallow Foundations 15 Continuous Footings 8 Foundation Walls 7 Deep Foundations 3 Spread Footings 2 Basements 2 Slab-on-Grade 2 Footing Reinforcement 1 Mat Foundations 1 Piles 1 Drilled Piers 1 Crawl Spaces 1 Retaining Walls 1 Foundation Drainage 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 6: Structural Loads and Load Paths
  • Chapter 8: Concrete and Masonry
  • Chapter 9: Site Work, Soils, and Groundwater

From Soil Report to Solid Footing

Chapter 9 told you what the ground can carry. Now you get to decide how a building meets it, from a simple strip of concrete under a wall to a forest of piles driven through soft soil. By the end you will be able to read a foundation plan and explain why each piece is there. Let's build it right!

Chapter 6 traced loads from the roof down to the base of the structure, and Chapter 9 measured what the soil beneath can support. This chapter connects the two. We follow the same invented Riverbend Youth Center from Chapters 2 and 9, with the same illustrative soil: a silty sand with an allowable bearing capacity of about 2,000 psf, a frost depth of 42 in, and groundwater well below the foundation. Every load and quantity below is illustrative.

docs.title: Foundation Systems
docs.text:
A foundation system is the part of a building, partly or entirely below grade, that transfers the building's loads to the soil or rock. It does four jobs. It supports the structure by spreading load over enough soil area that the soil is not overstressed, as Chapter 9 showed. It anchors the structure against wind uplift and sliding. It separates the framing from ground moisture and frost. And it provides a level, durable base on which the rest of the building is built. A foundation also completes the load path from Chapter 6, since every force that enters the roof must leave through here.

Foundations fall into two families. Shallow foundations deliver load to soil close to the surface, and deep foundations reach down through weak soil to stronger soil or rock. The choice depends on four inputs: the size of the loads, the bearing capacity and uniformity of the soil, the frost depth and groundwater level, and the cost. Designers start with the cheapest option that works, which is almost always a shallow foundation, and move to a deeper solution only when the soil forces them to.

Worked example: choosing the Riverbend foundation. The structural engineer reviews the geotechnical report. Silty sand with an allowable bearing of 2,000 psf begins 4 ft below grade, and groundwater is 12 ft down. The loads are modest for a one-story, wood-framed building with glulam beams. Every input points to shallow footings. If the report had instead found 15 ft of soft peat above firm sand, shallow footings would have settled badly, and the engineer would have recommended piles that pass through the peat. The decision follows the soil, which is why Chapter 9 came first.

docs.title: Diagram: Foundation Type Selector
docs.text:
Run Foundation Type Selector Fullscreen

Foundation Type Selector

Type: microsim sim-id: foundation-type-selector Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Learning objective: Students will evaluate (Bloom Level 5, Evaluate) which foundation type best fits a given combination of soil, load, water, and frost conditions, and will justify (Bloom Level 5, Evaluate) the choice with the rule that applies.

Visual: A cross-section of a ground profile with up to three soil layers whose depth and type the user can change, with a building outline above it. Beneath the profile, a row of foundation icons (spread footing, continuous footing, mat, driven pile, drilled pier) light up green when suitable, yellow when marginal, and red when unsuitable. The canvas is responsive, 480 px tall, and redraws on window resize.

Controls: A dropdown for the top soil layer (firm sand, soft clay, peat, gravel) and a slider for its thickness from 0 to 25 ft. A slider for column load from 10 to 400 kips. A checkbox for "high groundwater." A dropdown for frost depth (none, 42 in, 60 in). A "Riverbend defaults" button and a "Soft peat site" button.

Interactions: Hovering over an icon shows the foundation's definition and the main reason it was rated green, yellow, or red. Clicking an icon opens an infobox with a typical use and one cost or constructability concern. A justification line beneath the profile restates the governing rule, such as "soft layer deeper than 10 ft, so load must reach firm soil."

Default state: Riverbend defaults, with spread and continuous footings green.

Implementation: p5.js with built-in select, slider, checkbox, and buttons, a rule-based rating function, and a responsive canvas.

A Foundation Doesn't Hold the Building Up

Soil can only push back with so much pressure per square foot, so a foundation is really a load-spreading device. Ask of every foundation element, "How much soil area does this give the load to push against?"

docs.title: Shallow Foundations
docs.text:
Shallow foundations, also called spread foundations, carry load to the soil near the surface through the bearing area of a concrete element called a footing. Each footing is wider than the wall or column above it, and the extra width lets the load spread over a larger area of soil. The three common shallow types are the spread footing under a single column, the continuous footing under a wall, and the mat foundation under a whole building. The table below summarizes them. Each is explained in its own section that follows.

Type Supports Typical use Spread footing One column Columns of a steel or glulam frame Continuous footing A line of wall Exterior and interior bearing walls Mat foundation The whole building Heavy loads or weak soil

The word shallow describes how the load reaches the soil and not how deep the concrete sits. In Minneapolis, the bottom of an exterior footing must be below the frost depth, commonly 42 in, so even a "shallow" footing sits more than 3 ft below the surface. Chapter 9 explained that freezing soil heaves, so a footing placed above the frost depth would be lifted each winter and drop back each spring.

Worked example: bearing versus frost. Riverbend's silty sand is strong enough to support a footing at 2 ft, but the building code requires exterior footings to bear at 42 in below finished grade. The frost requirement therefore sets the depth, and the bearing requirement sets the width. A designer must satisfy both. An interior footing in the heated building is protected from frost by the warm space above it, so the frost rule may not apply there, although soil conditions still do.

Watch Out: Shallow Does Not Mean Above the Frost Line

A footing set at the depth that merely reaches good soil can still be inside the zone that freezes, and then it will heave. Check the frost depth requirement first, and then check bearing. The deeper of the two governs.

docs.title: Spread Footings
docs.text: A spread footing is an isolated pad of concrete, usually square, that supports a single column and spreads its load over the soil. The required area is the column load divided by the allowable bearing capacity, as in the Chapter 9 sizing example. Riverbend's 40 kip column on 2,000 psf soil needs 20 ft², so a footing 4 ft 6 in square (20.25 ft²) carries it. Spread footings are common under steel columns and under the posts that support glulam beams, where loads are concentrated at points instead of spread along walls. A short concrete pier often rises from the footing to lift the column base above the floor and moisture. Spread footings are also used for isolated loads such as a canopy post or a rooftop unit support, and each must still reach below frost depth if it is exterior.

docs.title: Continuous Footings
docs.text:
A continuous footing, also called a strip footing, is a long, narrow concrete strip under a loadbearing wall, running the length of the wall. Its job is to convert the wall's line load, which is the weight per linear foot of wall, into a pressure the soil can carry. Because the footing has a uniform cross-section, we can analyze a 1 ft slice of it. The required width equals the line load divided by the allowable pressure:

\[ b = \frac{w}{q_{\text{allow}}} \]

where \( b \) is the footing width in feet, \( w \) is the line load in pounds per linear foot (plf), and \( q_{\text{allow}} \) is the allowable bearing capacity in psf. Footing thickness is set separately, commonly 8 in or more for a light-frame building, so the footing is stiff enough to spread the load without cracking.

Worked example: the Riverbend perimeter footing. Assume the exterior wall and roof deliver 2,400 plf (an illustrative value that includes snow). On 2,000 psf soil, \( b = 2{,}400 / 2{,}000 = 1.2 \) ft, which is 14.4 in, rounded up to 16 in. On weaker 1,500 psf clay the width would be \( 2{,}400 / 1{,}500 = 1.6 \) ft, or 19.2 in, rounded to 20 in. The Riverbend perimeter is \( 2 \times (120 + 75) = 390 \) ft, so a 16 in wide, 8 in thick footing needs \( (16/12) \times (8/12) \times 390 = 347 \) ft³, or about 12.8 yd³ of concrete, before the footings under columns and the thickened areas are counted.

Learning objective: Students will identify (Bloom Level 1, Remember) the parts of a typical cold-climate foundation and explain (Bloom Level 2, Understand) the job of each part.

The canvas is responsive, 480 px tall, and redraws on window resize.

Clicking a part opens an infobox with its function, a typical dimension (marked "typical" and not required), and the section of this chapter where it is explained. Changing the dropdown rebuilds the cross-section and highlights the parts that are new.
