docs.title: Gypsum Board
docs.text: Gypsum board, also called drywall or wallboard, is a panel made of a gypsum core, a mineral that holds water chemically, pressed between sheets of heavy paper. It is the standard interior finish for walls and ceilings because it is inexpensive, smooth, and fire-resistant. Panels are commonly 4 ft wide and 8 to 12 ft long, and they are 1/2 or 5/8 in thick. Board is fastened to studs, the joints are covered with tape and joint compound, and the surface is sanded and painted. The surface finish is rated in levels, with Level 4 a common choice for painted walls. Type X gypsum board has a core with added glass fibers that helps it hold together in a fire, and it is used to build the fire-resistance-rated assemblies of Chapter 18. Moisture-resistant types are used in wet areas, and plain paper-faced board should be kept dry because wet paper supports mold. Gypsum board also helps sound reduction by adding mass.

docs.title: Interior Finishes
docs.text:
Interior finishes are the surface materials applied to the inside of the enclosure and floors, including paint, tile, flooring, ceilings, and wall base. They are the last materials installed, and they are what building occupants touch and see. Selection weighs durability, cleaning, appearance, acoustics, and fire behavior. Codes assign interior finish materials a flame-spread classification, commonly Class A, B, or C, and limit the class that may be used in corridors, exits, and assembly rooms. Low-emitting products reduce the chemicals released into the air inside. Timing matters, since flooring and paint are damaged by moisture and should not be installed until the building is enclosed, the concrete slab is dry, and the air sealing and inspections are complete. This ordering follows the same sequence the construction process established in Chapter 2.

You Can Finish a Wall Right

You can now choose a cladding and see what it adds to the footing, flash a window in the right order, size a sealant joint for thermal movement, read a window's U-factor and SHGC, and explain what a blower door test measures. That is the skill of connecting the outside of a wall to the control layers behind it.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Cladding is the first line of defense against water, and most modern walls use a drained design, with a gap behind the cladding, flashing at the base, and a water-resistive barrier behind it. A rainscreen adds drying.
  • Cladding weight affects the foundation. Brick veneer adds many times the line load of siding.
  • Flashing must lap in shingle fashion, with each layer over the one below. Caulk is a backup and not a substitute for flashing.
  • Sealant joints must be sized for the movement of the materials, with a backer rod and adhesion on two sides only.
  • A window is a hole in all four control layers. Its U-factor sets heat loss and inside surface temperature, its SHGC sets solar gain, and low-E coatings improve both. Safety glazing is required in hazardous locations.
  • Doors need sills, weatherstripping, and thermal breaks, and curtain wall and storefront systems must supply their own control layers.
  • Air sealing closes the leaks at joints and penetrations before the drywall goes up, and the blower door test measures the result as CFM50 and ACH50.
  • Gypsum board and other interior finishes complete the inside and are installed last, after the enclosure is closed and dry.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Cladding, Windows, Doors, and Air Sealing
docs.text: Test your understanding of the concepts in this chapter with these review questions, one for each of the 19 concepts covered.

docs.title: 1. Why is cladding described as the first line of defense and not as the water control layer?
docs.text:
1. It is applied last in the sequence, so it is installed only after the water control layer is no longer needed
  2. It sheds most rain and snow, but some water gets behind it, where the weather-resistive barrier acts as the second line
  3. It is face-sealed in every cladding system, so water that gets past the surface cannot reach the layers behind
  4. It is the only layer that must be continuous, so the barrier behind it may have gaps without consequence
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Cladding is the exterior skin that sheds water, protects the layers behind from sunlight, impact, and wear, gives the building its appearance, and contributes to fire performance. Most modern walls use a drained strategy that assumes some water will get behind it and provides a path out. A face-sealed system tries to keep all water out, so every joint must stay watertight for the wall's life.

Concept Tested: Cladding

See: Cladding

docs.title: 2. A joint must accommodate 0.30 in. of thermal movement, and the sealant is rated for plus or minus 25 percent. What is the minimum joint width?
docs.text:
1. 0.6 in.
  2. 0.3 in.
  3. 1.2 in.
  4. 0.15 in.
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The minimum width equals the movement divided by twice the movement capability: 0.30 / (2 × 0.25) = 0.6 in. Using the movement alone ignores the sealant's capability, 1.2 in. doubles the result, and 0.15 in. uses a rating of 100 percent. A narrow 1/8 in. joint would tear on the first cold night, and sealant should adhere on two sides only, with a backer rod behind it.

Concept Tested: Sealants

See: Sealants

docs.title: 3. Which type of glass is heat-treated to be about four times stronger and breaks into small, blunt pieces?
docs.text:
1. Annealed glass
  2. Laminated glass
  3. Insulating glass
  4. Tempered glass
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Tempered glass is heat-treated for strength and safety. Annealed glass is ordinary, slowly cooled glass that breaks into sharp shards, and laminated glass has a plastic layer between two panes that holds pieces together and improves sound reduction and security. An insulating glass unit is two or three panes separated by a sealed gap, not a strength treatment. Codes require safety glazing where people are likely to strike glass.

Concept Tested: Glazing

See: Glazing

docs.title: 4. Why is air sealing done before the drywall is installed?
docs.text:
1. The air barrier material is installed only on the outside of the wall, so the drywall would block it
  2. The drywall must be sealed with spray foam on both faces, which requires the framing to be open
  3. Most leakage occurs at joints and penetrations, and open framing lets the crew reach every one cheaply
  4. Building codes require an inspection of the framing before drywall regardless of air leakage
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A wall can have a perfect air barrier material and still leak at the top plate, rim joist, window and door gaps, penetrations, and electrical boxes. Sealants, gaskets, tape, and foam close them. Leaks hidden behind finished drywall are expensive to find and repair, and nearly impossible to do well afterward. Low-expansion foam is used around windows to avoid bowing the frame.

Concept Tested: Air Sealing

See: Air Sealing

docs.title: 5. On a design day, indoor air is 70°F and outdoor air is −10°F. A window with U-0.55 has an inside film resistance of 0.68. The room's dew point is 45°F. What happens at the glass?
docs.text:
1. The inside surface is about 26°F, but condensation does not occur because the glass is dry
  2. The inside surface is about 54°F, above the dew point, so the glass stays clear
  3. The inside surface is about 40°F, below the dew point, so moisture condenses
  4. The inside surface is about 70°F, equal to the room air, so no heat flows
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The surface temperature is T_in − U × ΔT × 0.68 = 70 − 0.55 × 80 × 0.68 ≈ 40°F, below the 45°F dew point, so moisture condenses and may freeze. Leaving out the film resistance gives about 26°F, and a low-U window such as U-0.28 would stay near 55°F. The glass edge is colder than the center, so real condensation starts earlier.

Concept Tested: Windows

See: Windows

docs.title: 6. A blower door holds 50 Pa at 4,500 CFM50 in a building of 90,000 ft³. What is the ACH50?
docs.text:
1. 30
  2. 0.05
  3. 1.5
  4. 3.0
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. ACH50 = CFM50 × 60 / volume = 4,500 × 60 / 90,000 = 3.0. Forgetting the factor of 60 gives 0.05, and 30 and 1.5 are order-of-magnitude and halving errors. A calibrated fan depressurizes the building by 50 pascals, and natural leakage is commonly estimated by dividing ACH50 by 15 to 20. Cold-climate residential codes commonly require about 3 ACH50 or less.

Concept Tested: Blower Door Test

See: Blower Door Test

docs.title: 7. What distinguishes Type X gypsum board?
docs.text:
1. Its core has added glass fibers that help it hold together in a fire, so it builds rated assemblies
  2. Its core has added moisture-resistant additives, so it can be used in showers and other wet areas
  3. Its paper facing is replaced with foil, so it also acts as both a vapor barrier and an air barrier
  4. Its thickness is limited to 1/4 in., so it is used only as a covering over existing walls and ceilings
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Gypsum board has a core of gypsum, a mineral that holds water chemically, pressed between sheets of heavy paper. Type X is used to build the fire-resistance-rated assemblies described in Chapter 18. Moisture-resistant types serve wet areas, and plain paper-faced board should be kept dry because wet paper supports mold. Panels are commonly 1/2 or 5/8 in. thick.

Concept Tested: Gypsum Board

See: Gypsum Board

docs.title: 8. What is the function of weep holes in a brick veneer wall?
docs.text:
1. They hold the brick to the backup wall to resist wind pressure on the wall
  2. They let water collected on the flashing drain out of the cavity
  3. They support the brick above windows and doors at the top of each opening
  4. They allow air to circulate in the cavity so the brick can expand freely
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A brick veneer wall has an air space, metal ties, flashing, weep holes, and lintels. Flashing at the base and above openings catches water running down the cavity, and weep holes in the mortar joints just above the flashing let it out. Ties hold the brick to the backup, and steel angle lintels hold the brick above openings. Veneer carries only its own weight.

Concept Tested: Brick Veneer

See: Brick Veneer

docs.title: 9. Why are vinyl siding nail holes slotted and the nails not driven tight?
docs.text:
1. Vinyl is soft, so tight nails would crush it during installation
  2. Vinyl is a drainage layer, so tight nails would block water paths
  3. Vinyl is combustible, so loose nails reduce the spread of fire
  4. Vinyl expands and contracts with temperature, so it needs room to move
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Siding is a family of thin, lapped cladding boards or panels fastened in courses, with each course overlapping the one below to shed water by the shingle principle. Vinyl moves with temperature, so the nails must allow it to slide. Fiber cement resists rot and fire, but cutting it creates silica dust that can harm lungs, so dust control is required.

Concept Tested: Siding

See: Siding

docs.title: 10. In a traditional three-coat stucco system, what is the correct order of the coats?
docs.text:
1. Brown coat, scratch coat, finish coat
  2. Scratch coat, brown coat, finish coat
  3. Finish coat, brown coat, scratch coat
  4. Scratch coat, finish coat, brown coat
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Stucco is a cement-based plaster applied in layers over lath. The scratch coat is pressed into the lath and scored for grip, the brown coat levels and builds thickness, and the finish coat provides the colored or textured surface. Stucco is hard and fire-resistant but cracks as the building moves, so over wood framing it needs a water-resistive barrier and often a drainage mat.

Concept Tested: Stucco

See: Stucco

docs.title: 11. Which two design problems must be addressed in a metal panel wall because of the properties of metal?
docs.text:
1. Thermal bridging at clips and girts, and movement of panels with temperature changes at the joints
  2. Moisture absorption in the panels, and rot of the supporting framing behind the panels over time
  3. Combustibility of the panels, and shrinkage of the panels as they dry out after installation
  4. Low strength of the panels, and galvanic corrosion caused by contact with the wood framing
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Metal panels are light, durable, and common on commercial and industrial buildings. Because metal conducts heat well, the clips and girts create thermal bridges unless thermal breaks are used, and because it moves with temperature, the joints must be sized for that movement, as in the sealant calculation. Panels are normally installed as a rainscreen, with an air space behind them.

Concept Tested: Metal Panels

See: Metal Panels

docs.title: 12. Which three benefits does the gap in a rainscreen provide?
docs.text:
1. Insulation, air sealing, and vapor control
  2. Fire resistance, sound reduction, and structural support
  3. Drainage, drying by moving air, and a capillary break
  4. Weight reduction, cost savings, and faster installation
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A rainscreen has a gap, often 3/4 in. or more, between the cladding and the water-resistive barrier. Water that gets past the cladding falls down the gap, moving air dries the wall, and the gap stops capillary action. A pressure-equalized rainscreen also matches the gap pressure to wind pressure outside so wind has less force pushing rain through joints. Riverbend mounts siding on vertical furring strips to form the gap.

Concept Tested: Rainscreen

See: Rainscreen

docs.title: 13. Why can a curtain wall be thin and highly glazed?
docs.text:
1. It is a load-bearing wall made of glass panels, and the glass carries the floor loads in compression
  2. It is attached to the foundation, and the foundation carries the wind load directly into the ground
  3. It is made of aluminum, which is strong enough to replace the structural frame of the building
  4. It hangs from the structure and carries only its own weight and wind, since the structure carries the floors
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A curtain wall is typically an aluminum frame with glass or panels as infill, and it is the usual exterior of a multi-story commercial building. Because it is a complete enclosure, its frame must include water, air, vapor, and thermal control layers, and it needs thermal breaks, strips of low-conductivity plastic, because bare aluminum conducts heat very well. A storefront is the one-story version.

Concept Tested: Curtain Wall

See: Curtain Wall

docs.title: 14. At the head of a window opening, how should the weather-resistive barrier be installed relative to the head flashing?
docs.text:
1. Tucked under the head flashing, so the barrier is protected from the sun and from impact
  2. Lapped over the head flashing, so water on the barrier runs onto the flashing and outward
  3. Omitted above the flashing, so the sheathing can dry upward through the opening toward the attic
  4. Replaced with a bead of caulk across the top of the window, which seals the joint
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Flashing directs water out of the wall. The top of the flashing tucks behind the weather-resistive barrier, and the bottom laps over the cladding below, which is the shingle principle. If the barrier were under the head flashing, water would flow behind the flashing and into the opening. Caulk is only a backup, because sealant ages, cracks, and leaves a gap.

Concept Tested: Flashing

See: Flashing

docs.title: 15. Why do designers commonly place a low-E coating on surface 3 in a heating climate and on surface 2 in a cooling climate?
docs.text:
1. Surface 3 reflects visible light into the room, and surface 2 absorbs visible light from outdoors
  2. Surface 3 protects the coating from the weather, and surface 2 exposes it for easier cleaning
  3. Surface 3 keeps heat in the room while admitting solar heat, and surface 2 rejects more solar heat
  4. Surface 3 reduces the glass's emissivity to zero, and surface 2 increases the glass's emissivity
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A low-E coating is a microscopically thin metal or metal-oxide layer that reflects long-wave infrared radiation, or heat, while passing visible light, lowering emissivity from about 0.84 to roughly 0.04 to 0.20. It is placed inside the sealed unit where it is protected. It can lower the U-factor of a double pane by about a third.

Concept Tested: Low-E Coatings

See: Low-E Coatings

docs.title: 16. Two windows with a combined 100 ft² of glazing have whole-window U-factors of 0.48 and 0.28. On a design day with an 80°F temperature difference, how much more heat does the 0.48 option lose?
docs.text:
1. 1,600 BTU/h
  2. 2,240 BTU/h
  3. 3,840 BTU/h
  4. 640 BTU/h
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Heat flow is U × A × ΔT. The 0.48 window loses 0.48 × 100 × 80 = 3,840 BTU/h and the 0.28 window loses 2,240 BTU/h, so the difference is 1,600 BTU/h. The other values are the individual losses or a slip. The NFRC label reports the whole-window value, which is higher than center-of-glass because the frame and edge conduct more heat.

Concept Tested: Window U-Factor

See: Window U-Factor

docs.title: 17. What does the solar heat gain coefficient measure?
docs.text:
1. The rate of heat flow through the whole window per square foot per degree of temperature difference
  2. The percentage of visible light that passes through the glass and the frame into the room
  3. The fraction of the sun's energy striking a window that passes through as heat, from 0 to 1
  4. The fraction of long-wave infrared radiation that the coating reflects back into the room
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. SHGC helps predict solar gain: heat gained equals SHGC × glass area × solar irradiance. A low SHGC reduces cooling loads and glare, while a high SHGC helps heat a building in winter, so Minneapolis designers commonly use a high SHGC on the south side and a low one where sun would cause overheating. The heat-flow rate is the U-factor, and visible light is visible transmittance.

Concept Tested: Solar Heat Gain Coefficient

See: Solar Heat Gain Coefficient

docs.title: 18. Why do busy building entries often include a vestibule with two sets of doors?
docs.text:
1. Doors opened by many people cause the largest bursts of air leakage, and two sets keep one closed
  2. Doors need two sets so that the sill pan can be sloped outward on both sides of the vestibule
  3. Egress codes require two doors in series so that occupants can exit the building in two steps
  4. Two sets of doors provide a thermal bridge that helps warm the entry during the winter months
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. An exterior door is a slab, a frame, a threshold, and weatherstripping, and it is another hole in the control layers. Water enters under the threshold, so it needs a sill pan and sloped threshold, and air leaks around the perimeter, so it needs weatherstripping and a sweep. A thermal break in the frame and threshold avoids thermal bridging. An egress door typically needs a clear opening of at least 32 in. wide.

Concept Tested: Doors

See: Doors

docs.title: 19. Why should flooring and paint be installed only after the building is enclosed and the slab is dry?
docs.text:
1. They are the first layer of the air barrier, so they must be completed before the drywall is hung
  2. They are required to pass the blower door test, so they must be finished before the test begins
  3. They cure by absorbing moisture from the slab, so a wet building improves their bond to the floor
  4. They are damaged by moisture, and finishes are the last materials installed in the construction sequence
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Interior finishes are surface materials such as paint, tile, flooring, ceilings, and wall base, selected for durability, cleaning, appearance, acoustics, and fire behavior. Codes assign flame-spread classes A, B, or C and limit the class allowed in corridors, exits, and assembly rooms. Low-emitting products reduce chemicals in indoor air. They are not part of the air barrier and are installed after air sealing and inspections.

Concept Tested: Interior Finishes

See: Interior Finishes

docs.text:
1. Rainscreen - Wikipedia - Traces rainscreen walls from 1960s Norwegian research and explains the drainage cavity and pressure equalization principle, supporting the chapter's treatment of cladding as a rain-shedding layer separated from the wall.

  2. Low emissivity - Wikipedia - Explains emissivity and how thin coatings on glass cut radiant heat loss, with a table comparing material emissivities, which supports the chapter's low-E coatings and glazing sections.

  3. Blower door - Wikipedia - Describes blower door history, the power-law airflow model, and metrics such as CFM50 and ACH50, giving students the underlying physics for the chapter's air leakage test.

  4. Fundamentals of Building Construction: Materials and Methods (7th Edition) - Edward Allen and Joseph Iano - Wiley - Allen's clear, hand-drawn construction detail drawings of wall sections, flashing, and window installation show how layers are sequenced, making cladding and opening details easy to follow.

  5. Residential Windows: A Guide to New Technologies and Energy Performance (3rd Edition) - John Carmody, Stephen Selkowitz, Dariush Arasteh, and Lisa Heschong - W. W. Norton - Explains glazing performance through U-factor, solar heat gain, and low-E coatings, drawing on Berkeley Lab research, so students can compare windows quantitatively.

  6. Drainage Plane Behind Exterior Wall Cladding - Building America Solution Center, U.S. Department of Energy - Details house wrap, taped foam, and membranes behind siding, with air gaps for wood siding, a one-inch cavity for masonry veneer, and stucco cautions, supporting the cladding sections.

  7. Windows and Doors Are Fully Flashed - Building America Solution Center, U.S. Department of Energy - Shows sill pan, jamb, and head flashing lapped over the drainage plane, with backer rod and caulk air sealing from inside, directly illustrating the chapter's flashing and sealants content.

  8. Purchasing Energy-Efficient Residential Windows, Doors, and Skylights - U.S. Department of Energy, Federal Energy Management Program - Defines U-factor, solar heat gain coefficient, visible transmittance, and air leakage ratings, with cold-climate selection advice, which supports the chapter's window, door, and glazing performance concepts.

  9. Tight Air-Sealed Homes - Building Science Education Solution Center, U.S. Department of Energy - Lists key air sealing locations such as window perimeters, rim joists, top plates, and penetrations, with blower door verification, giving a practical checklist for the chapter's air sealing section.

  10. Enclosure Leakage Test - Building America Solution Center, U.S. Department of Energy - Describes blower door procedures following RESNET Chapter 8, with single-point and multi-point CFM50 and ACH50 results, smoke and infrared leak finding, and code compliance uses.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: How low-slope and steep-slope roofs shed water, drain, ventilate, and resist ice dams, including green roofs. It builds on the prerequisite concepts from Chapters 3, 4, 7, 11. After completing this chapter, students will be able to define, explain, and apply the 10 concepts listed below.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 10 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Roof Assemblies 13 Steep-Slope Roofs 5 Low-Slope Roofs 4 Roof Drainage 3 Roofing Membranes 2 Attic Ventilation 2 Shingles 1 Metal Roofing 1 Ice Dams 1 Green Roofs 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 3: Forces, Heat, and the Physics of Buildings
  • Chapter 4: Moisture, Air Movement, and Thermal Comfort
  • Chapter 7: Wood and Steel Framing
  • Chapter 11: Enclosure Control Layers and Insulation

The Hardest-Working Surface on the Building

The roof takes the sun, the wind, the snow load, and every storm first, and it has to keep all of it out for decades. Once you understand how a roof sheds water and manages heat, you can read a roof section and spot the detail that will leak before it does. Let's build it right!

A roof is the part of the building enclosure that faces the harshest conditions and is hardest to repair once it fails. Chapter 11 described the four control layers that every enclosure needs: water, air, vapor, and heat. This chapter applies those layers overhead, where gravity pulls water toward every joint, snow adds weight, and warm indoor air rises directly into the assembly. In Minneapolis, where winter lasts for months and snow can sit on a roof through repeated freeze-thaw cycles, getting the roof right is a matter of both comfort and durability.

docs.title: Roof Assemblies
docs.text:
A roof assembly is the complete stack of materials, from the structural deck to the weathering surface, that together keep water out, control heat, air, and vapor, and carry loads to the walls below. A shingle or a membrane does not keep a building dry by itself, and a leak almost always traces to a joint between layers rather than to the middle of a material.

Every roof assembly performs the same six jobs, regardless of its type:

  • Shed or drain water. Rain and melting snow must leave the roof quickly, by slope, by drains, or both.
  • Carry loads. The structure resists the weight of the assembly (dead load), snow and rain (Chapter 6), and wind uplift, which tries to peel the roof off.
  • Control heat. Insulation limits winter heat loss and summer heat gain, following the heat-flow principles of Chapter 3.
  • Control air and vapor. An air barrier and, in cold climates, a vapor retarder keep warm, moist indoor air from condensing inside the assembly (Chapter 4).
  • Resist fire. Roof coverings are tested for fire exposure from outside and rated Class A, B, or C, with Class A giving the best resistance.
  • Last. The covering must withstand ultraviolet light, temperature swings, hail, and foot traffic.

Roofs fall into two families defined by slope, and the slope drives almost every other decision. Steep-slope roofs shed water by gravity over overlapping units, so the layers are discontinuous. Low-slope roofs hold a continuous waterproof membrane, so the layers are sealed into one sheet. The table below compares the two stacks, listed from the structure outward. Each term in the table is defined later in this chapter.

Layer Steep-slope (shingle) roof Low-slope (membrane) roof Structure Wood rafters or trusses Steel deck, wood panels, or concrete Deck Wood sheathing The structural deck Air/vapor control Ceiling air barrier at attic floor Vapor retarder or air barrier over the deck Insulation Batts or blown-in on the attic floor Rigid board above the deck Water control Underlayment, ice barrier at eaves Continuous membrane Covering Shingles or metal panels Membrane is the covering

Worked example: reading a roof section from the inside out. A Minneapolis house has a ventilated attic with R-49 of blown insulation on the ceiling. Starting at the room, the layers are drywall, a sealed air barrier at the ceiling plane, the insulation, the open attic air space, roof trusses, plywood sheathing, a synthetic underlayment, and asphalt shingles. Heat flows upward through the insulation, and the attic stays near outdoor temperature because it is ventilated. Water flows down and out over the shingles. Air that leaks upward through ceiling penetrations carries moisture into the attic, which is why the air barrier sits at the ceiling and not at the roof. The insulation controls heat and the covering controls only water, a division of labor that is the key to reading any roof section.

docs.title: Steep-Slope Roofs
docs.text:
A steep-slope roof is a roof pitched steeply enough that water runs off by gravity over overlapping layers of covering, with no continuous sealed surface. Slope is stated as rise over run, the vertical rise in inches for every 12 inches of horizontal run. A 6:12 roof (read "six in twelve") rises 6 inches over each 12 inches of run, which is an angle of about 27 degrees. Building codes and manufacturers commonly treat roofs steeper than about 3:12 as steep-slope, and each covering has its own minimum slope. Asphalt shingles, for example, are commonly allowed down to 2:12, with special underlayment required between 2:12 and 4:12, so the 3:12 line is a rule of thumb for the general case and the manufacturer's minimum governs for each product.

The shape of a steep-slope roof, usually a gable or a hip, also creates the attic space discussed under Attic Ventilation. Steep slopes shed water and snow efficiently, and they are the typical choice for houses and for many small commercial buildings.

Worked example: area and material quantity. A house is 28 ft wide and 40 ft long with a 6:12 gable roof whose ridge runs along the 40 ft length. Each side of the roof spans a horizontal run of 14 ft. The rise is \( 14 \times 6/12 = 7 \) ft, so each rafter slopes along a length of \( \sqrt{14^2 + 7^2} \approx 15.65 \) ft, ignoring the overhang. The two roof planes then total \( 2 \times 15.65 \times 40 \approx 1{,}252 \) ft². Roofers measure area in squares, where one square is 100 ft², so the roof is about 12.5 squares. Adding about 10 percent for waste at hips, valleys, and cut ends gives roughly 13.8 squares, so the buyer orders 14. Note that the sloped area is larger than the 1,120 ft² floor footprint by the factor \( \sqrt{12^2 + 6^2}/12 \approx 1.118 \), which is why estimating from a floor plan alone under-counts material.

Beau's Tip: The Slope Factor

To get roof area quickly from a plan, multiply the footprint by the slope factor: about 1.03 for 3:12, 1.12 for 6:12, and 1.41 for 12:12. Then add 10 percent for waste before you order.

docs.title: Shingles
docs.text:
Shingles are small, overlapping units of roof covering laid in courses from the eave upward so that each course sheds water over the joint beneath it. The most common type in North America is the asphalt shingle, made from a fiberglass mat saturated with asphalt and topped with ceramic-coated mineral granules that protect against sunlight and give color. Wood shakes, slate, and clay or concrete tile follow the same overlap principle.

Shingles are not waterproof as a surface. They shed water, and the layers beneath them provide the backup. In a cold climate the system typically includes a drip edge at the eaves and rakes, a self-adhering waterproof underlayment along the eaves to resist ice dams, a synthetic or felt underlayment over the rest of the deck, and flashing (thin metal or membrane that directs water around joints) at valleys, chimneys, walls, and penetrations. Most roof leaks start at flashing rather than at the shingle field. Asphalt shingles commonly last roughly 20 to 30 years, depending on climate, ventilation, and quality, and they are sold with ratings for wind resistance and for fire class.

docs.title: Metal Roofing
docs.text:
Metal roofing is a steep-slope covering made of formed steel, aluminum, copper, or zinc panels that run from ridge to eave. The two common systems are standing seam, in which adjacent panels interlock with raised seams and are held by concealed clips, and exposed-fastener panels, in which screws with sealing washers pass through the face of the panel. Standing seam costs more but avoids the fasteners that eventually loosen and leak. Metal roofs commonly last 40 years or more and shed snow readily.

Two properties of metal matter in design. First, metal expands and contracts with temperature (Chapter 5), so panels must be free to slide on their clips. Steel expands about 0.0000065 inch per inch per degree Fahrenheit, so a 20 ft steel panel that sees a 100 degree temperature swing changes in length by \( 0.0000065 \times 240 \times 100 \approx 0.16 \) inch; aluminum changes about twice as much. Second, snow can slide off a smooth metal roof suddenly, endangering people and damaging items below, so cold-climate designers commonly add snow guards above entrances and walkways.

docs.title: Low-Slope Roofs
docs.text:
A low-slope roof is a roof so shallow, commonly below about 3:12 and often nearly flat, that water cannot be trusted to run off over overlapping units and must be kept out by a continuous waterproof membrane. Most commercial, institutional, and industrial buildings have low-slope roofs because they cover large rectangular areas economically and provide a place for rooftop mechanical equipment. A low-slope roof is not flat. Designers slope the surface, commonly at least one-quarter inch per foot (about 2 percent), toward drains so that water does not stand.

The most common cold-climate arrangement places the insulation above the structural deck and the membrane on top of the insulation. Rigid foam boards, such as polyisocyanurate, are laid in layers with staggered joints, covered by a cover board that protects the foam and gives the membrane a firm base. Because the insulation is continuous and sits outside the structure, it limits thermal bridging and keeps the deck warm, which reduces condensation risk. In a protected membrane (or inverted) roof, the insulation sits above the membrane and is held down by ballast or pavers, which shields the membrane from temperature swings and damage.

The slope often comes from the insulation rather than the structure. Manufacturers supply tapered insulation, boards cut with a slope so that a structurally level deck can still drain.

Worked example: tapered insulation and heat loss. Assume for illustration that the designers of the Riverbend Youth Center (about 9,000 ft² on one story) choose a low-slope roof with the roof plan area equal to the floor area. Drains sit in valleys, and the longest distance from a high point to a drain is 30 ft. At a quarter inch per foot, the tapered insulation must change in thickness by \( 30 \times 0.25 = 7.5 \) inches over that distance, a quantity the designer must carry into the roof edge and parapet details. For heat loss, suppose two 3 in layers of polyisocyanurate at an illustrative R-5.7 per inch give a total of \( R = 2 \times 3 \times 5.7 = 34.2 \), using the average thickness for simplicity. The U-factor is \( 1/34.2 \approx 0.029 \) Btu/h·ft²·°F. With an indoor temperature of 70 °F and an outdoor temperature of 10 °F, the heat loss is \( Q = UA\Delta T = 0.029 \times 9{,}000 \times 60 \approx 15{,}800 \) Btu/h. The result is a quick check on whether the insulation level matches the energy code, which is the subject of Chapter 19.

The MicroSim below draws a low-slope warm roof from the sky down to the room. Name the layer that keeps rain out and the layer that keeps room vapor out of the insulation. Then remove or puncture each one and watch where the dots go.

docs.title: Roofing Membranes
docs.text:
A roofing membrane is a continuous, flexible, waterproof sheet or built-up layer that forms the weathering surface of a low-slope roof. The main families are listed below.

  • EPDM is a black synthetic rubber sheet with taped or adhesive seams. It is flexible in cold weather and has a long record of use.
  • TPO (thermoplastic polyolefin) is a single-ply sheet, commonly white, whose seams are welded with hot air to form a continuous bond.
  • PVC is also heat-welded and offers good chemical resistance, which suits roofs over restaurant kitchens.
  • Modified bitumen is asphalt reinforced with polymers and fabric, installed in one or two plies by torch, adhesive, or self-adhering backing.
  • Built-up roofing (BUR) alternates layers of reinforcing felts and hot bitumen, commonly topped with gravel.

A membrane is held in place by one of three methods. In a fully adhered system it is glued to the substrate, in a mechanically attached system it is fastened through the seams, and in a ballasted system it is held down by stone or pavers. The attachment method determines the roof's resistance to wind uplift. Most membrane failures occur at seams, penetrations, and edges, so seam quality and flashing details deserve as much attention as the membrane itself.

docs.title: Roof Drainage
docs.text:
Roof drainage is the system that collects water from the roof surface and carries it away from the building. On steep-slope roofs, gutters and downspouts do this job. On low-slope roofs, water flows to interior drains, to scuppers (openings through a parapet wall), or to edge gutters. Codes commonly require a secondary or overflow drain on a roof where a parapet could trap water if the primary drains clog, because a blocked drain loads the roof with the weight of standing water.

Worked example: sizing the load of a clogged roof. Rainfall is measured as an intensity in inches per hour. One inch of rain over one square foot is 0.623 gallons, so a roof must carry away about 0.0104 gallons per minute per square foot for each inch per hour of intensity. Assume the 9,000 ft² Riverbend roof and an illustrative design intensity of 3 inches per hour (the real value comes from the code and local rainfall data). The flow is \( 9{,}000 \times 3 \times 0.0104 \approx 280 \) gallons per minute, so four equal drains must each handle about 70 gpm. Now suppose all drains clog. Water weighs about 5.2 pounds per square foot for each inch of depth, so just 2 inches of ponding adds about 10.4 psf, or about 94,000 pounds over the whole roof. Ponding bends the deck, and the dip holds more water, a feedback loop that can lead to collapse. Structural engineers therefore check roofs for rain load (Chapter 6).

Watch Out: Ponding Is Progressive

A roof that holds water deflects, and the deflection holds even more water. Always ask where the water goes if the primary drain clogs, and confirm that a secondary drain or scupper sits slightly higher to act as the safety valve.

docs.title: Attic Ventilation
docs.text:
Attic ventilation is the intentional flow of outdoor air through the attic of a steep-slope roof, entering at low intake vents (soffits) and leaving at high exhaust vents (ridge or gable). It has two purposes. In winter it keeps the roof deck cold and carries away moisture that leaks up from the house. In summer it removes heat that builds up beneath a sun-heated roof. The airflow works best when it is balanced and continuous, with about half the vent area low and half high, because warm air rises and draws cool air in from below.

Model codes commonly set the net free vent area, meaning the open area after screens and louvers are subtracted, at 1 square foot for every 150 square feet of attic floor, and allow 1 for every 300 when the ceiling has a vapor retarder and the vents are split between high and low. As an example, an attic with 1,120 ft² of floor area at the 1:300 ratio needs about \( 1{,}120/300 \approx 3.7 \) ft², or 538 in², of net free area, split as roughly 269 in² at the soffit and 269 in² at the ridge. Insulation must never block the soffit vents, and baffles (rigid channels at each rafter bay) keep an air path open above the insulation.

docs.title: Ice Dams
docs.text:
An ice dam is a ridge of ice that forms at the eave of a sloped roof and traps meltwater behind it. The cause is heat escaping from the house. Warm air and conducted heat raise the temperature of the roof deck above freezing, so snow melts from beneath. The meltwater flows down the roof until it reaches the eave, which overhangs the exterior wall and stays cold. There the water refreezes, builds a dam, and the water behind it backs up under the shingles and into the building.

The cure targets the heat source, not the ice. In priority order, the remedies are to air seal the ceiling plane so warm air stops entering the attic, to add insulation, to ventilate the attic so the deck stays near outdoor temperature, and to install a self-adhering ice-and-water barrier at the eaves as a backup. Heating cables can melt channels through ice, but they add cost and do nothing about the underlying heat loss.

Visual: A side section of a house eave and attic with a snow layer on the roof. Color shading shows temperature, from warm orange near the ceiling to cool blue at the soffit. Arrows show heat flow and air movement. Ice appears at the eave when conditions allow it.

Controls: A slider for outdoor temperature (-20 to 30 °F), a slider for insulation R-value (R-19 to R-60), a checkbox "Air leaks at ceiling," a checkbox "Soffit and ridge vents open," and a checkbox "Ice-and-water barrier at eave."

Interactions: As controls change, the roof deck temperature updates and snow melts on the part of the roof above 32 °F. Meltwater flows to the eave and freezes if the overhang is below 32 °F. A readout says "Ice dam: forming, minor, or none" and a second readout says "Water reaching interior: yes or no." The first fix suggested by the status line is always air sealing, and the ice-and-water barrier checkbox shows that it protects the interior but does not stop the dam from forming.

Seal First, Then Ventilate

Notice that ventilation is the third remedy, not the first. Ventilation only dilutes heat that has already escaped, while air sealing and insulation stop the heat from escaping at all, so fix the source before the symptom.

docs.title: Green Roofs
docs.text:
A green roof is a roof assembly topped with a layer of living vegetation grown in a lightweight soil called growing medium. Beneath the plants the stack typically includes a filter fabric, a drainage layer that moves excess water to the drains, a root barrier that protects the membrane from penetrating roots, the waterproofing membrane, insulation, and the deck. The green layer does not replace the membrane. It sits on top and protects it from sunlight and temperature swings.

Extensive green roofs use a thin medium, commonly 3 to 6 inches, planted with hardy sedums and grasses that need little care. Intensive green roofs use deeper soil and can support shrubs, small trees, and walkable gardens, but they weigh much more and need irrigation. Benefits include reduced stormwater runoff, lower roof surface temperatures, and extended membrane life. The main design constraint is weight.

As an illustration, a 4 in layer of growing medium at a saturated density of 90 pounds per cubic foot adds \( (4/12) \times 90 = 30 \) psf before the drainage layer and plants are counted. That load is comparable to or larger than the entire dead load of an ordinary roof, so the structural engineer must design for it from the start, and it is rarely practical to add a green roof to a roof that was not designed for one.

You Can Read a Roof Section

You can now trace the layers of a steep-slope and a low-slope roof, size the water load on a roof drain, calculate attic vent area, and explain why air sealing comes before ventilation in stopping ice dams. That is the vocabulary a roofer, an architect, and an inspector all use.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A roof assembly is a system of layers, not a single material. Most failures occur at the joints between layers, at flashing, and at penetrations.
  • Steep-slope roofs shed water by gravity over overlapping units such as shingles and metal panels. Low-slope roofs rely on a continuous membrane and a slight slope toward drains.
  • Slope is stated as rise per 12 inches of run. Sloped roof area equals footprint multiplied by a slope factor, which is about 1.12 for a 6:12 roof.
  • Asphalt shingles shed water and depend on underlayment and flashing. Metal roofs must be free to expand and often need snow guards.
  • Low-slope roofs commonly place continuous insulation above the deck, with a membrane such as EPDM, TPO, PVC, modified bitumen, or built-up roofing on top.
  • Roof drains must carry the design rainfall, and a secondary overflow protects the structure, because standing water weighs about 5.2 psf per inch of depth.
  • Attic ventilation keeps the deck cold in winter and relieves heat in summer. Balanced intake and exhaust at about 1:300 of attic floor area is a common code ratio.
  • Ice dams result from heat loss through the ceiling. Air seal and insulate first, ventilate second, and add an ice-and-water barrier as a backup.
  • Green roofs add vegetation above the membrane and add significant weight, so the structure must be designed for them from the start.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Roof Assemblies
docs.text: Test your understanding of the concepts in this chapter with these review questions, one for each of the 10 concepts covered.

docs.title: 1. Why does a ventilated-attic roof place the air barrier at the ceiling plane and not at the roof covering?
docs.text:
1. Air leaking upward through ceiling penetrations carries moisture into the attic, so air must be stopped there
  2. The covering must be left open so that the roof deck can absorb moisture from the shingles above it
  3. The ceiling is the coldest layer in the roof, so the barrier belongs there to prevent condensation on drywall
  4. The shingles act as the vapor retarder, so the barrier is placed at the ceiling to avoid any duplication
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A roof assembly is the full stack of materials from deck to weathering surface, and leaks almost always trace to joints between layers. In the example, the insulation controls heat and the covering controls only water. Moisture in leaking air is the reason the ceiling air barrier is critical, and the attic stays near outdoor temperature because it is ventilated.

Concept Tested: Roof Assemblies

See: Roof Assemblies

docs.title: 2. A 6:12 roof covers a building footprint of 1,000 ft². Using the slope factor of about 1.12, what is the sloped roof area before waste?
docs.text:
1. About 1,000 ft²
  2. About 1,030 ft²
  3. About 1,410 ft²
  4. About 1,120 ft²
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A steep-slope roof is pitched so water runs off by gravity over overlapping layers, and slope is stated as rise per 12 in. of run. For 6:12 the slope factor is √(12² + 6²)/12 ≈ 1.12, so the area is 1,120 ft². Using the footprint alone undercounts material, 1.03 is the factor for 3:12, and 1.41 is the factor for 12:12. Roofers then add about 10 percent for waste.

Concept Tested: Steep-Slope Roofs

See: Steep-Slope Roofs

docs.title: 3. A low-slope roof is not flat. Why do designers slope it, often with tapered insulation?
docs.text:
1. A slope lets water run off over overlapping units, as it does on a conventional shingled roof surface
  2. A slope allows the membrane to be omitted, because gravity removes the water before it can enter
  3. A slope of at least one-quarter inch per foot moves water to drains so it does not stand on the membrane
  4. A slope reduces the thickness of insulation needed over the whole roof, so the roof costs less
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Low-slope roofs rely on a continuous waterproof membrane and are common on commercial, institutional, and industrial buildings. The slope often comes from tapered insulation, boards cut with a slope, so a structurally level deck can still drain. Over a 30 ft run to a drain, a quarter-inch-per-foot slope changes thickness by 7.5 in., a quantity that must be carried into parapet details.

Concept Tested: Low-Slope Roofs

See: Low-Slope Roofs

docs.title: 4. Why do codes commonly require a secondary overflow drain on a low-slope roof with a parapet?
docs.text:
1. The primary drains are too small for any rainfall, so the secondary drain handles all normal storms alone
  2. If primary drains clog, ponding adds load, the deck deflects, and the dip holds more water, risking collapse
  3. Standing water on the roof improves insulation, so the overflow limits how much benefit it provides in winter
  4. Parapets prevent water from leaving the roof, so the overflow replaces the primary drains during the winter
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Water weighs about 5.2 psf per inch of depth, so 2 in. of ponding adds about 10.4 psf, roughly 94,000 lb over a 9,000 ft² roof. A secondary drain or scupper set slightly higher acts as the safety valve. Structural engineers also check roofs for rain load. The overflow is a backup, not the normal path, and standing water offers no useful insulation.

Concept Tested: Roof Drainage

See: Roof Drainage

docs.title: 5. A roof sits over a restaurant kitchen and is exposed to grease and chemicals. Which membrane family fits best, and why?
docs.text:
1. EPDM, which is a rubber sheet that dissolves in contact with grease
  2. Built-up roofing, which is held down by stone ballast that absorbs grease
  3. PVC, which is heat-welded and offers good chemical resistance
  4. Modified bitumen, which is applied only by mechanical fasteners and cannot resist chemicals
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A roofing membrane is a continuous, flexible, waterproof sheet or built-up layer that forms the weathering surface of a low-slope roof. EPDM is synthetic rubber with taped seams, TPO is a heat-welded single ply, PVC is heat-welded with chemical resistance, modified bitumen is polymer-reinforced asphalt, and BUR alternates felts and hot bitumen. Most failures occur at seams, penetrations, and edges.

Concept Tested: Roofing Membranes

See: Roofing Membranes

docs.title: 6. An attic has 1,500 ft² of floor area, a ceiling vapor retarder, and vents split between high and low. At the 1:300 ratio, what total net free vent area is required?
docs.text:
1. 720 in²
  2. 360 in²
  3. 5 in²
  4. 1,440 in²
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. At 1:300, the net free area is 1,500 / 300 = 5 ft², which is 5 × 144 = 720 in², split about half at the soffit and half at the ridge. The value 360 in² is only the soffit half, 5 forgets the unit conversion, and 1,440 uses the 1:150 ratio, which applies when the conditions for the lower ratio are not met. Baffles keep an air path open above the insulation.

Concept Tested: Attic Ventilation

See: Attic Ventilation

docs.title: 7. Which statement about shingles is correct?
docs.text:
1. They form a continuous waterproof surface, so the underlayment beneath them is optional on any roof slope
  2. They are laid from the ridge downward so each course sheds water over the joint above it on the roof
  3. They are made of metal panels that run from ridge to eave and are held by concealed clips on the deck
  4. They shed water over overlapping courses and rely on underlayment and flashing, and most leaks start at flashing
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Shingles are small overlapping units laid in courses from the eave upward. Asphalt shingles are a fiberglass mat saturated with asphalt and topped with mineral granules, and they commonly last about 20 to 30 years. A cold-climate system includes a drip edge, self-adhering underlayment at the eaves, underlayment over the deck, and flashing at valleys, chimneys, walls, and penetrations.

Concept Tested: Shingles

See: Shingles

docs.title: 8. Why must metal roof panels be free to slide on their clips, and why do designers add snow guards?
docs.text:
1. Metal absorbs moisture and swells, and snow guards keep the panels from corroding when snow melts
  2. Metal expands and contracts with temperature, and snow can slide off a smooth roof suddenly above walkways
  3. Metal conducts lightning strikes, and snow guards ground the roof to protect the occupants below
  4. Metal is soft and bends under load, and snow guards support the panels against the weight of snow
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A 20 ft steel panel with a 100°F swing changes length by about 0.16 in., and aluminum by about twice as much. Standing seam systems use concealed clips that let panels move and avoid fasteners that loosen and leak, while exposed-fastener panels use screws with sealing washers. Metal roofs commonly last 40 years or more and shed snow readily, which is why snow guards are used.

Concept Tested: Metal Roofing

See: Metal Roofing

docs.title: 9. Why do air sealing and insulation come before ventilation and heating cables when preventing ice dams?
docs.text:
1. Ice dams are caused by cold air entering the attic, so ventilation addresses the cause only last
  2. Ice dams are caused by shingles that are too thin, so extra insulation thickens the roof covering
  3. Ice dams are caused by heat escaping from the house, so remedies must first stop the heat source
  4. Ice dams are caused by rain falling on the eave, so the ice barrier should be installed first
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Heat warms the deck above freezing, snow melts from beneath, and the meltwater refreezes at the cold overhanging eave and builds a dam that backs water up under the shingles. Ventilation only dilutes heat that has already escaped. A self-adhering ice-and-water barrier is a backup that protects the interior but does not stop the dam, and heating cables do nothing about the heat loss.

Concept Tested: Ice Dams

See: Ice Dams

docs.title: 10. What distinguishes an extensive green roof from an intensive one?
docs.text:
1. An extensive roof replaces the waterproofing membrane, while an intensive roof sits above the membrane
  2. An extensive roof uses a thin growing medium of 3 to 6 in. with hardy plants, while an intensive roof uses deeper soil
  3. An extensive roof supports small trees and walkable gardens, while an intensive roof supports only hardy sedums
  4. An extensive roof needs constant irrigation and weighs more, while an intensive roof needs none and is lighter
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A green roof is a roof assembly topped with vegetation in a lightweight growing medium, with filter fabric, a drainage layer, a root barrier, the waterproofing membrane, insulation, and the deck beneath. The green layer sits above the membrane and protects it. A 4 in. medium at 90 pcf adds about 30 psf, so the structure must be designed for it from the start.

Concept Tested: Green Roofs

See: Green Roofs

docs.title: References: Roof Assemblies
docs.text:
1. Roof - Wikipedia - Surveys roof forms, supporting structure, weatherproof layers, insulation, and drainage. Useful for the chapter's opening vocabulary, especially the contrast between flat and pitched roofs and the five core functions every roof performs.

  2. Ice dam (roof) - Wikipedia - Explains how heat escaping into the roof melts snow that refreezes at the cold eave. Covers the mechanism, insulation and ventilation mitigation, removal methods, and why membranes are required at eaves in cold climates.

  3. Green roof - Wikipedia - Describes extensive and intensive vegetated roofs, their stormwater and thermal benefits, costs, and disadvantages. Directly supports the green roof concept and the chapter's warning that planted roofs add significant structural weight.

  4. Fundamentals of Building Construction: Materials and Methods (7th Edition) - Edward Allen and Joseph Iano - Wiley - Allen's hand-drawn, layer-by-layer sketches of roof sections separate steep-slope water-shedding roofs from low-slope membrane roofs. Those sections show students exactly where deck, insulation, membrane, flashing, and drains sit.

  5. Building Science for Building Enclosures (1st Edition) - John Straube and Eric Burnett - Building Science Press - Applies a systematic hierarchy of rain-control strategies, including drainage and drying, to roofs and walls. Its heat, air, and vapor flow analysis explains why cold-climate roofs condense and form ice dams.

  6. BSD-135: Ice Dams - Building Science Corporation - John Straube's digest explains ice dams as a heat-loss problem, not a gutter problem. It recommends an airtight ceiling plane, generous insulation, and then ventilation, matching the chapter's priority order.

  7. Construct Roofs and Attics for Ice Dam Prevention - Building America Solution Center - A Department of Energy guide with construction details for air sealing, insulation depth, baffles, and ventilated over-roofs. Includes step-by-step checklists and cold-climate drawings that builders can follow on a Minnesota job site.

  8. About Attic Ventilation - ENERGY STAR - Explains how balanced soffit intake and ridge exhaust keep an attic cold in winter and relieve heat in summer. Pairs with the chapter's attic ventilation concept and warns against insulation blocking airflow.

  9. Using Green Roofs to Reduce Heat Islands - U.S. Environmental Protection Agency - Describes extensive and intensive green roofs, how evapotranspiration cools the roof surface, and the stormwater benefits. Its cost and comparison sections help students weigh green roofs against cool roofs and conventional membranes.

  10. Types of Roof Membranes for Flat or Low-Slope Roofs - Archtoolbox - Compares built-up roofing, modified bitumen, EPDM, TPO, PVC, spray foam, and liquid-applied membranes. Also covers minimum slope and tapered insulation for positive drainage, supporting the chapter's low-slope roofs and roofing membranes concepts.

docs.title: HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
HVAC, Plumbing, and Fire Protection Systems
Summary
docs.text: The heating, cooling, ventilation, plumbing, and fire protection systems that make a building habitable and safe. It builds on the prerequisite concepts from Chapters 1, 3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 13. After completing this chapter, students will be able to define, explain, and apply the 25 concepts listed below.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 25 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score HVAC Systems 24 Plumbing Systems 11 Fire Protection 11 Ventilation 9 Heating Systems 5 Water Supply 5 Cooling Systems 3 Mechanical Ventilation 3 Drain-Waste-Vent System 3 Ductwork 2 Heat Recovery Ventilator 2 Indoor Air Quality 2 Plumbing Fixtures 2 Radon Mitigation 1 Furnace 1 Boiler 1 Heat Pump 1 Air Conditioning 1 Air Distribution 1 Radiant Heating 1 Heating and Cooling Loads 1 Water Heating 1 Stormwater Management 1 Sprinkler Systems 1 Smoke Control 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Introduction to the Built Environment and Construction Terminology
  • Chapter 3: Forces, Heat, and the Physics of Buildings
  • Chapter 4: Moisture, Air Movement, and Thermal Comfort
  • Chapter 5: Properties of Building Materials
  • Chapter 9: Site Work, Soils, and Groundwater
  • Chapter 10: Foundation Systems
  • Chapter 13: Roof Assemblies

The Systems Behind the Walls

A building that stands up is only half a building. The other half keeps the air fresh, the water running, the temperature comfortable, and a fire from becoming a tragedy. By the end of this chapter you will be able to look at a mechanical room or a ceiling full of pipes and know what each system does and why it is there. Let's build it right!

Chapter 1 described a building as something that supports, separates, serves, and protects. The structure supports, and the enclosure separates. This chapter covers the systems that serve and the system that protects occupants when something goes wrong: heating, ventilating, and air-conditioning (HVAC); plumbing; and fire protection. Together with the electrical systems of Chapters 15 and 16, they are called the building systems, and the engineers who design them must fit them into the space the architect and structural engineer leave behind.

The running example is again the Riverbend Youth Center from Chapter 2, a one-story, roughly 9,000 ft² building in Minneapolis with a multipurpose room and three 600 ft² classrooms. All quantities for Riverbend are illustrative, chosen to make the arithmetic clear.

docs.title: HVAC Systems
docs.text:
An HVAC system (heating, ventilating, and air-conditioning) is the set of equipment, pipes, ducts, and controls that maintains the indoor temperature, humidity, and air quality within a range occupants find comfortable and healthy. The three functions in the name are separate jobs. Heating adds heat when the building loses more than it gains. Cooling removes heat when the building gains more than it loses. Ventilation replaces stale indoor air with outdoor air. Most HVAC systems are built from four parts, which are listed below.

  • A source that produces heat or cooling, such as a furnace, a boiler, a heat pump, or a chiller.
  • A distribution system that carries the heat or cooling to the rooms, either through ducts (air) or pipes (water).
  • Terminal devices that deliver it to the space, such as supply diffusers, radiators, or radiant floor loops.
  • Controls such as thermostats and building automation, which switch the equipment on and off to hold the target conditions.

The key idea is that HVAC is a response to the building. The enclosure designed in Chapters 11 and 12 decides how much heating or cooling the building needs, and the HVAC system supplies it. A better enclosure means smaller equipment, smaller ducts, and a lower energy bill for the life of the building.

Worked example: how much air does a classroom need for heating? A heated space is warmed by supplying air hotter than the room. The heat carried by moving air depends on airflow in cubic feet per minute (cfm) and the temperature difference between supply air and room air. For ordinary air, the sensible heat (heat that changes temperature but not humidity) is

\[ Q = 1.08 \times \text{cfm} \times \Delta T \]

where \( Q \) is in Btu per hour and \( \Delta T \) is in degrees Fahrenheit. The constant 1.08 comes from multiplying air density (0.075 lb/ft³), 60 minutes per hour, and the specific heat of air (0.24 Btu/lb·°F). Suppose one 600 ft² Riverbend classroom has an illustrative design heating load of 8,000 Btu/h and the system supplies air at 100 °F to a room held at 70 °F. Then \( \Delta T = 30 \) °F and

\[ \text{cfm} = \frac{8{,}000}{1.08 \times 30} \approx 247 \text{ cfm} \]

The fresh air this classroom needs for ventilation, calculated later in this chapter, is larger than that. In winter, the system must therefore heat more outdoor air than the walls alone would require, a result that explains why ventilation is such a large part of heating load in a cold climate.

Beau's Tip: Memorize 1.08

The formula \( Q = 1.08 \times \text{cfm} \times \Delta T \) lets you sanity-check any duct or heater in seconds. If a drawing says 1,000 cfm of air is heated by 30 degrees, you should expect about 32,000 Btu/h. If the equipment on the schedule is far from that, ask why.

docs.title: Diagram: Heating Load and Ventilation Explorer
docs.text:
Run Heating Load and Ventilation Explorer Fullscreen

Heating Load and Ventilation Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: hvac-heating-load-ventilation-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Visual: A cutaway of a 600 ft² classroom with wall, window, and roof areas labeled. Arrows show conduction heat loss through each surface and a separate large arrow shows heat lost with ventilation air. A stacked bar to the right shows the total load divided into walls, windows, roof, and ventilation, with a numeric readout in Btu/h and in tons of equivalent capacity.

Controls: Sliders for outdoor temperature (-20 to 40 °F), wall U-factor (0.03 to 0.30), window U-factor (0.15 to 0.60), roof U-factor (0.02 to 0.10), number of occupants (5 to 40), and heat recovery effectiveness (0 to 85 percent). A checkbox labeled "Add heat recovery ventilator" enables the last slider. A button labeled "Reset to Minneapolis design day" restores the default values.

Interactions: Changing any slider updates the arrows, the stacked bar, and the readouts immediately. Hovering over any arrow or bar segment shows a tooltip with the calculation (for example, "Walls: U x A x delta T = 0.05 x 400 x 70 = 1,400 Btu/h"). The status line states which component dominates at the current settings.

Colors: Walls in brown, windows in light blue, roof in gray, ventilation in orange. Segments also carry text labels for readability without color.

Responsive design: The canvas follows the container width and redraws on window resize. Height is 480 px on wide screens.

Implementation: p5.js with updateCanvasSize() as the first statement in setup(), built-in createSlider, createCheckbox, and createButton controls, created before any positioning function runs.

docs.title: Heating and Cooling Loads
docs.text:
The heating and cooling loads are the rates, in Btu per hour, at which heat must be added to or removed from a building to hold the indoor design conditions under the worst expected outdoor conditions. Equipment is sized from loads, never the other way around. A heating load has two main parts. Conduction loss is heat passing through the enclosure, which Chapter 3 gave as \( Q = U \times A \times \Delta T \). Infiltration and ventilation loss is heat carried away by air that leaks out or is deliberately exhausted and replaced.

A cooling load adds the heat from sunlight through windows, from occupants, lights, and equipment (internal gains), and the moisture that must be removed to control humidity. Cooling capacity is commonly stated in tons, where one ton equals 12,000 Btu/h. Methods such as ACCA Manual J for houses and ASHRAE procedures for larger buildings turn drawings into loads.

As a quick example, 3,000 ft² of net exterior wall at an illustrative U-factor of 0.05 Btu/h·ft²·°F, with a 70 °F difference between 70 °F indoors and 0 °F outdoors, loses \( 0.05 \times 3{,}000 \times 70 = 10{,}500 \) Btu/h.

Watch Out: Bigger Is Not Safer

Adding a "safety factor" to equipment size is a common instinct, and it backfires. An oversized air conditioner cools the room quickly, shuts off, and never runs long enough to remove humidity, so the space feels clammy. Calculate the load first and select equipment close to it.

docs.title: Heating Systems
docs.text:
A heating system is the source and distribution equipment that adds heat to a building when outdoor conditions would otherwise let it cool below comfort. Minnesota buildings spend most of their energy on heating, so this choice has a long financial tail. Heating systems differ in how they make heat, which fuel or energy source they use, and how they deliver heat to the rooms.

Efficiency is stated differently for each type. Combustion equipment is rated by AFUE (annual fuel utilization efficiency), the fraction of fuel energy that becomes useful heat over a season. A heat pump is rated by its coefficient of performance (COP), the ratio of heat delivered to electrical energy used. A COP of 3 means three units of heat for each unit of electricity, which is possible because the heat pump moves heat that already exists rather than creating it.

Worked example: input energy for 80,000 Btu/h of heat. Suppose a building needs 80,000 Btu/h of heat delivered to the rooms. An 80 percent AFUE furnace needs fuel input of \( 80{,}000/0.80 = 100{,}000 \) Btu/h. A 95 percent condensing furnace needs \( 80{,}000/0.95 \approx 84{,}200 \) Btu/h. To compare with electricity, convert using 1 kW = 3,412 Btu/h, so 80,000 Btu/h is \( 80{,}000/3{,}412 \approx 23.4 \) kW of heat. Electric resistance heating converts each kilowatt of electricity into one kilowatt of heat, so it draws 23.4 kW. A heat pump at COP 3 draws \( 23.4/3 \approx 7.8 \) kW, and at a colder-weather COP of 2 it draws about 11.7 kW. The heat pump uses a third to a half as much electricity because it moves heat, but its COP falls as the outdoor temperature falls, which is why cold-climate models and sizing matter in Minnesota.

The table below summarizes the four main heating types that the following subsections define.

Type Heat source Delivers heat by Typical cold-climate note Furnace Combustion or electric element Warm air through ducts Common in houses and small buildings Boiler Combustion or electric element Hot water or steam through pipes Pairs with radiators or radiant floors Heat pump Electricity moving heat Warm air or water Use models rated for low outdoor temperatures Radiant system Hot water or electric elements Warm surfaces Comfortable at lower air temperatures

Interactions: Moving the sliders updates the bars and the COP marker on the curve. Hovering over any bar shows the input energy, the efficiency used, and a one-sentence explanation of how the system makes heat. A status line reports when the heat pump input exceeds the 95 percent furnace input for the selected temperature, with the message "Heat pump COP has fallen below the break-even point for equal energy."
