docs.title: Renovation and Retrofit
docs.text:
Renovation is the work of altering, repairing, or upgrading an existing building to extend its life or improve its performance, and a retrofit is the addition of new components or systems to an existing building to improve a specific performance, such as energy use, safety, or accessibility. A renovation might replace a worn roof and refinish interiors, while an energy retrofit adds attic insulation, air sealing, new windows, and a heat pump. Chapter 19's strategies are often applied as retrofits, since a large share of the buildings that will be in use for decades already stand.

Existing buildings bring constraints that new ones do not. The condition of hidden structure and materials is uncertain, which makes the assessment step above essential. Older buildings may contain hazardous materials such as asbestos and lead paint, which require licensed handling. The building code treats existing buildings through provisions for alterations, with requirements that scale with the extent of the work, so the team confirms with the building official, as Chapter 17 taught, which provisions apply.

docs.title: Adaptive Reuse
docs.text:
Adaptive reuse is the conversion of an existing building to a use other than the one for which it was built, such as turning a warehouse into apartments or a factory into offices. Minneapolis has many examples, including former flour mills and warehouses that now serve as housing, offices, and museums. Reuse saves the embodied carbon of the existing structure (Chapter 20), preserves a community's character, and may qualify for historic preservation incentives.

The challenge is that a new use means new code requirements. A change from warehouse to residential changes the occupancy classification and so triggers the requirements of Chapter 18: fire separations, egress, and sprinklers. The floors may not carry the new loads, the windows and walls may not meet the energy code, and the building may need accessibility upgrades. A feasibility study tests the structure, the code path, and the cost before the owner commits.

docs.title: Deconstruction
docs.text:
Deconstruction is the careful, selective dismantling of a building, in roughly the reverse order of its construction, to recover materials for reuse and recycling instead of demolishing it and sending the debris to a landfill. It puts the salvage strategies of Chapter 20 into practice at the end of a building's life. Crews remove fixtures, doors, windows, flooring, and structural timber, and sort the materials for resale, donation, or recycling.

Deconstruction takes longer and more labor than demolition, so it competes on avoided disposal costs, the resale value of the materials, and sometimes tax benefits for donations. It also needs a survey for hazardous materials before work begins. The approach works best when a building was designed for it, with mechanical fasteners and accessible connections, so designers who think about reuse at the start make deconstruction easier at the end.

docs.title: Building Resilience
docs.text:
Building resilience is the ability of a building to withstand, adapt to, and recover quickly from disruptive events, such as severe storms, flooding, extreme heat or cold, and loss of power or water. It treats rare but severe events as design inputs, in the same way the structural chapters treated snow and wind loads. A related idea is passive survivability: how long a building stays livable without power or fuel. In a Minnesota January, a well-insulated and airtight building loses heat slowly and gives occupants more time before pipes freeze.

Resilient design adds margin and recovery paths. Examples include placing equipment above flood levels, specifying durable enclosures, providing emergency power for critical functions, as Chapter 18 described, using shading and insulation to limit temperature swings, and arranging systems so that the failure of one does not disable the others. Resilience connects durability, energy efficiency, and life safety, because the buildings that cope best with disruption are those that were built well in all three.

You Finished the Whole Journey

You can now diagnose a leak from stain to flashing, estimate a component's service life and life-cycle cost, assess a building with a condition index, and plan its reuse. Across this book, you also learned to trace a load path, read a wall section, apply the code, estimate heat loss, and weigh materials with life-cycle data. That makes you a builder who can justify a decision with evidence, so go build it right!

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Durability is performance over time in a specific environment, and it is designed by identifying each agent of degradation, giving each a defense, and noting where the defense is most likely to fail.
  • Service life depends on the component, the environment, the quality of the work, and the maintenance, and the factor method shows which of these decisions most affects the estimate.
  • Preventive maintenance costs far less than the damage it prevents, and life-cycle cost, discounted to present value, shows that the cheapest first cost is often not the cheapest to own.
  • Failures rarely have a single cause. They are chains of design, material, construction, maintenance, environment, and use conditions, and water is involved in most enclosure failures.
  • Water intrusion, freeze-thaw damage, rot, mold, and efflorescence all follow from moisture, while cracking, settlement, and fire damage come from movement, loads, and heat.
  • Assessment describes the condition of a building, and forensics finds the cause of a failure by testing competing hypotheses against evidence.
  • Renovation, retrofit, adaptive reuse, and deconstruction extend a building's value and keep embodied carbon and materials in use.
  • Resilient buildings combine durability, efficiency, and life-safety systems so that they can withstand and recover from disruption, which is the sum of what this book has taught: loads, heat, moisture, materials, systems, codes, and sustainability working together in one well-built building.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Durability, Maintenance, and Building Failure
docs.text: Test your understanding of the concepts in this chapter with these review questions, one for each of the 20 concepts covered.

docs.title: 1. Why is it incorrect to call a material durable in general?
docs.text:
1. Durability is the same as strength, so any strong material is durable in every environment and every climate zone
  2. Durability depends only on cost, so an expensive material is durable in any environment and under any exposure conditions
  3. Durability applies only to metals and coatings, so other materials cannot be described as durable in any climate
  4. Durability is performance in a specific environment, so brick lasting centuries in a dry climate may crumble in freeze-thaw
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Durability is the ability to keep performing a required function in the service environment with only planned maintenance. It is not the same as strength, since a strong material can still decay if it stays wet, and it has a cost dimension because a material that needs frequent expensive repair is not durable in any useful sense. Water is the most important agent of degradation, followed by temperature swings, sunlight, chemicals, organisms, wear, and fire.

Concept Tested: Durability

See: Durability

docs.title: 2. A stain on a ceiling traces back to a missing flashing detail on the drawings. What does this illustrate about how building failures occur?
docs.text:
1. Failures usually result from a chain of conditions, so a stain may begin on a drawing, and breaking any link prevents loss
  2. Failures have a single cause, which is always found at the location of the visible symptom in the building
  3. Failures occur only through collapse of the structure, so a stain on a ceiling is not a failure of any kind
  4. Failures are caused by environmental loads alone, so the drawings and the construction cannot contribute to them
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Building failure is the condition in which a building or part no longer meets its required performance, from rare collapse to common serviceability failures such as leaks, cracks, and mold. The cause categories are design, materials, construction, maintenance, environment, and use. In the flashing example, the detail was omitted, installers worked from the drawings, wind-driven rain entered the wall, and decay followed over several years.

Concept Tested: Building Failure

See: Building Failure

docs.title: 3. Why does a forensic investigator propose several competing hypotheses and protect the evidence before repairs begin?
docs.text:
1. Only one hypothesis can be tested at a time, so the investigator must pick the cheapest one to test first
  2. The evidence is created by the repair itself, so repairs should be completed before any investigation can begin
  3. Each hypothesis is tested against the evidence, and repairing the failed part first could destroy evidence of the cause
  4. Hypotheses are written for legal reasons only, so the testing of each one against the evidence is optional
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Building forensics investigates what happened, why, and who or what was responsible, unlike a building assessment, which describes condition. The steps are to define the problem and protect the evidence, collect facts, propose competing hypotheses, test each by observation, sampling, laboratory work, analysis, or a water test, and write a conclusion. In the Riverbend example, a bottom-up water test leaked only at the window head.

Concept Tested: Building Forensics

See: Building Forensics

docs.title: 4. A component has a reference service life of 30 years. Using the factor method, the design factor is 0.9, outdoor environment 0.8, and maintenance 1.1, with all other factors 1.0. What is the estimated service life?
docs.text:
1. About 21.6 years
  2. About 23.8 years
  3. About 30 years
  4. About 33 years
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The factor method multiplies the reference life by every factor: 30 × 0.9 × 0.8 × 1.1 ≈ 23.8 years. Leaving out the maintenance factor gives 21.6, and ignoring all factors returns the reference life. Factors below 1.0 shorten life and above 1.0 lengthen it. The result shows which decisions move the number, such as improving drainage details or skipping maintenance, and it lets the owner schedule a replacement fund.

Concept Tested: Service Life

See: Service Life

docs.title: 5. A condition assessment finds $450,000 of needed repairs, and the replacement value is $6,000,000. What is the facility condition index, and how is it commonly described?
docs.text:
1. 7.5 percent, commonly described as fair
  2. 7.5 percent, commonly described as good
  3. 13.3 percent, commonly described as poor
  4. 0.75 percent, commonly described as good
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The FCI equals the cost of needed repairs divided by current replacement value: 450,000 / 6,000,000 = 0.075, or 7.5 percent. Owners commonly describe about 5 percent or less as good, 5 to 10 percent as fair, and above that as poor, though bands differ among organizations. Assessments combine record review, interviews, visual walk-throughs, non-destructive tools such as moisture meters and infrared cameras, and destructive investigation where needed.

Concept Tested: Building Assessment

See: Building Assessment

docs.title: 6. What are the four strategies for controlling water intrusion, sometimes called the four Ds?
docs.text:
1. Design, demolish, dehumidify, and discard the wet materials
  2. Dig, dam, dilute, and divert groundwater away
  3. Detect, document, defer, and dispute claims
  4. Deflect, drain, dry, and use durable materials
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Water intrusion is the unwanted entry of liquid water and the most common cause of enclosure failures. Sources include rain driven through gaps, roof leaks, ice dams, groundwater, plumbing leaks, and capillary rise. Deflecting uses overhangs, flashings, and slopes; draining uses a drainage plane; drying lets vapor escape; and durable materials are used where wetting is unavoidable. Finding the point of entry can be difficult.

Concept Tested: Water Intrusion

See: Water Intrusion

docs.title: 7. How does a retrofit differ from a renovation, and what makes existing buildings harder to work on than new ones?
docs.text:
1. A retrofit replaces the entire building with a new one, while existing buildings have no hidden conditions at all
  2. A retrofit adds new components to improve specific performance, while hidden conditions and hazardous materials add uncertainty
  3. A retrofit applies only to new buildings under construction, while existing buildings are exempt from the code
  4. A retrofit removes all hazardous materials from a building, while a renovation never encounters any of them
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A renovation alters, repairs, or upgrades a building to extend its life or improve performance, while a retrofit adds new components, such as attic insulation, air sealing, new windows, and a heat pump, to improve energy, safety, or accessibility. Codes treat existing buildings through alteration provisions with requirements that scale with the extent of the work, so the team confirms with the building official.

Concept Tested: Renovation and Retrofit

See: Renovation and Retrofit

docs.title: 8. Vibration monitoring of a motor, which triggers servicing when measurements show a failure approaching, is an example of which maintenance style?
docs.text:
1. Reactive maintenance
  2. Preventive maintenance
  3. Predictive maintenance
  4. Deferred maintenance
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Maintenance has three styles. Reactive maintenance fixes something after it fails, costs nothing until the failure, but failures occur at the worst times and can damage other parts. Preventive maintenance services components on a schedule to avoid failure. Predictive maintenance services when measurements show a failure approaching. A well-run building uses all three, and the owner budgets for them at the outset.

Concept Tested: Building Maintenance

See: Building Maintenance

docs.title: 9. Option 1 costs $6 per ft² and lasts 15 years, and Option 2 costs $12 per ft² and lasts 30 years. Both total $24 per ft² undiscounted over 60 years. At a 3 percent discount rate, which has the lower present value?
docs.text:
1. Option 2, because it lasts longer and so always has the lower present value at any discount rate
  2. Option 1, because it spreads its spending over time and later costs are worth less today
  3. They tie, because discounting affects both options equally when the totals are the same undiscounted
  4. Neither can be determined without knowing the initial cost of the maintenance over the full study period
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Life-cycle cost converts future costs to present value with PV = cost / (1 + r)ⁿ. Option 1 is installed in years 0, 15, 30, and 45, giving about 6 + 3.85 + 2.47 + 1.59 ≈ $13.91 per ft². Option 2 is installed in years 0 and 30, giving 12 + 4.94 ≈ $16.94. The discount rate matters because a larger first cost is not discounted at all.

Concept Tested: Life-Cycle Cost

See: Life-Cycle Cost

docs.title: 10. What is passive survivability, and why does it matter in a Minnesota January?
docs.text:
1. How long a building's roof lasts without any maintenance, and a snow-covered roof is stronger because of the added weight
  2. How quickly occupants can evacuate a building in a fire, and a cold building has fewer exits that can be used
  3. How long a generator can run on one tank of fuel, and a cold building uses less fuel while it is running
  4. How long a building stays livable without power or fuel, and an insulated, airtight building loses heat slowly, delaying frozen pipes
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Building resilience is the ability to withstand, adapt to, and recover quickly from disruptive events, such as severe storms, flooding, extreme heat or cold, and loss of power or water. It treats rare severe events as design inputs. Examples include placing equipment above flood levels, providing emergency power for critical functions, using shading and insulation to limit temperature swings, and arranging systems so one failure does not disable the others.

Concept Tested: Building Resilience

See: Building Resilience

docs.title: 11. Why is a preventive task such as clearing gutters in spring and fall considered economical?
docs.text:
1. A small planned task costs far less than the water damage that follows if it is neglected
  2. It costs more than the repairs it avoids, but it is required by the building code in every jurisdiction
  3. It replaces the need for flashing, so the roof can be built more cheaply by omitting the metal flashings
  4. It prevents all failures from ever occurring, so no other kind of maintenance is needed in the building
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Preventive maintenance is scheduled servicing and inspection at set intervals to keep components working and to find small problems before they become large ones. The schedule follows manufacturer recommendations, building exposure, and history. A typical schedule includes roof, flashing, and drain inspections twice a year, sealant checks yearly, HVAC filter replacement often quarterly, and testing emergency lights and the fire alarm.

Concept Tested: Preventive Maintenance

See: Preventive Maintenance

docs.title: 12. A 50 ft (600 in.) concrete wall with α = 5.5 × 10⁻⁶ per °F experiences a 100°F seasonal temperature swing. How much does its length change if it is free to move?
docs.text:
1. About 0.033 in.
  2. About 3.3 in.
  3. About 0.33 in.
  4. About 0.66 in.
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Thermal movement follows ΔL = α L ΔT = 5.5 × 10⁻⁶ × 600 × 100 = 0.33 in. Using 0.66 in. would apply to a 100 ft wall, and the others are decimal slips. This explains why designers place control joints and expansion joints, which give a material a planned place to move. A wall without joints will find its own place to crack, and width, direction, and pattern point to the cause.

Concept Tested: Cracking

See: Cracking

docs.title: 13. Two columns 30 ft (360 in.) apart settle differently by 0.5 in. Compared with a rule-of-thumb limit of 1/500 (0.0020), what is the angular distortion and what does it suggest?
docs.text:
1. About 0.0014, above the limit of 0.0020, so cracking is expected in the walls
  2. About 0.72, far above the limit, so collapse of the frame is expected
  3. About 0.0028, above the limit of 0.0020, so cracking is expected in the walls
  4. About 0.0014, below the limit, so cracking is not expected from the rule of thumb
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Angular distortion is differential settlement divided by the distance between the points: 0.5 / 360 ≈ 0.0014, or about 1/720, which is below 1/500. The rule of thumb is not a code limit, and the foundation engineer designs to actual criteria. Uniform settlement is usually harmless, while differential settlement distorts the frame and causes cracks, sticking doors, and sloping floors.

Concept Tested: Settlement

See: Settlement

docs.title: 14. Why does dry wood last for centuries even though the wood is a food source for decay fungi?
docs.text:
1. Fungi need only moisture to grow, and wood always contains too little of it unless it is submerged in water
  2. Fungi need only a food source, and dry wood is not food for them because its cell walls are sealed
  3. Fungi need food, moisture above about 20 percent, oxygen, and moderate temperature at once, and removing one stops growth
  4. Fungi cannot live in wood above 40°F, so dry wood is always too cold for the fungi to establish growth
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Decay fungi turn wood into a crumbly, weak mass, and wood-boring insects such as carpenter ants and termites also damage wet wood. The remedies follow from the four needs: keep wood dry through detailing, separate it from soil and concrete, use preservative-treated or naturally durable wood where wetting is expected, and provide a drying path. The steel counterpart is corrosion.

Concept Tested: Rot and Decay

See: Rot and Decay

docs.title: 15. What should be done first when mold is found growing on a damp wall?
docs.text:
1. Correct the moisture source, then dry the area and remove or clean the affected materials
  2. Paint over the mold so that the spores cannot spread to other surfaces in the building
  3. Bleach the surface and leave the moisture source in place until the next season
  4. Seal the area with an air-tight membrane until it dries out by itself over a long time
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Mold is a fungus that grows on damp organic surfaces, such as the paper facing on gypsum board, dust, or wood, and it can start within a couple of days of a material becoming wet. Condensation on a cold surface, a leak, or a flood can supply the moisture. Wiping a stain without fixing the leak only hides the problem, and the damage keeps growing out of sight.

Concept Tested: Mold

See: Mold

docs.title: 16. A white powdery band appears along the base of a brick wall. Brushing removes it, but it returns. What does this indicate?
docs.text:
1. Mold is growing on the brick surface, so the wall must be treated with a fungicide and then sealed again
  2. Water is moving through the wall and carrying salts to the surface, so a leak or drainage problem should be investigated
  3. The brick is deteriorating from sunlight, so it must be coated with a protective sealer on all of its faces
  4. The salts come only from the cleaning product used on the wall, so no investigation of the wall is needed
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Efflorescence forms when water dissolves soluble salts and carries them to the surface, where the water evaporates and leaves the salts behind. It is not mold and does not damage the material by itself. It is a signal that water is passing through the wall. Washing removes the deposit but it returns if the water source remains.

Concept Tested: Efflorescence

See: Efflorescence

docs.title: 17. Why is air-entrained concrete the standard defense against freeze-thaw damage for exterior concrete in cold climates?
docs.text:
1. Microscopic bubbles give freezing water, which expands about 9 percent, room to expand without cracking the concrete
  2. Microscopic bubbles stop all water from ever entering the concrete, so that freezing never occurs inside it
  3. Microscopic bubbles increase the compressive strength of the concrete to well above 10,000 psi in all cases
  4. Microscopic bubbles make deicing salts harmless, so the salts can be used freely on young concrete surfaces
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Freeze-thaw damage is the cracking, flaking, and crumbling of porous materials such as concrete, brick, and stone caused by water freezing inside them. It appears as spalling and as scaling, which deicing salts make worse. A low water-to-cement ratio also makes concrete less permeable, brick is selected for freeze-thaw resistance, and flashings, copings, and drainage keep water out of masonry.

Concept Tested: Freeze-Thaw Damage

See: Freeze-Thaw Damage

docs.title: 18. After a fire, a steel beam looks sound and unwarped. What should happen before the building is reoccupied?
docs.text:
1. The beam should be accepted as sound, because steel is a noncombustible material that cannot be harmed by heat
  2. A structural engineer should assess every damaged member, because a member can look sound yet have lost strength
  3. The beam should be painted and reoccupied, because the damage from the fire is only cosmetic in appearance
  4. The beam should be tested only if it is wood, because only wood chars and loses section in a fire
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Fire damage is the harm done by heat, flame, smoke, and the water used to extinguish a fire. Steel loses roughly half its strength near 1,100°F, concrete loses strength and may spall, and wood chars on the surface while the core remains sound. Smoke and soot spread beyond the burned area, and firefighting water often causes more widespread damage than the flames. Repairs trigger permits and inspections.

Concept Tested: Fire Damage

See: Fire Damage

docs.title: 19. Why does converting a warehouse into apartments often trigger major code upgrades?
docs.text:
1. A new use never changes the code requirements, because the building already exists and was previously approved
  2. A new use removes the need for a certificate of occupancy, because the structure has already been inspected
  3. A new use changes the occupancy classification, bringing new requirements for fire separations, egress, and sprinklers
  4. A new use applies only to the roof and has no effect on any of the other parts of the building
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Adaptive reuse is the conversion of an existing building to a use other than the one for which it was built, such as a flour mill that becomes housing or a museum. It saves the embodied carbon of the existing structure, preserves a community's character, and may qualify for historic preservation incentives. A feasibility study tests the structure, the code path, and the cost before the owner commits.

Concept Tested: Adaptive Reuse

See: Adaptive Reuse

docs.title: 20. How does deconstruction differ from demolition, and what makes it competitive?
docs.text:
1. Fast, mechanical destruction of the building so the debris can be hauled away, competing through lower labor cost
  2. Conversion of a building to a new use while keeping the structure, competing through historic preservation incentives
  3. Installation of new systems in an existing building to improve its performance, competing through energy savings
  4. Careful, selective dismantling to recover materials for reuse, competing through avoided disposal costs and resale value
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Deconstruction proceeds in roughly the reverse order of construction, with crews removing fixtures, doors, windows, flooring, and structural timber and sorting them for resale, donation, or recycling. It takes more labor than demolition and needs a hazardous-material survey before work. It works best when a building was designed for it, with mechanical fasteners and accessible connections, which is why designers who think about reuse at the start make it easier.

Concept Tested: Deconstruction

See: Deconstruction

docs.title: References: Durability, Maintenance, and Building Failure
docs.text:
1. Forensic engineering - Wikipedia - Surveys how investigators determine causes of failures in materials and structures, from the 1847 Dee bridge collapse to modern microscopy and photogrammetry. Directly supports the chapter's building forensics and building failure concepts.

  2. Adaptive reuse - Wikipedia - Explains converting existing buildings to new uses, with benefits, challenges, methodology, and global examples. Relevant to the chapter's adaptive reuse and renovation concepts, including embodied-energy and heritage arguments for keeping old structures.

  3. Frost weathering - Wikipedia - Explains how freezing water fractures porous material through ice segregation and volumetric expansion, including the roughly nine percent expansion of ice. Gives the physical mechanism behind the chapter's freeze-thaw damage in Minnesota masonry and concrete.

  4. How Buildings Learn: What Happens After They're Built (First Edition) - Stewart Brand - Viking Press - Brand popularized "shearing layers" (site, structure, skin, services, space plan, stuff), adapting Frank Duffy's idea. Each layer changes at its own pace, a clear lens for service life, maintenance, and adaptive reuse.

  5. Why Buildings Fall Down: How Structures Fail (First Edition) - Matthys Levy and Mario Salvadori - W. W. Norton - Levy and Salvadori explain structural failures through readable case studies and everyday analogies, without heavy mathematics. Their stories of settlement, decay, and fire illustrate the chapter's building failure and forensics concepts.

  6. RR-0103: Water Management - Building Science Corporation, Joseph Lstiburek - Presents the principle of shedding water by layering materials downward and outward, from site grading through roofs, walls, and openings. A concise guide to preventing water intrusion, rot, and mold.

  7. A Brief Guide to Mold, Moisture and Your Home - U.S. Environmental Protection Agency - Explains that controlling moisture is the key to preventing mold, with cleanup guidance and moisture-control steps. Supports the chapter's mold, water intrusion, and preventive maintenance topics with practical homeowner-level detail.

  8. Preservation Brief 39: Holding the Line: Controlling Unwanted Moisture in Historic Buildings - National Park Service - Diagnoses moisture sources in older buildings and describes signs such as efflorescence, eroding surfaces, and freeze-thaw spalling. Directly relevant to the chapter's efflorescence, freeze-thaw, and building assessment concepts.

  9. Best Practices for Reducing, Reusing, and Recycling Construction and Demolition Materials - U.S. Environmental Protection Agency - Covers design for disassembly and deconstruction as alternatives to demolition, including which building types suit salvage and how to handle hazards like asbestos and lead. Supports the chapter's deconstruction concept.

  10. Preservation Briefs - National Park Service Technical Preservation Services - Index of 50-plus technical guides on masonry, wood, roofing, and mechanical systems in older buildings, plus guidance on building codes for existing buildings. A practical resource for the chapter's renovation, retrofit, and adaptive reuse topics.

docs.title: Learning Graph for The Science of the Built Environment
docs.text:
Open Learning Graph Viewer Fullscreen

This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text:
We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

Concepts 381 through 448 were added later from the appendices on rapidly evolving technologies. They form their own category and depend on concepts from the chapters.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Course Description Quality Assessment
docs.text:
This report rates the overall quality of the course description for the purpose of generating a learning graph.

  • Course description fields and content depth analysis
  • Validates course description has sufficient depth for generating 300-600 concepts
  • Compares course description against similar courses
  • Identifies content gaps and strengths
  • Suggests areas of improvement Vew the Course Description Quality Assessment

docs.title: Learning Graph Quality Validation
docs.text:
This report gives you an overall assessment of the quality of the learning graph. It uses graph algorithms to look for specific quality patterns in the graph.

  • Graph structure validation - all concepts are connected
  • DAG validation (no cycles detected)
  • Foundational concepts: 6 entry points
  • Indegree distribution analysis
  • Longest dependency chains
  • Connectivity: percent of nodes connected to the main cluster

View the Learning Graph Quality Validation

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
In order to see patterns in the learning graph, it is useful to assign colors to each concept based on the concept type. We use generative AI to create about a dozen categories for our concepts and then place each concept into a single primary classifier.

  • A concept classifier taxonomy with approximately 12 categories (+/- 1 or 2)
  • Category organization - foundational elements first, course capstone project ideas last
  • Balanced categories (3.5% - 15% each)
  • All categories under 30% threshold
  • Pedagogical flow recommendations
  • Clear 3-5 letter abbreviations for use in CSV file
  • A Miscellaneous (MOSC) category is sometimes added View the Concept Taxonomy

docs.title: Taxonomy Distribution
docs.text:
This reports shows how many concepts fit into each category of the taxonomy. Our goal is a somewhat balanced taxonomy where each category holds an equal number of concepts. We also don't want any category to contain over 30% of our concepts.

  • Statistical breakdown
  • Detailed concept listing by category
  • Visual distribution table
  • Balance verification

View the Taxonomy Distribution Report

docs.title: Checklist for every sim
docs.text:
Work through these in each sim, in a wide window (fullscreen landscape) and again at 640 px wide, which is the minimum test width unless the author says otherwise. 640 px is a realistic column for a sim in an iframe inside the textbook. The book targets students on standard laptops, so phone widths are not a goal in these early phases; below 640 px the layout is best-effort (control rows crowd and labels can overlap), and that is not a bug to report.

  • [ ] It loads with no blank canvas, and the browser console shows no errors.
  • [ ] Click each numbered label and each layer. The panel under the drawing explains what it is, why it is there, and what happens if it fails.
  • [ ] Every layer box is ticked when the sim loads. Untick each one with Remove the layer, retick it, then repeat with Punch a hole. Dots that were stopped should now pass, and the status line should change. Reset ticks them all again.
  • [ ] Slide Explode. Layers separate and the flows still cross the gaps.
  • [ ] Untick and retick each flow checkbox.
  • [ ] Tick Temperature (slab and wall only) and move its slider.
  • [ ] Tick Line art. The drawing should become black and white and print cleanly.
  • [ ] Legend is on when the sim loads. The hatch swatches match the layers drawn. Untick it and the legend disappears; Reset turns it back on.
  • [ ] Switch the unit selector to SI. Thickness, R-value, and temperature should change units.
  • [ ] Tick Quiz me. Layer names turn into numbers and a question appears. Click a wrong layer (it outlines red and the right one green), press Next question, then click a right layer. The score should read like 1 / 2. Untick Quiz me to return.
  • [ ] Select a layer. The bottom of the panel shows its typical materials and its MasterFormat section.
  • [ ] Press Reset. Everything returns to the starting state.
  • [ ] No callout text overlaps another, runs off the canvas, or is crossed by a leader line.

docs.title: What to try in each sim
1. Heated Slab on Grade
docs.text:
Side A is the heated room, side B is the ground. Layers run top to bottom: slab, rigid foam, vapor retarder, sand cushion, compacted gravel, subgrade soil.

  • Intact: ground water should read as stopped at the gravel, vapor as stopped at the retarder, and heat as slowed at the foam.
  • Untick the vapor retarder: some vapor should now get through, slowed by the foam.
  • Untick the foam: heat should reach the ground.
  • Untick the gravel alone: water should still be stopped, now at the retarder. Untick gravel and retarder together and water should reach the slab.
  • Temperature on: the profile should run from the warm room (80 °F start) down to 40 °F ground, with most of the drop across the foam. The slider caption should name "Heated room" and "ground".

Please confirm with the chapter:

  1. The retarder is drawn under the foam. Many details put it directly under the slab, above the foam. Which order should the book teach?
  2. Chapter 10's slab list does not mention foam, a sand cushion, or in-slab tubing, so the chapter text needs a sentence or two to match.
  3. Assumed values: sand R-0.2, gravel R-0.4, soil R-1, surface films 0, ground at 40 °F.

docs.title: 2. Fire-Rated Partition Explorer
docs.text:
Side A is the fire side, side B the far side. Layers: two boards, a steel-stud cavity with mineral wool, then two boards. No temperature profile on purpose, because a steady-state profile would mislead for a fire.

  • Intact: flame should be stopped at the first board.
  • Remove boards one at a time: the stop point should move inward. Remove all four and flame should reach the far side.
  • Remove the mineral wool: heat and sound should now get through more than before. (The engine was changed after the first test round so slowing layers add up. Please check that this is now visible.)
  • Punch a hole in a board: flame should pass only through the hole.

Please confirm:

  1. The "one-hour" label. Two layers of Type X board on each side is described by the test agents as usually heavier than a one-hour design (one layer per side is the common one-hour build). Should the sim show the one-layer wall, or be relabeled?
  2. The 5/8 in boards, 3 5/8 in studs, and noncombustible wool are illustrative. Chapter 18 gives no layer list for this partition.
  3. The dots show which layers stop which flows, not a rating or a time.

docs.title: 3. Brick Veneer Rainscreen Wall
docs.text:
Side A is outside, side B the framed wall. Layers: brick veneer, air gap, weather barrier, taped sheathing.

  • Intact: rain should be slowed at the brick and stopped at the weather barrier. Air should be stopped at the sheathing.
  • Remove the weather barrier: rain should reach the sheathing (slowed at the brick first).
  • Remove or puncture the sheathing: air should now reach the framed wall.
  • Remove the air gap: only the text changes. The engine cannot draw drainage.

Please confirm:

  1. Overlap. Chapter 12 already has cladding-rainscreen-water-path-explorer (and chapter 11 has control-layer-wall-section-explorer). Keep this as a second sim, or add air leakage to the existing one?
  2. Title. The chapter calls brick veneer a "drained cavity" and keeps "rainscreen" for the vented, pressure-equalized wall. This sim does not model pressure equalization.
  3. The weather barrier is credited with stopping water only. Some real barriers are also air barriers.

docs.title: 4. Example: Cold-Climate Exterior Wall
docs.text:
Eight layers from siding to gypsum, with the temperature profile and a 37 °F dew point.

  • Untick the rigid foam with Temperature on: the sheathing outline should turn red if its temperature falls below the dew point. Try outdoor temperatures from -20 °F to 40 °F.
  • Punch a hole in the weather-resistive barrier: rain should reach the sheathing only through the hole.
  • Remove the vapor retarder: vapor from the inside should pass further into the wall.
  • Compare with the hand-built control-layer-wall-section-explorer and decide whether the engine version could replace it.

docs.title: 5. Example: Low-Slope Warm Roof
docs.text:
Vertical stack from the sky down to the room: ballast, membrane, insulation, vapor retarder, steel deck.

  • Puncture the membrane: rain should pass only through the hole.
  • Remove the vapor retarder: vapor from the room should rise into the insulation.
  • Check the label column on the right: names and the "stops: ..." lines should not overlap.

docs.title: Also to test: Structural Span Ranges
docs.text:
This one comes from the new range-explorer skill, not the layered-assembly engine. Run fullscreen or open its lesson page.

  • [ ] It loads with the red marker at 24 ft and a headline like "Span 24 ft: 10 of 13 options reach it".
  • [ ] Drag the red marker in the chart, and move the slider. Both move the same marker.
  • [ ] Rows whose bar contains the marker are dark and bold; the rest fade. Light bar is possible, dark bar is typical.
  • [ ] Put the marker on 40 ft (the Riverbend girder line). Wood joists and flat plate slabs should fade; glulam, steel beams, and trusses should stay dark.
  • [ ] Click a row name: the panel shows what it is, why choose it, and what to watch out for. Click it again to clear.
  • [ ] Untick Wood, Steel, or Concrete; change Sort; switch IP to SI and watch the numbers and axis change.
  • [ ] The span ranges are my illustrative values, not the book's. Tell me which ones to change.

docs.title: Known limits of the engine
docs.text:
• Drainage and time cannot be drawn. A layer that works by draining (a rainscreen gap) or by time (a fire rating) shows its effect in the text only.
  • The temperature profile is steady-state, one-dimensional, and ignores thermal bridging and moisture.
  • The dots are schematic. They show which layers stop or slow a flow, not rates.
  • Up to 12 layers and 5 flows per sim.
  • Designed for laptop screens and iframe columns of 640 px and up. Narrower screens still draw, but the controls crowd.

docs.title: Where the files are
docs.text: Each sim is a folder under docs/sims/<sim-id>/ with main.html, <sim-id>.js (the layer data), layered-assembly-engine.js (a copy of the shared engine), index.md, and metadata.json. Edit the layer data in <sim-id>.js to change content. To change drawing or behavior, edit the engine in skills/layered-assembly-infographic/assets/ and run python skills/layered-assembly-infographic/scripts/assembly_tool.py sync --apply so every sim gets the fix.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
This page is the working list of improvements we plan to explore for The Science of the Built Environment. We take them one at a time, and each item gets a status so we can see what is decided, what is built, and what is still an idea.

The ideas come from a review of Francis D.K. Ching's Building Construction Illustrated (see References). Ching's page design is a strong model for teaching how assemblies go together. His pages are static and black-and-white, and they show the object but not the invisible flows (heat, air, moisture, current, load) that explain why the assembly works. Our job is to keep his clarity and add the explanation.

docs.title: Strategy: build tools, not one-off sims
docs.text:
The same teaching patterns will recur in every trade book we write: electrical, HVAC, plumbing, framing, finishes, and others. So we do not build a single MicroSim and then copy it. For each pattern we build a project skill that carries four things:

  1. A data format that describes one instance (one wall, one panel, one drain run).
  2. A shared engine that draws and animates any instance of the pattern.
  3. Conventions (hatches, colors, label style) so every diagram reads the same way.
  4. A validator that catches mistakes before a student sees them.

These skills live in the repo's skills/ folder and are only for this book and its sister trade books. They are not general-purpose intelligent-textbook skills, so they do not belong in the global skills folder.

docs.title: Core design rules
docs.text:
• Line art is the object; color is the invisible flow. Base drawings stay black-and-white line work with a fixed hatch legend. Color appears only for flows (heat, air, water, vapor, current).
  • Every label has two levels: what it is (a short noun phrase) and why it is there (the physics or code reason). Ching gives the first; the second is our contribution.
  • One idea per diagram, with a stable section ID so a sim, a poster, a quiz item, and a glossary term can all point to it.
  • Predict, then test. Each interactive asks the learner to commit to a prediction before showing the result.
  • Self-contained sims. Each sim folder holds its own copy of the engine, stamped with a version, so it still runs when pasted into the p5.js editor. A sync command refreshes the copies.

docs.title: 1. Layered-assembly infographic skill
docs.text:
What. A skill that turns a short data file describing a stack of layers into a finished MicroSim: thickness-proportional layers with hatching, numbered leader-line callouts with two-level labels, layer toggles, an explode slider, animated flows that stop at the layers that block them, an optional temperature profile from R-values, and an IP/SI toggle.

Why. Our wall, roof, slab, and cladding chapters each need this diagram. Writing it once as a skill means each new assembly takes minutes, looks the same as the others, and stays correct.

Trades. Version 1 handles stack assemblies (wall, roof, floor, slab). The data format has a kind field so later versions can add other shapes. See idea 11 for linear systems.

Open questions.

  • Which assemblies get built first? Candidates: exterior wall (already built by hand), low-slope roof, slab-on-grade, fire-rated partition.
  • Do we convert the existing hand-built control-layer-wall-section-explorer to the engine, or leave it as is?
  • How do we show a material change along the layer (for example studs and cavity in the same layer)?

docs.title: 2. Draw the flow, not just the object
docs.text: Heat, air, water, and vapor are invisible, and a static page cannot show them. The skill draws them as animated dots on a black-and-white base. This is a design rule in idea 1, not a separate build.

docs.title: 3. Clickable exploded building as the table of contents
docs.text: Our building-systems-cutaway sim could become the chapters page, with each exploded layer linking to its chapter. It follows the same orientation idea as the opening drawing of a classic construction text.

docs.title: 4. Turn tables and charts into controls
docs.text:
Status: the range-explorer skill (skills/range-explorer) turns a list of options with ranges into a chart with a movable marker. The pilot is structural-span-range-explorer (chapter 7). The book has no span table, so its ranges are illustrative values I supplied; they are on the review list below. Candidates for the next charts are in skills/range-explorer/references/trade-applications.md.

  • A structural span-range chart becomes an interactive chart: enter a span and load, see which systems qualify.
  • Exposure and dimension tables become sliders.
  • Soil classification becomes a sort-the-sample exercise.

docs.title: 5. CSI MasterFormat tags
docs.text: Tag each concept, glossary term, and MicroSim with a MasterFormat division, and add a filter on the MicroSims page. This links our physics to the way builders and specifiers look things up. Minnesota code sections could be tagged the same way. This needs a decision on where the tag lives (learning-graph columns, sim metadata.json, or both).

docs.title: 6. Shared hatch and symbol legend
docs.text: One convention for earth, concrete, masonry, wood, insulation (batt and rigid), membrane, air space, gypsum, metal, and glass, used in every sim and poster. Version 1 of the hatch set ships inside the idea 1 engine. Later we may publish it as its own legend page. Includes a line-art-only mode for printing and accessibility.

docs.title: 7. IP/SI unit toggle
docs.text: North American trade practice uses inch-pound units; most of the world and the science literature use SI. The idea 1 engine includes the toggle. Later, non-sim pages could follow the convention of showing both units.

docs.title: 8. Date-stamp what ages
docs.text: Separate timeless principles (heat flow, load paths) from content that changes (code editions, product names, energy-use statistics). Tag the second kind with an edition year so readers and future editors can see what to check.

docs.title: 9. Sustainability earlier
docs.text: Add a short operational-versus-embodied carbon thread to chapters 1-2, ahead of the dedicated sustainability chapters. Use current, cited data.

docs.title: 10. "Read the drawing" quiz items
docs.text: Quiz questions that use an assembly drawing: identify the layer, say what it controls, or drag a label to the right part. Builds on the layer data from idea 1 (the same data file can generate the questions).

docs.title: 11. A "run" skill for linear systems
docs.text:
Electrical distribution, plumbing drain-waste-vent, and HVAC duct runs are not stacks; they are chains of components along a path. The same four-part pattern applies:

  • Electrical: stages (service, meter, main, panel, breaker, circuit, device). Flows: current and fault current. "Break a stage" (remove the ground, oversize the breaker) and see what happens.
  • Plumbing: drain, trap, vent, stack. Flows: water, sewer gas, air. Break the vent and watch the trap siphon.
  • HVAC: supply, return, filter, coil, duct. Flows: air and heat. Restrict the duct and watch the pressure.

This would be a second skill (for example run-system-infographic) that shares the legend, callout style, and unit toggle with idea 1. We should build it after idea 1 has been used on several assemblies, so we know what actually generalizes.

docs.title: Review at the end
docs.text:
Items I deferred or wrote from memory, collected here so you can review them together. Nothing here blocks the work.

  • MasterFormat section numbers and titles on every layer (csi fields in the five layered-assembly sims). Checked against nothing yet; skills/layered-assembly-infographic/references/csi-masterformat.md lists them. Decide the edition (2004 or 2018) the book will cite, then verify each one.
  • Structural span ranges in structural-span-range-explorer (thirteen systems, possible and typical ranges). Illustrative; the chapters do not give them. Replace with values from a span reference you trust, or keep them labeled illustrative.
  • "What ages" notes in all six sims (currency blocks). They say what to check, but I have not checked any of it against the codes.
  • Engineering claims in the layered-assembly sims raised during testing: the one-hour partition label (two layers per side), the vapor retarder order under slab foam, and the rainscreen title.

docs.title: How we work through this list
docs.text:
1. Pick one idea.
  2. Write down the decision and any open questions answered in the idea's section above.
  3. Build it (usually as a skill plus one pilot sim).
  4. Update the status in the table above.

docs.title: Scoring Note
docs.text: The quality score is a heuristic computed from format and link checks (20), concept coverage (20), Bloom's alignment (up to 25), answer balance (up to 15), distractor length parity (up to 10), and explanation length (up to 10). It does not measure whether each question is unambiguous or whether each distractor is plausible. Those judgments were made by the generating model while writing the questions and have not had an independent human or second-model review.
